stories.Headline: Akamai launches AI inference & agent sandbox tools
stories.Summary:
On October 27, 2026, Akamai, the Nasdaq-listed cloud company, introduced two new AI products for its cloud platform, Akamai Inference and Akamai Agent Sandbox. Akamai Inference gives customers managed access to open-weight and custom models through APIs that work with existing OpenAI-compatible applications, so those applications can move over without rewrites. Akamai Agent Sandbox gives developers a separate environment where code written by AI agents can run, away from the agent's own runtime. The company says the two services are meant for organisations moving AI from trials into production, where model serving, latency, data access and agent security become harder to manage. Customers of Akamai Inference can choose either serverless, pay-per-use inference or dedicated deployments.

At launch the catalogue holds 12 open-weight models, ranging from 8 billion to 2.8 trillion parameters, including NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra, OpenAI gpt-oss-120b and Google Gemma 4, along with embedding models for retrieval-augmented generation. Agent Sandbox is an open-source component of the Spin framework and uses WebAssembly isolation to limit compute, memory, outbound connections and system access. Both products are available in beta, and the Inference beta includes the serverless options. Akamai also added NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra GPU clusters to its dedicated GPU fleet, where each eight-GPU node carries 288 GB of HBM3e memory per GPU, or 2.3 TB in total, and it keeps NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs for low-latency inference. It is also preparing its data centers for the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform in 2027, and customers should contact Akamai Sales about availability of the B300 clusters.

Adam Karon, Chief Operating Officer and General Manager of Akamai Cloud, said the company had built its AI strategy on the idea that inference would take the largest share of enterprise focus and spending, and that customers had proved this and pushed it further. He said customers want to build, run and protect AI on one platform, and that the two new products add the inference and execution layers that make Akamai's AI infrastructure a full stack, with its security portfolio covering every layer. Jon Alexander, Senior Vice President of Cloud Technology, said enterprises should not have to choose between speed and control when they put AI into production. He described some teams wanting to ship an AI feature quickly on a managed platform, others needing dedicated GPUs to run large open models on their own terms, and every team running agents needing a boundary around the code those agents write. The announcement builds on infrastructure that Akamai says has already secured multiyear Akamai Cloud contracts worth more than $14 billion collectively.

Its cloud network spans more than 4,350 edge locations and supports both CPU and GPU workloads, alongside storage, networking and security services. Requests to Akamai Inference run across that global network to cut latency, and the service connects to managed databases, object storage, and private and public clouds so models can use enterprise data. Akamai said it also plans to add capabilities that govern what agents can reach and what can reach them. Developers can pick the isolation approach that fits their workload, including dedicated CPU systems, NVIDIA-accelerated infrastructure, managed Kubernetes and serverless execution across edge and core.

stories.Headline: OpenAI's Scientific Breakthroughs Spark Backlash as Researchers Demand Greater Access
stories.Summary:
OpenAI announced three AI-generated research results in October 2026, covering mathematics, theoretical computer science, and physics. In mathematics, the company says its systems produced a proof of the local smoothing conjecture in every spatial dimension on October 18, and that it also resolves the Kakeya conjecture and Stein's restriction conjecture in all dimensions. In computer science, it claims a result that disproves the exponential time hypothesis, a long-standing assumption used to argue that some problems cannot be solved much faster than by brute force. The physics work concerns quantum chromodynamics and Yang-Mills theory, with OpenAI saying it finished the Lean formalization of its Yang-Mills existence result on October 16. The company also said it generated a proof related to quantum chromodynamics in September.

The three results were released in different ways. For the mathematics proof, OpenAI published a natural-language write-up and a formal Lean proof, formalized the day after the proof was generated, on its public GitHub repository. For the computer science result, it set up a review group made up of Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi of the University of California, San Diego, and Ryan Williams of MIT, and it agreed to make the underlying data public and fund a conference on the finding. The physics materials were initially withheld, with the company saying it would defer to an external group of experts on how to release them. OpenAI said it consulted outside experts, which it calls shepherds, to decide how each result should be shared.

Researchers who spoke to The Verge were critical of that approach, even as they praised the science. Some described the findings as huge, major breakthroughs and significant, and Brown University mathematician Brendan Hassett said the Kakeya claim looks well supported, though he had not yet checked the Lean formalization. Many experts welcomed OpenAI's decision to consult outsiders but argued that a public announcement should come with materials anyone can examine, and they questioned why the company was handpicking who gets to look first. One researcher said it makes no sense for only a few distinguished scientists to see the work at first. The Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence has likewise warned against giving selected researchers privileged access, and has urged public releases, formal proofs, information on how problems were chosen, and support for those trying to understand the results.

The dispute follows earlier friction, since OpenAI published work on hundreds of problems at the start of October, which left mathematicians with a large amount of material to check. The proofs have a prior history, as Larry Guth, Hong Wang and Joshua Zahl proved a two-dimensional local smoothing result in 2019, and Wang and Zahl proved the three-dimensional Kakeya conjecture in 2025. The articles stress limits on the claims, saying the Yang-Mills work does not address the unresolved mass gap and that disproving the exponential time hypothesis does not mean every hard problem is now easy. The results still face independent checking, and Lean formalization, while it lets proofs be verified by computer, does not replace expert judgment of what they mean. OpenAI says its release approach is still evolving and involves trade-offs, while researchers continue to press for open access so the claims can be tested.

stories.Headline: IATA - IATA's 2026 Global Passenger Survey: Travelers Embrace Biometrics and AI but Entry Requirements Remain a Barrier
stories.Summary:
The International Air Transport Association (IATA) released the results of its 2026 Global Passenger Survey on 28 October 2026, announcing them from Macao. The survey points to three main trends: biometric identification is becoming mainstream and interest in digital passports is growing, passengers are using artificial intelligence to plan their travel, and immigration rules are discouraging more people from visiting destinations. The findings are based on over 10,000 responses from more than 200 countries. The survey aims to show what passengers want from their air travel experience.

On biometrics, 58% of passengers said they had experienced them at some point in their airport journey over the past 12 months, up from 50% in 2025 and 24 percentage points higher than in 2022. Among those who had used biometrics, 87% were happy with the experience, up from 86% last year, and 78% of travelers would share biometric data if it meant skipping a passport or boarding pass check. Of those willing, 75% prefer to register once in advance. Interest in digital passports is strong, with 84% interested in using one for online check-in, and 82% each interested in sharing one with an airline at booking or in using a phone that combines a digital wallet, digital passport and loyalty cards. The main worries about biometrics are data breaches at 59%, information being shared with other organizations at 49%, and unclear handling of personal data at 41%.

On AI, 49% of travelers have used it for travel planning, with 21% using it to search for flights to a specific destination, 19% to find the cheapest flights and 17% for inspiration on where to go. On entry rules, 43% of passengers said immigration requirements had put them off visiting a destination, up from 33% in 2025. Among those deterred, 53% said the process is too complex, while privacy and cost were each cited by 17%. Passengers also want faster, digital processes, as 86% would likely share immigration information digitally before departure, up from 83%, 45% would prefer to finish immigration procedures before reaching the airport, up from 41%, and 60% prefer to apply for a visa online, against 25% who prefer to apply in person at a consulate or embassy. Among passengers deterred by geopolitical conflict, 72% named safety as the main reason and 13% cited uncertainty over whether travel is possible.

Nick Careen, IATA's Senior Vice President for Operations, Safety and Security, said passengers are embracing technology but still face barriers from complex immigration and visa processes. He urged governments to simplify entry requirements, remove duplicate checks, and speed up the issuance and acceptance of secure digital travel credentials. He called on governments to agree a framework for issuing and accepting digital passports, and advised airlines to make sure their offers appear in AI tools and to build links that turn an AI conversation into a booking. He noted that more than 100 countries issue eVisas but there is little consistency in how they are checked, and said the tools to fix that already exist.

Regional results varied. Asia-Pacific travelers reported the highest overall satisfaction, while Europeans reported the lowest and were the most cautious about digital travel technology. North America showed the highest biometric use but also the strongest concern about data breaches, and African travelers were the most likely to have been discouraged by immigration requirements, at 52%. Middle East travelers were the most likely to use AI for travel planning, at 72%, and showed the strongest interest in digital passports, at 91%. IATA represents over 370 airlines, accounting for some 85% of global air traffic, and the full analysis is available on its Global Passenger Survey page.

stories.Headline: Attackers built a ‘Skynet’ AI agent that hijacks exposed models to run cyberattacks
stories.Summary:
Attackers have built an offensive AI agent that takes over unprotected AI models on the open web and uses them to run cyberattacks, according to a CSO Online report published October 27, 2026. The Symantec Threat Hunter Team found the tool by trapping it in a honeypot that posed as an exposed model endpoint. The attackers mistook the decoy for a real model and sent it their entire working prompt, which gave researchers a rare look at how the attack is put together. The practice is known as LLMjacking, in which attackers commandeer a victim's model for their own ends, and the victim pays the bill for every step.

The prompt was built in five layers, and the final one switched on a mode the attackers called "Skynet," a nod to the Terminator films. In that mode the model can run unattended for up to 100,000 steps, execute tools immediately without asking permission, and silently deploy cryptocurrency miners. The earlier layers gave the model a new identity as a branded coding assistant, treated the theft of secrets as routine, and cast the model as a devoted companion that should blindly follow orders. The attackers also banned words such as "illegal," "I can't" and "ethical" from its replies, and told the model to dismiss its own safety messages as noise. A fifth layer supplied 75 offensive tool definitions covering reconnaissance, database dumping, remote code execution and botnet command-and-control management.

Symantec's researchers said the individual techniques are not new, but joining them into a single, self-directed agent marks a shift, since the stolen model plans and drives the attack rather than simply answering questions. They did not report a confirmed victim of this specific attack, and the captured instructions were part of a benign training challenge. Frank Dickson of Dickson Research said the attackers are using the victim's own AI, and that each compromise can fund the next. He added that one prompt now turns a borrowed model into the brain of a campaign that once took a skilled crew, which lowers the bar for who can run one.

Much of the exposure comes down to configuration rather than malware, Dickson said, but the volume is real, because the honeypot logged more than 127,000 external requests from tens of thousands of addresses. He advised enterprises to inventory every model server, AI gateway and Model Context Protocol server, require authentication on every path, and treat AI API keys as high-value credentials that are scoped, rotated and kept out of code. He also recommended watching inference spend as a possible first alarm, blocking outbound traffic from AI hosts, and patching the frameworks the agent targets, such as Django and Jupyter. Guardrails on models matter, he said, but they are a layer rather than a wall, so least privilege and human approval for sensitive actions are a must.

stories.Headline: Big Tech earnings to test AI boom amid market turmoil
stories.Summary:
Big Tech companies are heading into a heavy week of earnings with investors pressing them to show that their enormous artificial intelligence spending can deliver quick returns. According to a Reuters report relayed by TechGig on October 28, 2026, a turbulent market selloff has revived warnings of an AI bubble, including from Citadel founder Ken Griffin. That turmoil has also pushed some companies to delay their IPOs. Wall Street expects Amazon, Microsoft and Alphabet to report faster growth in their cloud businesses this week, though optimism is tempered by worries over the rising cost of financing AI.

The growth forecasts are large. Google Cloud is expected to lead the three in the September quarter, with revenue projected to jump 95.1 per cent to $29.57 billion, according to LSEG data, up from 81.8 per cent growth in the previous quarter. Amazon Web Services, the market leader in cloud, is forecast to grow 38.2 per cent, compared with 36.8 per cent in the prior quarter. Microsoft Azure is predicted to expand 47.7 per cent, speeding up from 42 per cent three months earlier, based on Visible Alpha data. On cash, Alphabet and Amazon are expected to report cash burn for the second and third straight quarters respectively, while Microsoft is likely to generate more than $8 billion in cash flow.

Microsoft will also change how it reports its results this week. It will fold cloud, AI and business software into a division called "Agents and Infra," while Windows, gaming and ad sales will form a second division called "Devices and Consumer." The new structure will include a disclosure of Azure's quarterly revenue in absolute terms, answering investor requests for actual figures rather than only growth rates. Citizens analyst Andrew Boone said that what executives say on their calls is as important as the numbers this quarter, given growing competition in search and concerns about whether AI capital spending will pay back.

The pressure comes as investors debate whether the recent AI correction is over and how the earnings will affect the market rally. CNBC's Halftime Report, hosted by Scott Wapner with the Investment Committee, took up that question on October 27. The articles do not say what the companies will report or how markets will react. Results from the three cloud giants, along with Microsoft's first look at Azure's absolute revenue, are due this week.

stories.Headline: Wall Street prepares for AI's "day after"
stories.Summary:
US stocks closed higher on Tuesday, Oct 27, as a technology rally driven by artificial intelligence revived, with the Nasdaq leading the way. Buzz around details of Anthropic's planned initial public offering lifted chip stocks for a third straight session. The Nasdaq Composite gained 308.43 points, or 1.18 per cent, to 26,477.81, the S&P 500 rose 45.83 points, or 0.6 per cent, to 7,722.6, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average edged up 15.99 points, or 0.03 per cent, to 52,377.57. Technology was the top-performing sector in the S&P 500, while energy shares fell the most as crude prices eased and attention turned to Middle East peace talks.

Third-quarter earnings season gathered pace, with nearly half of S&P 500 companies having reported and 83 per cent of them beating expectations, according to LSEG data. Boeing tumbled 10.7 per cent after a larger-than-expected quarterly loss, and Xylem slid 14.2 per cent after trimming its full-year forecasts. Sherwin-Williams fell 2.7 per cent after missing on quarterly profit, while United Parcel Service rose 5.8 per cent and Royal Caribbean gained 5.5 per cent after both raised their annual outlooks. Economic data showed rising new orders for computers and peripheral equipment, which supported the idea of strong AI-related spending. Advancing stocks outnumbered decliners by 1.83 to 1 on the NYSE and 1.86 to 1 on the Nasdaq, and volume on US exchanges was 16.1 billion shares, against a 20-day average of 17.18 billion.

Chuck Carlson, chief executive of Horizon Investment Services in Hammond, Indiana, said the Anthropic news was giving AI stocks, particularly chipmakers, a bit of a relief rally. He noted that those shares had been hit hard in recent weeks and were probably due for a bounce. He also said investors seemed more confident the Federal Reserve would do nothing at its meeting, partly because of an election on Tuesday, and that there was likely some relief that interest rates would not get in the way of a rally. The Fed began its two-day October policy meeting on Tuesday, and markets widely expect it to hold the fed funds target rate at 3.75 to 4 per cent, according to CME's FedWatch tool.

The AI trade has been under pressure this month from concerns about whether debt-funded spending is sustainable as borrowing costs rise. The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor index remains more than 20 per cent below its June 22 record close, though it is up 62.1 per cent so far in 2026 against a 12.8 per cent gain for the S&P 500. To pay for its AI expansion, Meta raised its largest-ever equity fundraising to US$97.5 billion, and its shares fell 1.6 per cent. Markets had opened higher on Monday as Anthropic's IPO filing drew investor attention. Microsoft and Alphabet are due to report results on Wednesday and Amazon.com on Thursday, and the Fed is expected to save its second rate hike of 2026 for its December meeting.

stories.Headline: Samsung aims to cut chip material development time using AI
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics said on Monday, Oct. 26, that it aims to use artificial intelligence to shorten the development of new semiconductor materials. The goal was announced by Choi Young-sang, an official at the Samsung Advanced Institute of Technology, the company's research and development center, at a forum hosted by the Korea Industry Association Forum. Participants at the event were discussing how AI can be used in industrial research and development. Choi said the company wants to bring the development period down by three years.

Under the target, development of new semiconductor materials would fall from five years to two years, while the number of promising material candidates identified would rise by more than fivefold. Samsung also wants to cut the number of experiments needed to find optimal conditions by more than 80 percent. Choi explained that semiconductor materials are built from multiple thin-film layers, which means a seven-layer structure can have more than 100 million possible material combinations. Researchers, however, can run only about 50 experiments a month, so working through those options is slow.

Choi described the conventional approach as one that leans on the experience and intuition of researchers, and said it can take months or even years to pinpoint candidate materials. He added that data from failed experiments has so far not been fully put to use, which is part of what the AI approach is meant to address. The company expects the method could also lower development costs. Samsung further anticipates that it could carry AI into other industries, with battery materials named as one example.

The announcement comes as Samsung's wider corporate family benefits from the AI boom. Samsung Electro-Mechanics, an electronic components affiliate, reported record third-quarter results on Oct. 28, with operating profit up 165 percent to 691 billion won and revenue up 30 percent to 3.76 trillion won. The company credited demand for products used in AI data centers, and said it plans to meet long-term supply agreements with major global technology companies. The articles do not say what steps Samsung Electronics will take next to put its AI material development goal into practice.

stories.Headline: Indian AI companies showcase homegrown technologies at Dubai AI Festival 2026
stories.Summary:
Indian artificial intelligence companies are showing off homegrown technologies at the Dubai AI Festival 2026, a two-day event that opened on Monday, 26 October, in the United Arab Emirates. The festival runs on 26 and 27 October at the Dubai World Trade Centre under the theme "Where Intelligence Meets Opportunity." Xinhua described it as a showcase of the latest AI advances and applications. Indian firms are presenting work in AI computing infrastructure, enterprise automation, cybersecurity, computer vision and intelligent digital solutions.

The Bharat Pavilion hosts 23 Indian companies, and their offerings cover the full AI value chain. That includes the cloud and GPU infrastructure needed to train and deploy models, as well as applications built for specific industries. The showcase also features AI-ready computing infrastructure, GPU cloud services, data-centre capabilities and enterprise cloud management platforms. The pavilion was inaugurated on Monday by Dr. E. Vishnu Vardhan Reddy, the Consul General of India in Dubai.

The festival is organised by Dubai AI Campus, a business and technology incubator initiative of the Dubai International Financial Centre, in partnership with the UAE Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence, Digital Economy and Remote Work Applications. This is the third edition of the event. It brings together technology companies, investors, policymakers and industry leaders to discuss how AI is developed and adopted. The programme covers AI governance, enterprise transformation, computing infrastructure, investment, ethics and the use of AI across different sectors.

Indian exhibitors said they are confident that the solutions they built in India can be deployed in other countries too. They regard the festival as an important platform for meeting potential clients and partners, widening their global reach and taking their technologies into newer markets. The reporting notes that Indian technology companies are looking to expand their international footprint and explore new business partnerships. The festival gives them a chance to present their capabilities to markets beyond India.

stories.Headline: Crusoe Partners with Araico on AI Cloud in Paraguay
stories.Summary:
Crusoe, a builder and operator of artificial intelligence infrastructure and cloud platforms, announced on October 22, 2026 a strategic partnership with Araico, a Paraguayan energy and infrastructure developer. Together they plan to build high-performance AI computing infrastructure powered by the Itaipú Hydroelectric Dam. The agreement was finalized while a US trade delegation led by Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau was visiting Asunción from October 19 to 21. The State Department described it as potentially one of the largest private investments in Paraguay's history, and Landau said it could be the largest private foreign investment the country has seen.

The facility will sit next to the Itaipú substation, drawing power directly from the dam. An initial deployment is due to come online in mid-2027, with a path to 106 MW of IT capacity and long-term options to grow to roughly 280 MW. It will serve customers in the United States and Latin America through Crusoe Cloud, and it is Crusoe's first AI cloud deployment in Latin America. Araico will lead local development and site infrastructure, while Crusoe will manage, operate and deliver the physical computing capacity. The articles do not give a total investment figure for the project.

Cully Cavness, Crusoe's chief strategy officer, president and co-founder, said Paraguay's geography and history have produced one of the world's most abundant renewable power sources, and that Crusoe's energy-first strategy is built to add value to exactly that kind of resource. Araico chief executive Alejandro Zuccolillo said pairing Itaipú's hydroelectric capacity with Crusoe's expertise would keep more of the value of Paraguay's renewable power at home, turning it into industrial growth, local jobs and digital innovation. President Santiago Peña said the project brings jobs, investment, technology and innovation, and could help Paraguay become a regional leader in AI infrastructure. Landau added that American capital and know-how would help establish Paraguay as a technology powerhouse.

The deal was one of several commitments tied to the US visit. Uranium Energy Corp announced a $12 million investment to develop a uranium concession in Paraguay, and the two governments signed agreements on airspace monitoring and border screening. The State Department also said it is providing $5.5 million in foreign assistance and $6.25 million in security assistance, and that negotiations have begun toward a civil nuclear cooperation agreement known as a 123 Agreement. A CBRE report on 2026 data center trends has noted that Paraguay's hydroelectric power and regulatory environment are drawing investors. Mordor Intelligence projects that the South American data center construction market will grow from US$5.72 billion in 2026 to US$8.88 billion by 2031.

stories.Headline: Tech and AI leaders expand China’s 2026 rich list as DeepSeek founder makes debut
stories.Summary:
China's population of mega-wealthy people hit an all-time high this year, according to the annual Hurun China Rich List released on Tuesday. The number of people worth more than 5 billion yuan, about $750 million, rose to a record 1,529. That figure far exceeds the previous peak of 1,460, which was set in 2021. Tech founders helped drive the increase as China widens its reach in artificial intelligence. Among the new entrants was Liang Wenfeng, founder of the AI startup DeepSeek, who debuted at number seven with an estimated fortune of $41.7 billion.

He was one of 263 newcomers on the list, and most of them came from sectors such as semiconductors, AI and robotics. His wealth was boosted by DeepSeek's R1 reasoning model, which was released last year and set off a sell-off in US tech stocks. The model's release is described as having shaken the industry. Rupert Hoogewerf, who is named in the article, said the roster reflected what he called China's two-speed economy, in which tech fortunes have surged while traditional wealth has declined. The article text available here cuts off at that point, so his full comments are not given.

The Hurun list is described as a closely watched annual ranking of the country's richest people. Liang also appears on a separate ranking published the same day, AI Magazine's Top 250 AI Leaders 2026 list, where he is named alongside frontier lab figures such as OpenAI's Sam Altman and Anthropic's Dario and Daniela Amodei. stories.Headline: build ai agents with function calling using python
stories.Summary:
A new tutorial published by TechGig in mid-October 2026 shows how to build an AI agent framework from scratch in Python, using function calling so that large language models can act rather than only generate text. Function calling, also called tool use, lets a model output structured JSON that triggers predefined functions. The tutorial's framework includes a WebSearchTool for web queries, a PythonExecutorTool for running code, a CalculatorTool for math, and FileReadTool and FileWriteTool for working with the file system. A separate PersistentAgent class gives agents memory so they can retain information across interactions.

The framework works with both the OpenRouter and Groq APIs and relies on free-tier models, namely google/gemini-2.0-flash-exp:free and llama-3.1-70b-versatile. The agent core handles communication with the model, runs the tools, and keeps conversation context across multiple turns. The tutorial stresses clear tool descriptions, strict parameter validation with JSON Schema, and error handling in which tools return strings instead of raising exceptions. It also adds a cap on the number of turns to prevent infinite loops, and it includes worked examples of web search, calculation, code execution, and file operations.

Separately, Anthropic published a study of how AI agents influence expert decisions. It recruited 61 professional analysts with causal-inference experience, 50 of whom used Claude Code on a task for a fictional farming cooperative, deciding whether an advisory program that about 40% of members had joined should be expanded. The board would expand it only if productivity improved by roughly 3 to 4%. Analysts faced four analytical choices, such as measuring yield per hectare or per unit of operating cost, and each agent was secretly set by coin flip to favor one option. Analysts went with the agent's lean 86% of the time, against the 50% expected if it made no difference.

The paper reports that analysts who had already stated a preference switched away from it 60% of the time when the agent disagreed, versus 6% when it agreed, though that rests on only 38 cases. When the agent leaned toward a full rollout, 54% of analysts recommended it, compared with 36% when it leaned the other way. Afterward, 77% of analysts repeated the agent's arguments, but only 15% credited the agent as their source. Those who followed the agent closely were about as confident, averaging 71 against 73, and 52% described the final recommendation as more their own than the agent's. Experience and expertise did not predict who deferred.

Anthropic notes it is unclear how far the results carry over to the real world, since the agents' preferences were deliberately strengthened for the experiment. It also says the findings are not a simple warning against AI, because analysts who used the agent finished faster and made far fewer serious errors than those who worked without it, although that comparison group was small and less experienced. The company argues the concern is that unexamined deference could let an agent's arbitrary or misaligned preferences shape policy or research decisions, which matters especially for AI safety research, where a human reviewer is only an independent check if the judgment is their own. A third article, from MarkTechPost, about Nace AI's Drex search tool for agents, reached the source material only as unreadable page code, so nothing beyond its headline can be reported from it.

stories.Headline: Wang Yi Calls for China-U.S. Cooperation to Develop and Govern AI
stories.Summary:
Foreign Minister Wang Yi said on Friday that China and the United States have both the capacity and the responsibility to work together on developing and governing artificial intelligence, so that the technology stays under human control and benefits people. He made the remarks in the Xiong'an New Area in Hebei province, during a meeting with John L. Thornton, co-chair of the Board of Trustees of the Asia Society, and New York Times columnist Thomas L. Friedman. Both men were in China to attend the 2026 Global Governance Forum (Xiong'an). China Daily reported the meeting on October 23, 2026.

Wang said that as two leading AI countries, China and the US should cooperate not only to guard against risks but also to discuss rules and standards that can apply worldwide. He said such work would let the technology promote shared prosperity and common security, and that China favors inclusive AI development that serves the common good. On global governance more broadly, he said the world faces several deficits, including in peace, development and security. He added that the Global Governance Initiative has offered an important public good and has won wide international recognition and support.

According to a press release from the Foreign Ministry, Thornton and Friedman said the malicious use of AI poses the greatest risk to building a constructive US-China relationship of strategic stability. They hoped the two countries would deepen cooperation on the issue and provide an important public good for the world. Wang, for his part, praised the two visitors for their long-standing efforts to advance China-US relations and expressed hope that they would help make the forum a success. The two guests also noted that the international community is closely watching the coming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Economic Leaders' Meeting hosted by China, and they hoped China would use it to play a distinctive and positive role on global challenges.

The call fits into a wider Chinese push on AI governance. A commentary in the Pakistan Observer on October 28 described the Belt and Road Initiative as an increasingly important arena for AI cooperation, citing Chinese efforts such as the Global Initiative on Artificial Intelligence Governance and the Inclusive Plan for Artificial Intelligence Capacity Building. The same piece said that initiative pledges 5,000 AI-specific training slots for developing countries over five years. Separately, India is due to host the 12th BRICS Parliamentary Forum in New Delhi on October 26 and 27, with ethical AI and global governance among the themes. The articles do not say whether any China-US talks on AI have been scheduled, so the next concrete step is not yet clear.

stories.Headline: Harmonic AI expands Aristotle model for software and chip design verification - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
Harmonic, the AI startup co-founded by Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev, said on Tuesday that it is expanding its Aristotle model beyond mathematical proofs into software and chip design verification. The announcement comes as the growing use of AI to detect software flaws is drawing more scrutiny. Researchers recently used the technology to uncover critical bugs in PHP, which set off a global rush to patch the vulnerabilities. Separately, Amazon is widening software support for its Trainium AI chips through its Neuron platform, a move reported by TechGig on October 20.

Under the expansion, Aristotle can now verify software written in C and chip designs written in Verilog. The tool is available with usage-based pricing. As an example of its capabilities, the US fusion lab DIII-D said Aristotle rebuilt part of its reactor-control software in four hours, working from one research paper and a 254-word prompt. Harmonic is developing what it calls mathematical superintelligence, a reasoning-focused AI system aimed at reducing hallucinations and factual errors.

On Amazon's side, the Neuron platform supports both Trainium AI chips and Inferentia accelerators. A key piece is the Neuron Kernel Interface, known as NKI, which gives programmers tools to create and fine-tune low-level operations for Amazon's custom silicon. AWS describes Neuron as a software development kit for building and running machine-learning workloads on its chips. NKI is aimed at developers who write specialized kernels, the small code segments that perform computations on the chip, and while that control can optimize particular workloads, it also requires them to learn new interfaces and adapt their code.

Harmonic is backed by Nvidia's venture capital arm, NVentures, along with Sequoia and Ribbit Capital. It raised $120 million in a funding round last November that valued the company at $1.45 billion. Amazon is the party behind the Neuron expansion, which it presents as a way for cloud customers to diversify computing supply and manage expenses. The articles do not include direct statements from either company's executives beyond the announcements themselves.

The Amazon effort targets Nvidia's CUDA ecosystem, whose mature tools and large developer community make switching hardware difficult even when alternatives are cheaper or offer more computing capacity. TechGig notes that customer adoption will hinge on software compatibility and the effort of migrating existing code. Companies weighing the platform will consider framework support, performance under their own conditions, reliability, availability and long-term support, and hardware savings could be offset if large application rewrites are needed. The articles do not say what comes next for either company beyond these adoption questions.

stories.Headline: Watch Nscale Anthropic in AI Computing Talks
stories.Summary:
Anthropic made its IPO filing public on Monday, October 26, 2026, in a registration statement lodged with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. The offering is widely expected in mid-November and could value the Claude developer at more than $2 trillion, which would challenge the record set by SpaceX, whose June IPO raised $75 billion at a $2.1 trillion valuation. The filing did not give a share price, a share count or a valuation, all of which will be set after a road show with investors and bankers. Anthropic plans to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker "ANT," with Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley leading the deal.

The numbers in the filing are large on both sides of the ledger. First-half revenue reached $16.286 billion, more than 14 times the figure a year earlier, and revenue in the quarter ended June 30 grew 1,368% from a year before, while computing and infrastructure costs rose 300%. Anthropic reported a net loss of $80.7 billion for the first six months of 2026, compared with $42 billion for all of 2025, though adjusted operating profit excluding one-off valuation losses was $1.618 billion, its first half-year profit. Infrastructure commitments total more than $800 billion and run through 2045, including at least $110 billion with Amazon through April 2036, $120 billion with SpaceX through 2029, $115 billion with Google and $45 billion with Microsoft, both through 2033. A five-year, $161.2 billion tensor processing unit lease with Broadcom is also part of the total.

Anthropic itself disclosed these figures and risks, describing its spending strategy as bold but rational. The company said current cash and sales should cover the next 12 months, but it warned that growth depends on factors such as infrastructure costs and that it may need extra financing sooner than expected. It said it has raised about $141 billion through the end of June and holds $112.4 billion in cash. Of the 335-page filing, 94 pages cover risks, including warnings that poorly safeguarded AI could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, and that reliance on Samsung Electronics, SK hynix and Micron for memory, plus TSMC for chip production, leaves it exposed to tariffs, sanctions and geopolitical conflict. It also said properly controlled AI could help treat diseases such as cancer and Alzheimer's, with a cumulative economic impact of $22.5 trillion by 2031.

The offering is arriving slightly later than expected, as recent market moves have made investors cautious about the AI boom. Seoul Economic Daily reported that Wall Street wants proof Anthropic can earn enough to cover its spending, noting its latest model, Claude Opus 5.5, cut token costs per task by about 40% from the previous version. The news lifted South Korean chip stocks, with the KOSPI closing at 5,638.34 on the 27th, up 3.09%, and brokerages projecting operating profit at the main chipmakers to rise about 50% next year. Next comes the road show, after which the share price, share count and valuation will be set ahead of the expected mid-November listing.

stories.Headline: Anthropic preps for initial public stock offering in major step for AI company - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, filed a registration statement with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on October 26, 2026, taking a major step toward a stock market listing. The public filing follows a confidential draft that the company submitted to the regulator on June 1, 2026. Anthropic says it intends to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol ANT. The number of shares to be offered and the price range have not been set, and the offering remains subject to regulatory review.

The filing lays out detailed financial figures. For the six months ended June 30, 2026, revenue reached $16.3 billion, up from $1.16 billion a year earlier, while the net loss widened to $80.7 billion from $13 billion, largely because of accounting charges tied to changes in the estimated value of certain financing instruments as the company's valuation rose. Anthropic reported an operating loss of $693 million, compared with $2.14 billion a year earlier, though on its own adjusted measure it showed operating income of $1.6 billion, a margin of about 10%. Computing and infrastructure costs came to $8.95 billion, and the company held $131.7 billion in cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments as of June 30. Revenue from a group of existing customers in the three months ended September 30 was about nine times higher than a year earlier, a calculation that excludes Claude Pro and Max subscribers.

Customer numbers also grew sharply. As of September 30, more than 11,900 customers had generated at least $100,000 in revenue over the preceding 12 months, up from more than 950 a year earlier. More than 1,900 customers produced at least $1 million, and roughly 250 produced at least $10 million. The filing describes a governance setup meant to protect the company's long-term public-benefit mission, under which an entity formed by its seven co-founders will hold a special share carrying 50.1% of general voting power. The Long-Term Benefit Trust will have the right to appoint a majority of the board, which would limit the influence of ordinary shareholders even after the company goes public.

The prospectus flags several risks, including reliance on computing infrastructure providers, competition and the high cost of building increasingly capable AI models. Major cloud providers supply Anthropic with computing capacity and help distribute its products while also developing rival AI services. ABC News described the filing as a developing story. What happens next depends on the regulatory review and market conditions, which will determine the timing and terms of the offering.

stories.Headline: Anthropic Unveils 335-Page Public Prospectus: Poised to Make History as the Largest-Ever IPO and the Most Loss-Making AI Company of All Time
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the parent company of Claude, has publicly filed its full S-1 prospectus with the SEC, a 335-page document seeking a NASDAQ listing under the ticker "ANT." The filing was published on October 27, 2026, after the company confidentially submitted a draft on June 1, 2026. Bloomberg, citing people familiar with the matter, has reported that Anthropic plans to complete the offering in mid-November. If it does, it would reach the market ahead of its rival OpenAI and become the first pure-play frontier model company to list in the United States.

The financial figures are striking. Revenue in the first half of 2026 reached 16.286 billion dollars, compared with about 1.16 billion in the same period a year earlier, and 41 million dollars for all of 2023. The net loss for the first half was 80.748 billion dollars, against about 41.965 billion for the whole of 2025, but roughly 72.4 billion of the half-year loss came from fair value changes on convertible notes, derivative liabilities and other financing instruments, which does not represent cash spent. About 80.2 percent of revenue, or 13.06 billion dollars, came from usage-based billing such as API calls, while subscriptions brought in about 3.2 billion, or 19.6 percent. The number of customers with trailing twelve-month revenue of at least 100,000 dollars rose to more than 11,900 as of September 30, 2026, from 950 a year earlier.

The public version also updates the company's computing commitments. Its commitment to Microsoft rose from 31.4 billion dollars to 44.9 billion, its commitment to Google is 114.5 billion, and its contract with SpaceXAI carries a ceiling of 120.5 billion. Two new suppliers, Nscale and Lambda, were disclosed for the first time. The two largest customers, each about 12 percent of revenue, turned out to be Amazon and Google rather than the Cursor and GitHub Copilot that had been rumored. Reports also say the company has signed computing orders worth about 5.18 trillion dollars over ten years, with some saying 80 percent is payable even if unused.

The company's leadership is described as a brother and sister pair, with CEO Dario Amodei and President Daniela acting together as chief operating decision-makers of a single operating segment. Amodei has said that growth is too fast for the company to handle. At an Investor Day in mid-October, Anthropic said third-quarter revenue hit 16.8 billion dollars, up 45 percent from the prior quarter, and that it reached profitability on an adjusted basis. The prospectus also says the company has chosen not to build image or video generation models, focusing its computing on programming, agent capabilities and safety research. Menlo Ventures data cited in the coverage puts Anthropic at 42 percent of the code generation market, ahead of OpenAI at 21 percent.

The size of the offering is not yet set. An earlier leaked draft pointed to a maximum raise of about 1 trillion dollars at a valuation near 2 trillion, which would top SpaceX's 1.77 trillion dollar issuance valuation from June, though some investors have cut their expectations to about 1.5 trillion amid pressure on AI stocks. Because the SEC requires a public S-1 at least 15 days before a roadshow, the roadshow could begin as early as the second week of November. The prospectus devotes 64 pages to the business and 94 to risk warnings, including that AI could harm humanity or resist shutdown.

stories.Headline: Open-source project aims for AI-assisted development control plane
stories.Summary:
Anthropic has moved its monorepo from Git to a new source control system called Scion, and it described the migration in a 13 October engineering post. A separate open-source project named SYSTEM-ENGINEERING is exploring an Engineering Control Plane for AI-assisted development, according to TechGig. Scion shifts commits, merges, rebases, history and blame queries to the server side, with clients keeping bounded object caches and virtualised checkouts that fetch files only when needed. Tools can also query diffs and perform some writes through APIs without checking out any code.

The numbers behind the move are large. Daily merged changes rose from around 2,500 in May to more than 30,000 in September, and the company's CI systems run roughly 25 million checkouts every day. The monorepo has nearly 100 GB of main-branch history and a compressed working copy above 25 GB. Anthropic reports cache-hit rates above 99% at each tier, an infrastructure footprint for CPU and memory 200 times smaller than its earlier Git mirrors, and checkout speedups of two orders of magnitude for CI and research jobs. Checkouts run through a node-local daemon that shares cached objects across jobs and fetches from regional caches, which in turn draw on authoritative servers backed by Spanner and cloud storage.

Anthropic is responsible for Scion, and it says the design trades offline independence for less local data and shared infrastructure. The company stresses that Scion is not a general-purpose replacement for Git, since it needs its own code-review, code-search and CI systems and its implementations are highly bespoke. It suggests that other teams instead bring selected ideas, such as comprehensive server-side APIs and improved fetch protocols, into existing Git platforms. InfoQ noted that the performance figures are company-reported results for Anthropic's internal workload, not general benchmarks against Git. On the SYSTEM-ENGINEERING project, TechGig says the aim is to add structure around AI-assisted workflows rather than simply adding more agents or connecting more tools, and the project asks for community feedback on its architecture, agent orchestration, reliability mechanisms, memory and continuity, and developer experience.

For context, the problems Anthropic describes had grown harder to manage over time. It had relied on shallow clones, sparse checkouts, promisor remotes, repository snapshots and several hundred Git mirrors, but found them harder to operate as merge rates climbed. InfoQ compared Scion with Uber's GitFarm, which centralises standard Git operations without replacing the source-control system, and said Scion goes further by changing the underlying data model. In a 15 October update, Anthropic credited Mononoke and its Bonsai data model with pioneering many of the techniques it uses. InfoQ's takeaway for architects is that repository queries do not always need local checkouts and that immutable objects can be shared through caches, though Scion depends on server availability and requires substantial integration work.

stories.Headline: Who’s Responsible When AI Agents Go Rogue?
stories.Summary:
On October 26, 2026, PYMNTS reported that J.D. Salbego, founder and CEO of the AI agent security firm ClawSecure, is warning that AI agents can be hijacked through hidden instructions planted in ordinary emails, shared documents or support tickets, a method known as indirect prompt injection. Two days later, the Daily Californian published a piece on research from Veeam showing that how a company assigns responsibility for agent risk affects whether it can catch an agent that goes off course. ClawSecure tested 14 models from five labs and told PYMNTS it found a recurring pattern across models and integrations involving Dropbox, Notion and Linear. Veeam's Data and AI Trust Gap report surveyed 600 senior executives, including CEOs, CIOs, CISOs and CDOs, across industries and regions, with fieldwork running from March 16 to April 6, 2026.

Veeam's numbers show a wide gap between adoption and readiness. Some 88% of organizations are using or piloting AI agents, and 95% say data challenges have already slowed their AI progress. Organizations where the CISO owns agent risk are 24% more likely to detect rogue AI behavior, while those that spread ownership across teams are 47% less likely to detect it, though these are relative comparisons from survey data, not a controlled experiment. Only 28% of respondents are confident they can detect AI systems operating outside approved parameters, and just 40% of leaders feel very confident they can isolate and precisely reverse an agentic failure. The report also found that 65% of CEOs believe their organization has a full AI inventory, against 48% of technical leaders, and that 95% of organizations report unauthorized AI use, with only 25% offering approved alternatives.

On who is responsible, Salbego argued that providers should say publicly where their protections end and what customers must supply, noting that getting answers during ClawSecure's disclosure process took repeated follow-ups. He said small businesses and consumers are especially exposed because simple setup tools let them connect financial accounts without any security staff. He called for continuous monitoring of the messages passing between a model and its tools, and advised bank technology executives to shut down every AI agent while they arrange security help. The Veeam research points instead to single ownership, with the CISO holding accountability, setting approved parameters for each agent and having the authority to pause one or revoke its access. It also recommends giving each agent its own credentials and a named human sponsor, and rehearsing how to reverse an agent's changes.

For context, Salbego acknowledged that ClawSecure sells security services in the same market its research examines. He wants a public, comparable safety rating program for models run by a government body such as the National Institute of Standards and Technology, with voluntary participation, and said ClawSecure has built a framework it is trying to hand to Washington. He said he has discussed agent security with congressional offices from both parties and spoken with the Federal Trade Commission. Because ClawSecure sells into the market, he said it will not administer the framework itself, and he expects it to take time to get an institutional testing program running, which he hopes to start without waiting for legislation.

stories.Headline: Oracle Deep Data Security Expands Authorization Across Analytics, APEX, ORDS, and AI Agents
stories.Summary:
Oracle announced a set of new enterprise AI products and a security framework called the Deep Trust AI Architecture, according to coverage published on October 26, 2026. The package includes 25 Claw-powered Fusion Agentic Applications, designed to analyse options, prepare actions and carry out approved work within company policies and controls. Oracle also launched two employee-facing interfaces, Fusion Companion and Fusion Agentic Home, which let staff set business goals, hand work to AI systems and track progress, including through supported external tools such as ChatGPT. The applications cover finance, human resources, supply chain, sales and service.

The Deep Trust framework applies security, privacy and business rules across four layers: the software platform, data, data access and application development. At the platform level, Oracle says Autonomous AI Database can apply security updates across the database engine, operating system, storage and firmware before they are made public, with rolling patching so applications keep running. At the data layer, Deep Data Security and SQL Assertions enforce user access rules and business limits inside the database rather than only in application code, which Oracle says stops AI-generated applications or direct database tools from bypassing policy. For data access, Deep Trust Data APIs limit AI systems to specific business objects instead of unrestricted SQL, and a new tool called Deep NL2SQL adds business and data context to natural-language queries, with verification tools meant to improve accuracy. In development, the APEX AI Application Generator lets AI coding systems turn natural-language requests into Oracle APEX application definitions rather than large volumes of executable code, so the runtime engine, not generated code, enforces core protections.

Oracle executives and an outside analyst explained the thinking behind the launch. Chris Leone, Executive Vice President of Applications Development, said enterprise software is shifting toward doing the work while people define objectives and set policies. Juan Loaiza, Executive Vice President of AI Database Technologies, called trust the biggest challenge in AI today and said the architecture builds trust into each layer so organisations keep control over what AI agents and AI-generated applications can do. Steven Dickens, Chief Executive Officer of HyperFRAME Research, said Oracle is moving the competitive battleground from model intelligence to architectural trust, pointing to Deep Data Security and Deep NL2SQL as ways of enforcing policy and verifying AI-generated answers at the source.

The launch comes as other industries wrestle with the same question of how far to trust agentic AI. A Thomson Reuters Institute report cited in a separate piece dated October 28, 2026, found that 40% of organizations are already using or planning to use agentic AI tools. That article also cited the 2026 INTERPOL Global Financial Fraud Threat Assessment, which found that criminal groups using agentic AI generate profits more than four times higher than with earlier digital methods. Investigators quoted there stressed keeping humans in the loop, which echoes Oracle's emphasis on approval steps for higher-stakes processes. The articles do not say when each of Oracle's individual features will be generally available.

stories.Headline: Webull and Sentinel AI Launch Pilot Program Bringing Public Companies to Retail Investors at the Point of Trade
stories.Summary:
Webull and Sentinel AI announced a joint pilot program on October 28, 2026, aimed at giving public companies a new way to reach retail investors. Under the program, a listed company gets a direct channel to investors through its page on Webull's Corporate Connect Service, where investors can interact with it at the point of trade. The company also gets real time visibility from Sentinel AI into the bullish and bearish narratives forming around its stock on social platforms and online news. Its investor relations team then shapes a response based on that read.

The announcement leans on the growing weight of individual traders, citing JPMorgan's finding that retail investors made up as much as 36% of US stock market trading in 2025, compared with a ten-year average of roughly 12%. Corporate Connect gives public companies a verified page inside the Webull app where they can publish news and updates, answer investor questions, and build a following among Webull's more than 29 million registered users worldwide. Investors who follow a company receive a notification each time it posts. Sentinel's tools link the narratives it detects to an issuer's SEC filings and supply draft responses, and the company's IR team turns that material into updates the company approves. The pilot begins with a select group of public companies, with expansion planned after the initial results.

Several executives commented in the announcement. Michael Christoph, Webull's Head of Capital Markets, said pairing Corporate Connect with Sentinel's narrative data means companies will post content that answers what users are actually asking, which he described as good for both the companies and the investors following them. Krishan Arora, Sentinel's founder and CEO, said retail investors act on stories before fundamentals, and that the program closes the loop by putting a company's response in front of investors at the point of trade. He said Webull brings the audience while Sentinel brings the intelligence. Mark Roberts, Managing Partner at The Blueshirt Group, said retail investors are a growing part of his clients' shareholder base and that real-time insight into what they are saying can improve the effectiveness of companies' messaging.

On background, Webull Corporation, listed on Nasdaq under the ticker BULL, offers investment services in 18 markets across North America, Asia Pacific, Europe, Africa and Latin America through a network of licensed brokerages. Sentinel AI describes itself as a retail sentiment and narrative intelligence platform and says more than 200 public companies, with over $250 billion in combined market capitalization, rely on it. It is part of the Narravance ecosystem. Public companies and investor relations firms interested in joining can contact the parties named in the announcement, and results from the first group of participants will shape how the program expands.

stories.Headline: Former Yahoo CEO Marissa Mayer Used AI to Describe Her Daughter for School, Sparking a Parenting Debate
stories.Summary:
Former Yahoo chief executive Marissa Mayer said she used her own AI assistant to come up with a description of her daughter for a school task. Ahead of her daughter Marielle's tenth birthday, a teacher asked parents for three bullet points on what made each child special. Mayer, who felt overwhelmed by the range of possible answers, asked Dazzle, a personal assistant built by her startup, which replied that her daughter was empathetic, creative and an animal lover. She shared the story in an interview with The New York Times, published on October 25, 2026, and called the answer perfect.

Dazzle has been available since late September and analyzes images in a user's camera roll to answer questions, perform tasks and make suggestions. Mayer has said it recognized Marielle's interest in magic and suggested a magic shop in San Francisco for an outing, and that it helped her choose skis for her mother. She has said it blends AI models with personal context and, for complicated requests, human help. The New York Post reported that the app shares camera roll data with third-party platforms for shopping and assistance features. Mayer is 51, runs a team of about 10 engineers, and led Yahoo from 2012 to 2017 after becoming Google's first female engineer.

Mayer is the one at the center of the reaction, and she has defended the broader idea behind her product rather than this particular use. She has pitched Dazzle as an "AI wife" aimed at women, meant to ease the mental load of domestic planning for busy parents, and she said she hopes it will help draw more women into AI. In the Times interview she said that as a woman she wants to see more people like her at the table where decisions are made. Critics, including commentators on X and Reddit, argued that the three descriptors were generic enough to fit millions of children and questioned why a parent needed software for such a personal question. The Post said it had reached out to Mayer for comment, and neither report included a response from her to the criticism.

Supporters of AI tools countered that organizing observations can save time for parents juggling work and childcare. It remains unclear whether the school knew AI had been involved, and there is no evidence of a complaint from the school. Mayer has not said that Dazzle replaced her own knowledge of her daughter. The episode adds to a history of criticism of Mayer, including her time at Yahoo, when she resigned after the company's core operations were sold to Verizon and lawmakers subpoenaed her over security breaches. The articles do not say what Mayer or Dazzle will do next in response to the debate.

stories.Headline: Dutch Government Plans to Cut 25,000 Jobs in AI-Led Overhaul
stories.Summary:
The Dutch government announced on Oct 26 that it plans to cut around 25,000 civil servant jobs, roughly 15% of its central government workforce, as part of an efficiency drive built around artificial intelligence. The cuts would be spread over several years and are meant to save €3.5 billion (S$5 billion) a year. Police and defence are exempt from the reductions. Government headcount reached a record 160,000 at the end of 2025, up 41% from 2018, despite earlier Cabinets promising to scale it back.

On the numbers, the government wants to save €900 million a year by 2027, rising to €3.5 billion a year from 2035. Ministries, inspectorates and implementing agencies would be hit hardest, with a letter to Parliament warning of "significant staffing implications," including reductions of 45% or even 60% in some departments. The Cabinet is due to present its plans for using AI to work more productively in early 2027. The cuts are tied to a flagship programme to scrap 500 unnecessary or overly bureaucratic rules each year, which is meant to reduce the need for staff. The government also says it will favour Dutch and European suppliers to avoid dependence on non-European technology.

State Secretary for Effective Government Eric van den Burg, who sent the letter to Parliament, said the state cannot keep doing what it has been doing and must become simpler, smarter and smaller. He pointed to several non-binding parliamentary motions urging the Cabinet to raise government productivity by 20% through AI as one reason for the push. He added that AI projects have already been launched in different parts of government in recent years, and that the aim is to apply the technology more broadly. Others have been more cautious about the plan's prospects. ING chief economist Marieke Blom said the big question is whether the government can meet its targets, noting that earlier headcount cuts were followed by more hiring, and that AI could also generate new demands, such as institutions being flooded with complaints filed by AI agents.

The Dutch plan is being watched as perhaps the most ambitious attempt yet to use technology to shrink a state payroll, though governments generally trail the private sector on AI, according to a September 2025 report by the OECD. Bloomberg calculated that a similar cut would mean about 150,000 jobs in the US, around 75,000 in the UK and slightly over 50,000 in France. Civil servants are often highly unionised, which could make cuts hard to deliver, and concerns about data security and reliance on foreign technology firms also loom. For now, the next step is the Cabinet's detailed AI deployment plan, expected in early 2027.

stories.Headline: Former GitHub CEO launches Entire, a Git forge for humans and AI agents
stories.Summary:
Thomas Dohmke, the former GitHub CEO, launched a new Git forge called Entire on October 26, 2026. The platform is built for humans and AI coding agents to work together, and it is positioned as an alternative to GitHub. It is available to developers now, and it aims to let teams merge changes as quickly as AI agents can generate them. Entire's backers include Felicis, which led a $60 million seed round in February 2026 at a $300 million valuation.

The platform has three core features: Trails, distributed Git hosting and Continuous Memory. Trails replaces traditional pull requests, and whenever code is pushed, review agents assess it in cloud sandboxes and return scores, explanations and suggested fixes, including checks on security, code quality and whether a human needs to look. Developers can set rules called Gates that block a merge until conditions such as human approvals or passing CI checks are met. Entire says its hosting is up to 89 times faster than GitHub and six times faster than Cursor Origin, with internal benchmarks of 418 pushes per second against 4.7 for GitHub. Repositories can be hosted in India, the United States, Europe and Australia, and Continuous Memory, which stores agent sessions and prompts in the repository, is claimed to cut token use by up to 71 percent.

Dohmke said the goal of Trails is to give people the information they need to judge whether enough loops between a coding agent and the review agents have happened for the work to reach a stable state. He added that merging should only happen when confidence is high, risk is low and all findings are cleared. He also argued that pull requests need to evolve because AI-generated code arrives so much faster. Kyle Galbraith, co-founder and CEO of Depot, said the bottleneck in software development has moved from writing code to building and testing. Entire has partnered with Depot and Buildkite so that build and test results appear inside Trails, and failed builds can block merges.

Developers can host repositories directly on Entire or mirror existing ones from GitHub, and they can keep GitHub as their source of truth while running Trails on Entire. The company also offers a migration option for teams that want to move over fully. Teams can convert existing GitHub Actions workflows without rewriting them, and repositories can be replicated across regions to meet data residency needs. Entire uses Claude Code and Codex for its review workflows, with isolated environments from Daytona and E2B. The company is building infrastructure around existing coding agents rather than its own foundation models, and it has said further hosting regions are planned.

stories.Headline: Majority of responses to consultation on smoking Bill ‘generated by AI bots’
stories.Summary:
More than three quarters of responses to a Government consultation on a smoke-free generation and tighter vape sales were produced by artificial intelligence bots, according to a study whose findings were published in the journal Tobacco Control. The responses were overwhelmingly aimed at opposing measures on disposable e-cigarettes. Researchers from the University of Edinburgh believe this is the first case of large-scale, automated interference in a formal public health consultation. The analysis drew on published consultation reports and Freedom of Information data from the Department of Health and Social Care, and it covered a consultation held in October 2023.

The consultation drew 118,756 responses, but the Department identified 76 per cent, more than 90,000, as fraudulent using bot-detection methods. Almost all of the bot responses targeted multiple-choice questions opposing plans to restrict disposable vape sales, and the same share said they had heard of the consultation through social media. Once the bot responses were removed, about 79.6 per cent of valid responses backed the plans on disposable vapes. The plans were later enacted in the Tobacco and Vapes Act, which received Royal Assent in April. That law makes it illegal to sell tobacco products to anyone born on or after January 1 2009, and it bans disposable vape sales, which took effect in June of the following year, along with curbs on e-cigarette flavours and marketing.

The researchers said the scale and consistency of the bot responses suggested a coordinated campaign, and they noted that tobacco companies have previously tried to flood public consultations with favourable submissions. They said it was not possible to determine who was behind this campaign. They also warned that detection tools must keep evolving as bots become more sophisticated, and that consultations in places with fewer resources to screen submissions may be more vulnerable to such influence. A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said its controls had worked in this case, that the fake responses were removed, and that the consultation still helped shape the action being taken toward a smoke-free generation. The department said it would stay alert to similar interference in future consultations.

stories.Headline: Sen. Blumenthal, teachers' union push back against Google AI in schools
stories.Summary:
U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat, and Kate Dias, president of the Connecticut Education Association, criticized Google's use of artificial intelligence in school technology at a press conference at the state Capitol in Hartford on Tuesday, Oct. 27. They said the tools risk undermining student learning because AI does the drafting, math and research that students need to practice themselves, and that schools find the features hard to turn off. Many Connecticut students use Google Chromebooks starting in kindergarten, and Blumenthal said Google is spreading AI through its Chrome browser, so students and teachers cannot avoid it. They called for more regulation of AI in classrooms and said Congress must take up the issue soon.

Blumenthal and Republican Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri sent a list of questions to Google CEO Sundar Pichai on Oct. 21 and asked for answers by Nov. 2. The questions ask what research Google has done on whether Gemini, AI Overviews, AI Mode and other products harm children's mental wellbeing, and why AI is the default and sometimes cannot be disabled on licensed education devices. They also ask whether schools, teachers or parents have raised concerns and how Google responded, how much money it has spent on programs that expand AI use in schools, and whether its classroom tools have encouraged harmful behavior or missed signs of self-harm. One question refers to a Maryland student who was hospitalized after developing an intense dependence on Google's AI.

Blumenthal said Google is selling products that lead students to test lower, think slower and have more behavior problems, while allowing that AI also holds great promise. He compared it with helping his four children, saying he made them do the work first and then checked it, rather than handing over answers. Dias said embedding AI that cannot be turned off into systems schools rely on to communicate and teach is a violation of trust. She noted that Google is a trusted partner for most schools and helped them reach children at home during the COVID-19 pandemic. CT Insider said it had asked Google for comment, and the company's education website says it is committed to protecting privacy with AI, helping with compliance and adapting to feedback.

Dias said some districts are pulling back from technology, with students bringing home pen and paper assignments, though she said technology will still be used and needs regulation. In Connecticut, the state Commission for Educational Technology has issued guidance telling districts to consider whether existing policies can cover AI, and lawmakers passed an AI law in June affecting schools, including chatbot and social media restrictions, new curriculum and teacher training. Concern is also surfacing elsewhere. In Australia, the Australian Education Union told a Senate committee that AI has shifted teacher workload rather than reduced it, and a Nine survey of 1,209 people found 85 per cent did not want AI chatbots in primary schools.

stories.Headline: Artificial intelligence use doubles in rural Nebraska, poll shows
stories.Summary:
The 2026 Nebraska Rural Poll found that most rural Nebraskans now use artificial intelligence tools, a sharp rise since the poll first asked about AI in 2024. Fifty-five percent of those surveyed said they have used any AI tool, up from 27% two years earlier. The findings were released in late October 2026 by Rural Prosperity Nebraska, which conducts the poll annually with funding from Nebraska Extension. Even so, many respondents remain doubtful about how reliable these tools are.

Use varies considerably across groups. At least three-quarters of respondents ages 19 to 39 have used AI tools, compared with just 23% of those 65 and older. People with higher education levels or higher household incomes, along with women, were also more likely to have used them. Heather Akin, an associate professor at the University of Nebraska–Lincoln, said the growth shows AI is becoming part of everyday life for many rural residents. She argued that rural people need chances to explore the technology, understand its limits and decide when to use it.

Although most respondents report using AI, few use it to learn about specific subjects. Just over one in 10 said they often use generative AI to learn about education and skill development (16%), topics affecting them or their family (14%), and science and technology (12%). Interest in learning more about AI is strong, with 45% of respondents wanting to know how to protect their privacy, 36% wanting to evaluate response accuracy, 33% wanting to understand bias and 28% wanting to learn ethical use. Mary Emery, director of Rural Prosperity Nebraska, said these concerns show residents want to use AI responsibly and that accessible learning opportunities could help them make informed choices.

The full "Artificial Intelligence" report will be the subject of a Rural Poll webinar at noon CST on Nov. 18, and the report is available on the Nebraska Rural Poll website. The 2026 poll is the 31st year of tracking rural Nebraskans' views on policy and quality of life, and it is described as the largest and longest-running poll of its kind. Questionnaires were mailed in April and May to nearly 6,900 households, and 881 households from 86 of the state's 93 counties responded. The poll carries a margin of error of plus or minus 3%.

stories.Headline: Today's poll: Should schools place limits on how students and teachers use artificial intelligence in the classroom?
stories.Summary:
The Havasu News ran a reader poll on October 28, 2026, asking whether schools should place limits on how students and teachers use artificial intelligence in the classroom. Readers were offered three choices: yes, no, or not sure. The poll was posted as an online feature of the paper's opinion section, and visitors could cast a vote and then view the running results. The articles give no vote totals, so the outcome of the poll is not known from these pages.

The poll itself does not require or change any rule, and it carries no policy, deadline, or penalty. The page simply invites readers to say whether they think limits are appropriate. Nothing in the pages sets out what limits might look like, which grades or districts they would cover, or who would enforce them. The site also offers a comment section, with posting guidelines about language, threats, honesty, and respect, but no comments appear in the captured text.

The poll is published by Today's News Herald and Parker Pioneer, which operate under River City Newspapers, LLC, and the copyright notices name the same papers for 2026. The articles do not name a reporter or editor responsible for the question's wording. They also contain no statements from school officials, teachers, or students about artificial intelligence. Both captures are near-identical copies of the same poll page, one posted at 6:45 p.m.

and one at 10:45 p.m. UTC on October 28, 2026. The pages show the poll still open for voting when captured, so its results may change. The articles do not say whether the newspaper will publish the final tally or any follow-up coverage.
