stories.Headline: Agentic AI can cut banks' transaction monitoring workload by up to 50% - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
Banks could cut the human effort needed for transaction monitoring investigations by 30 to 50 percent by deploying agentic artificial intelligence, according to a McKinsey report published on October 28, 2026. The same report says these systems could also improve the quality and consistency of compliance reports. In one case cited, banks achieved a reduction of more than 40 percent in human processing time. Unlike tools that help individual analysts with narrow tasks, agentic AI can coordinate an entire investigation from start to finish. Those figures come from the consultancy's own assessment, so they describe reported results rather than an independent test.

The approach would let AI agents handle data collection, research, analysis and report preparation, leaving experts to focus on complex cases, risk assessment and final decisions. McKinsey said AI-generated reports could use the same transaction analysis periods and report structures across cases, with each claim linked to its source data for review by quality teams, auditors and regulators. It recommended that banks build systems with quality checks, clear risk controls and traceable decisions. The report said 30 to 50 percent of an agent network may need to be dedicated to quality assurance and traceability. One large bank reportedly used a similar multi-agent system to prepare corporate credit risk assessments, halving the time credit officers spent on analysis.

McKinsey stressed that people must remain in charge, since AI agents can analyse evidence and make recommendations but staff must assess findings, fill information gaps and keep responsibility for decisions. Hans-Georg Beyer, Commerzbank's chief credit risk officer and former group chief compliance officer, was quoted in the report saying that AI supports the work but that all judgments remain with the team. The report advised banks to start with a focused use case, prove its value and then widen it to other compliance activities. It also said success depends on staff skills, collaboration between compliance experts and data scientists, and robust governance.

The report noted that the same approach could extend to fraud detection, know-your-customer checks and regulatory compliance. It said banks would need to monitor deployed systems closely, test their reliability and keep improving them as risks and business needs change. A separate Global Finance Magazine article published the same day offers a more cautious view of agentic AI in banking. It reports that JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citigroup, Wells Fargo and Morgan Stanley have restricted or blocked third-party AI agents from client accounts, because they cannot reliably tell customer-authorized activity from rogue agent activity. Industry bodies quoted there say verifiable digital identities for AI agents are still lacking, so that restriction is presented as temporary until agent management catches up.

stories.Headline: Trump vows to 'officially ban' phrase 'artificial intelligence' in the United States
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump has said he will ban the phrase "artificial intelligence" across the United States, replacing it with "super intelligence." He made the pledge in a Truth Social post on Tuesday, October 27, 2026, after previously calling anyone who uses the older term an enemy. Trump argued the name is inaccurate and said the government would be officially banning it in all relevant documents. The article notes that the term has become common in everyday life, making such a change hard to achieve. Trump is pursuing the change even though he has not yet issued any formal ban beyond the federal government's own terminology.

Trump had already ordered federal agencies to use "super intelligence" in an executive order issued in late September. That order said the term better reflects the transformative capabilities and limitless opportunities of the technology. The phrase "artificial intelligence" was coined in 1955 by Stanford University emeritus professor John McCarthy, who defined it as the science and engineering of making intelligent machines. The White House's stance and the rhetoric in Trump's posts have drawn attention, with Trump describing the ban as one he would carry out soon. The articles do not say how a ban on private or non-government use would be enforced.

The push drew a pointed response from The Wall Street Journal, whose opinion section ran a newsletter titled "Let AI Be AI," written from the perspective of AI systems. That piece argued the existing name is snappy and widely understood, and it pointed out that "SI" already refers to the International System of Units and that Sports Illustrated uses the abbreviation. Trump responded by directing his anger at the newspaper in his latest post. The articles report that Trump has brushed aside concerns about AI safety, even as experts warn about the technology's risks.

Those risks have been raised by people inside the industry. Former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon said when he resigned last month that people building AI believe it could kill everyone by the end of the decade. Trump has ties to figures such as Elon Musk and Sam Altman, and when asked in September whether AI should be slowed or regulated, he said America is leading China and wants to keep it that way. A University of Massachusetts Amherst survey published last month found that only 23 percent of Americans think Trump has handled artificial intelligence well, while 57 percent say he has handled it poorly.

stories.Headline: KT Unveils Token Factory Platform With Over 500 AI Models, Set for Oct. 30 Launch
stories.Summary:
KT unveiled its KT Token Factory platform on October 27, 2026, a service that brings more than 500 domestic and international AI models together in one place. According to THE ELEC, the platform lets businesses choose models suited to their tasks and manage usage and costs without opening separate accounts for each model. The Korea Times reports that the service will go live on Friday, October 30, with 73 models at launch. KT plans to expand the lineup to more than 500 models in November through a partnership with OpenRouter, a global AI model marketplace.

The platform includes KT's Auto Model Router, which picks the most suitable model by analyzing a query's complexity, required quality, and cost. Simple tasks go to lightweight models, while complex analysis goes to higher-performance ones. KT says its prompt compression, which is tuned for Korean and removes repetitive expressions, can cut token consumption by up to 25 percent. Guardrail technology checks prompts and responses for personal information, sensitive data, and harmful content, and blocks sensitive data from being sent overseas. Seven of the launch models, including Upstage's Solar, KT's Mi:dm, and Google's Gemma, run on domestic infrastructure.

KT will offer a standard plan with usage-based postpaid billing and prepaid credits, plus an enterprise plan where customers can negotiate lower rates by committing to a set usage volume. Enterprise options include dedicated network connections and service-level agreements. The Korea Times reports that KT is using its telecom billing experience to track token consumption and combine those charges with telecom fees. Lee Jin-hyung, head of the AX Business Division, said the company's main revenue comes from the margin on producing tokens on graphics processing units in its own data centers, not from commissions on third-party models. KT plans to open the service to individual developers and consumers in March 2027, when it also expects to introduce subscription pricing.

Park Sang-won, senior vice president and head of the AX Business Division according to THE ELEC and executive vice president according to the Korea Times, said at a press conference in Seoul that competition is shifting from building better models to helping users apply AI effectively. He said the central challenge is turning AI use across businesses and workflows into measurable results. The articles frame the launch as KT's push to build a new growth business by helping companies control AI costs. Both reports indicate the enterprise launch comes first, with the consumer market to follow.

stories.Headline: Law school puts AI 'Supreme Court' to the test
stories.Summary:
The Supreme Court of Nepal has ordered the government to draft a dedicated data protection law covering the personal and biometric data collected through the country's National Identity Card program. In a ruling issued on 9 October, the court said constitutional privacy protections require a comprehensive legal framework approved by Parliament, not administrative standards and committees. It also struck down a Nepal Rastra Bank directive that had made the National Identity Card the sole basis for opening or renewing bank accounts. The judges reasoned that biometric records such as fingerprints and retinal scans are highly sensitive, and that a compromise could have lasting consequences for individuals and national security.

The court asked for a standalone Data Protection Act that would clearly define the purposes of data collection, limits on its use, citizens' rights, oversight mechanisms, penalties and remedies for violations. It also warned against giving private banks broad access to biometric records and called instead for verification systems that return only a yes-or-no answer. Citizens may not be denied banking services because they lack a National Identity Card, the ruling states. The decision lands as the country has recently required citizens aged 16 and older to use their national ID to enrol in, renew and access health insurance services from December 16.

The case was brought by advocate Sarita Adhikari, who argued that the absence of a clear legal framework governing access to, use of and retention of biometric data violated constitutional privacy rights. The government defended existing safeguards, including a Data Security Committee and standards developed under the National Identity Card and Registration Act. The court found those safeguards inadequate. The ruling was reported by Setopati and carried by Biometric Update, which noted that it raises questions about expanding mandatory national ID use without stronger protections, particularly where private organizations take part in verification.

stories.Headline: New York Court System's New AI Rules for Lawyers Explained
stories.Summary:
New York's state court system has released a guide telling attorneys they can use generative artificial intelligence to help prepare court papers without telling a judge they did. The guide, called The Risks of Using Artificial Intelligence in Preparing Court Papers: What Every Attorney Should Know, was written by the court system's Advisory Committee on Artificial Intelligence and the Courts and released on October 27, 2026. It says lawyers must understand what their AI tools can and cannot do and must confirm independently that any information the software produces is accurate and reliable. Attorneys are not required to disclose AI use when they file or to provide separate certifications beyond what they already sign. Heidi Brown, an associate dean at New York Law School, said she is concerned that the guidance does not require disclosure to judges.

The guidance makes clear that responsibility for filings stays with the lawyer. Attorneys must make sure every factual and legal claim in a court submission is accurate and properly supported, and they should check all AI-generated citations and quotations with authoritative legal research tools. They should also record the steps they took to verify AI-assisted material. The same sanctions for false material apply whether or not AI was used, and the Rules of Professional Conduct and 22 NYCRR Part 130 still govern the attorney's obligations. The guidance also warns that common large language models do not check citations against verified databases and instead predict likely words, which is why independent checking matters.

Brown described "misgroundings," where real cases are cited but described inaccurately, as especially risky because they look legitimate. The guidance further warns that training data can carry bias and may not reflect recent legal developments. The guide builds on Part 161 of the Rules of the Chief Administrator of the Courts, which was adopted March 25, 2026 and took effect statewide June 1, 2026. Under that rule, attorneys may use AI in preparing papers without a blanket disclosure requirement, but they must verify that nothing filed contains fabricated cases, statutes, or other material. Individual judges can still impose their own AI requirements through their part rules.

Chief Administrative Judge Joseph Zayas, who appointed the advisory committee in 2024, said AI can improve efficiency but requires caution and informed oversight. First Deputy Chief Administrative Judge Norman St. George said safeguarding the integrity of filings is paramount. The court system chose not to ban generative AI or mandate disclosure, relying instead on attorneys' informed use. The stakes are already visible in court. Sanctions against lawyers for AI-generated errors have grown nationally, and a researcher has counted more than 1,200 cases involving erroneous AI information, roughly 800 from U.S. courts.

In New York, the Appellate Division, Third Department, imposed monetary sanctions in January 2026 over filings that cited 23 fabricated cases. Penalties elsewhere have been steeper, including an Oregon federal order requiring a lawyer to pay $109,700 in sanctions and costs. In March 2026, the 6th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals sanctioned two attorneys over more than two dozen fake citations and ordered each to pay $15,000 as a punitive sanction. Because AI tools are increasingly built into the software lawyers already use, New York's approach places the burden on individual attorneys to catch errors before a judge or opposing counsel does.

stories.Headline: Long Beach Schools Ask Families To Weigh In On AI In Classrooms
stories.Summary:
Long Beach Unified School District has opened two surveys asking students and families how artificial intelligence, screen time and classroom technology should be handled in its schools. The questionnaires went live on October 16 and remain open through Friday, November 6. The effort follows weeks of pressure from parents and students who want tighter limits on classroom technology. On October 7, students wearing zombie makeup told the school board at a public meeting that heavy reliance on AI could weaken independent thinking.

The surveys ask whether students use too many screens, how digital tools affect learning and attention, and whether AI helps students grasp hard concepts or instead raises concerns about accuracy, academic honesty, privacy and safety. Families are also asked whether students should spend more or less time on devices during the school day and whether the right amount should depend on age and the type of learning. The district has not announced an AI ban, and no new policy has been finalized. Its existing AI guidance already addresses responsible use, academic integrity and the protection of student information. Participation is voluntary, and the district says responses will be reviewed collectively.

According to the district's spokesperson, Eric Mitchell, a technology workgroup made up of teachers, students, parents and guardians, administrators and industry experts will review the results after the deadline and identify common themes. Local parents, including members of a Long Beach chapter of the national group Schools Beyond Screens, have pushed the district to limit classroom technology, and the district already adopted a 2025 policy restricting phones and personal devices. One parent, Kim Tashkin, has said she hopes the district passes an AI moratorium quickly. Reporting from Hoodline notes that the district spent $2.5 million on laptops in the 2025-26 school year and projects another $2.5 million for the current year.

The debate sits within a wider national trend. A 2025 RAND study found that 54 percent of students and 53 percent of surveyed teachers reported using AI for school, a rise of more than 15 percentage points over one to two years. The same research found that 61 percent of parents, 48 percent of middle schoolers and 55 percent of high schoolers worried that greater AI use could harm critical thinking, compared with 22 percent of district leaders. Other large districts have responded differently, with Los Angeles Unified and New York City Public Schools both reported to have adopted AI moratoriums. The articles say the workgroup's findings, along with focus groups and additional research, could shape future policy recommendations for Long Beach, though what those recommendations will be remains unknown.

stories.Headline: Chipmaker SK Hynix to return $75 billion to shareholders after record profit
stories.Summary:
SK Hynix, the South Korean memory chipmaker, unveiled plans on Wednesday to return a large amount of money to its shareholders after its profit surged to a level well above analysts' expectations. The company reported an operating profit of 83.3 trillion won for the September quarter, beating projections by more than 7%. It said it would pay out 60 trillion won more in the remainder of the fiscal year through share buybacks and dividends, on top of a previously announced 40 trillion won. Much of the payout stems from gains the company locked in after selling its stake in Kioxia Holdings earlier this year. Shares rose more than 4% in early Seoul trading.

The company also said it expects shortages of components crucial to Nvidia's AI accelerators to persist through at least 2030, which is keeping prices high. SK Hynix and rival Samsung Electronics are among the largest beneficiaries of the surge in demand for memory from artificial intelligence developers building data centers. Memory now makes up roughly a third of all expenses related to AI data centers, according to research from Macquarie, and that share is expected to grow as prices for high-bandwidth memory are set to more than double in 2027. Analysts at Counterpoint Research said quarterly earnings have not yet peaked and expect the upward trend to continue at least through 2027.

The announcement came from SK Hynix's management, which reaffirmed its outlook on the shortage and set out the payout plan. The company has also recently faced changes to its listing plans, having abandoned a potential U.S. listing of its Solidigm unit, a potential $10 billion offering, after shareholder opposition and regulatory scrutiny. Bloomberg News reported that Solidigm is in talks with the U.S. Commerce Department about investing $45 billion in a new chip plant on American soil. Solidigm had been among several AI-linked companies to shelve public offerings amid mounting concerns about an AI bubble that are rattling global markets.

stories.Headline: VNY Exclusive: De La Rosa Says Self-Regulation Fails, NYC Must Lead on AI
stories.Summary:
The New York City Council has become a focal point in the push to regulate artificial intelligence after a hearing on October 15, 2026, in which representatives from OpenAI, Google, Meta, and xAI testified under oath about their companies' policies. The Council's Technology Committee chair, Carmen De La Rosa, who represents Washington Heights, Inwood, and Marble Hill, is leading the effort. The hearing was reported as the first time a legislative body at any level of government had put such tech executives on the record in this way. xAI had initially declined the Council's invitation, so the Speaker used the Council's subpoena power to compel its appearance.

De La Rosa's central bill, Intro 161, would require a report on how AI is affecting the city's workforce, including changes to job duties and possible job losses. She said the goal is to identify which jobs are at risk, retrain workers for other city roles, and make sure the systems that handle benefits such as food stamps and housing stay accurate and fair. Related bills in the same package would protect personal data, require independent third-party audits of AI tools, and make sure residents know when they are dealing with a person rather than a chatbot. She also voiced concern about surveillance by the NYPD and about mixed-status families whose information could be misused.

De La Rosa said that federal oversight is needed, but she argued that the current administration's emphasis on self-regulation does not give cities confidence. She noted that many of these companies are headquartered in New York and said the city can ask them what their technology does and what safeguards they have in place. She criticized several witnesses for avoiding responsibility, and she said the xAI representative's answers were unsatisfactory, adding that the company did not appear eager to work with municipalities. She pointed to a whistleblower's testimony that only three employees were dedicated to safety at the company, which she said contradicted the claim that safety was everyone's responsibility.

Looking ahead, De La Rosa said the Council is holding oversight hearings and community roundtables, including one for teens, and that the results will shape legislation and the budget. She said she expects to testify in Albany and is waiting for the results of the November midterm elections before engaging further with Congress. She also framed public libraries as local hubs for digital and AI literacy, particularly for communities that still lack reliable internet access. The articles do not say when Intro 161 will be voted on or whether it will pass.

stories.Headline: What candidates in Arkansas’ US Senate race say about AI, data centers
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence and the data centers that power it have become a campaign issue in the midterm cycle, and Arkansas' U.S. Senate race is no exception. Republican Sen. Tom Cotton, who is up for reelection in November, faces Democrat Hallie Shoffner and Libertarian Jeff Wadlin. In interviews reported by the Arkansas Advocate on October 27, 2026, all three said Arkansans should get a vote on whether a data center is built near them. The reporting notes that a Pew Research Center poll in August found 71% of people surveyed worry AI will replace human jobs over the next 20 years, and that another poll found more than 70% of Americans do not want a data center built near them.

On specific proposals, the candidates differ. Shoffner said she would support a new federal agency to monitor and regulate the AI industry, comparing it to the way the Environmental Protection Agency oversees fertilizers used on crops. Cotton said the federal government does not need a "Department of Artificial Intelligence" or a big government bureaucracy, and that any legislation should be targeted, with clear guardrails such as protecting children from chatbot misuse and preventing fraud. Wadlin said he would back a ban on AI in public safety and transportation, and called for tougher rules on agentic AI, which acts with partial or full autonomy. He said he would accept either a government agency or a commercial auditing body, so long as there is nationwide oversight.

On data centers, Cotton has introduced a bill that would let them build their own power grid so they do not draw power from local communities or raise residents' utility bills. He also supported a measure from Republican Sen. Jon Husted of Ohio that would set standards for connecting data centers to the grid, but Senate Democrats blocked it, calling it toothless. Wadlin said data center companies should pay for their own electricity and water, and that decisions should come through town halls rather than backroom deals or nondisclosure agreements signed by state officials or county judges. Shoffner said Arkansans want jobs and industry but also transparency about the impacts, and that she hears questions about data centers at every campaign event. Cotton did not answer emailed questions from the Advocate, but he told 40/29 News in September that he has discussed both the promise and the risk of AI with the White House, the Pentagon and the CIA, and that AI companies should be transparent about their products and their effects on communities.

The debate unfolds amid wider concern about the industry. Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin recently sued OpenAI, alleging it hid ChatGPT's risks from users, and some states have barred chatbots from giving mental health advice after suicides among young users. Data centers' water and electricity use has caused local backlash across the country, including in several Arkansas communities where officials have clashed over regulations. Proposals to regulate AI and data centers have been floated in Congress, though President Donald Trump has dismissed calls for new guardrails. The articles do not say what will happen next beyond the November election.

stories.Headline: Bill Gates Predicts Some People Will Reject A.I. for Amish Lifestyle
stories.Summary:
Bill Gates has suggested that some people may eventually choose to live the way the Amish do, rejecting artificial intelligence in much of daily life. He made the remarks on The Verge's "Decoder" podcast, which aired around October 27, 2026, as Microsoft was reportedly offering buyouts to roughly 60,000 employees during its large AI push. Gates said people could use AI for certain tasks while keeping childcare, cooking, art and sports in human hands, even if machines could perform them better. The articles say the interview came as the company announced a voluntary exit offer on Monday, October 26.

Gates describes the coming two decades as a tumultuous transition with winners, losers and significant disruption before society reaches an era of abundance. He sees the potential payoff as a world where AI helps reduce shortages and makes healthcare and food more accessible. He has argued that AI needs government regulation, because once several competitors exist, responsibility cannot rest with the companies alone. He also warned that the technology could enable bioterrorism and dramatic harm, and that it will eventually reach physical and blue collar work through humanoid robots.

The articles attribute these views to Gates himself, who co-founded Microsoft and served as its CEO until 2000. He has said that humanity will have real choices about how far to let the technology advance, and that a lot of people may decide not to live at the technological frontier. He has also described the rise of AI as a period as turbulent as any in human history, and told the podcast that it is better to tell people this is coming than to stay silent. Earlier, according to TMZ, he had called AI the most dangerous technology humans have invented. PEOPLE reported that it reached out to Microsoft for comment, but the articles do not include a response.

stories.Headline: Exclusive | Broadcom CEO Intervened to Seal $63 Billion Anthropic Debt Deal
stories.Summary:
Bank of America, Blackstone, Citi and Morgan Stanley announced on Oct. 26, local time, a $63 billion transaction to supply AI computing resources to Anthropic. The arrangement runs through a newly established special purpose vehicle, or SPV, which will buy Broadcom's XPU-based AI accelerators and networking equipment and lease them to Anthropic. The four financial institutions will lend money to the SPV, and those loans will be secured by the Broadcom products it purchases. Equipment deliveries are set to begin in 2027. The article reports the deal as a financing structure built around the chips rather than a conventional sale.

Bank of America, Citi and Morgan Stanley will hold first-priority security interests, meaning they have the first claim on proceeds from asset sales if the SPV runs into financial trouble. Blackstone will hold the only second-priority security interest, which the article notes typically carries higher interest rates in exchange for lower repayment priority. Broadcom will guarantee the residual value of the collateralized equipment up to the amount of the first-lien loans. If the resale value of AI accelerators falls and the SPV cannot fully repay its first-lien debt, Broadcom will cover the shortfall. The article says this structure is designed to reduce the risk of losses for first-lien lenders.

Hock Tan, president and chief executive officer of Broadcom, described the transaction as evidence of the standing of advanced technology and strong confidence in the AI ecosystem. He said underlying demand for AI computing is growing at a tremendous pace and that enough capital exists to support that growth. The article presents these remarks as the company's public framing of the deal. The Elec's reporting places the arrangement within a broader wave of AI infrastructure spending, in which chipmakers and financial firms are finding new ways to fund large compute purchases. The article does not report any regulatory response, further financing steps, or additional details on the terms beyond those described above.

stories.Headline: Italy's AI Act framework takes shape: What Legislative Decree No. 179/2026 means for organizations
stories.Summary:
Italy's Legislative Decree No. 179/2026 took effect on October 23, 2026, giving national shape to the EU AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. The decree was dated October 7 and published in Italy's Official Journal on October 8, completing a two-step approach that began with Law No. 132 in September 2025. That earlier law set national AI principles and asked the government to align Italian law with the AI Act. The new decree answers that request by filling gaps the EU regulation leaves to member states.

The decree separates oversight of conformity-assessment bodies from market surveillance of AI systems. The Agency for Digital Italy, known as AgID, assesses, designates, notifies and monitors those bodies, including through periodic and extraordinary audits. If AgID finds shortcomings, it may begin proceedings to limit, suspend or revoke a body's designation after giving that body a chance to be heard. The National Cybersecurity Agency, known as ACN, holds general market-surveillance duties for AI systems and may inspect real-world testing remotely or on site without prior notice. ACN is also responsible for national registration of high-risk systems covered by point 2 of Annex III to the AI Act.

Other authorities receive narrower remits. The Bank of Italy, CONSOB and IVASS each have market-surveillance responsibilities for specified high-risk uses in banking, financial services, insurance and insurance distribution, within their stated remits. Italy's data-protection authority holds a limited market-surveillance role tied to a specific provision of the AI Act. Sanctioning powers follow the same logic: AgID may impose administrative fines for listed violations by notified bodies, and national market-surveillance authorities sanction within their own areas, with no single general fine amount set by the decree.

Organizations operating in Italy should note that several operational details remain for later instruments. A government regulation proposed by ACN is to define how its inspection powers are exercised, and a later decree by ACN's director general, agreed with AgID, is to set registration and information-management procedures. Until those instruments appear, companies can already map which authority would supervise their systems and which conformity-assessment bodies they may need to use. Because the decree assigns duties by authority and remit, compliance planning will depend on identifying the regulator relevant to each product or service.

stories.Headline: Prosecutors say Rhode Island agency used AI to create backdated Medicaid records in alleged $2 million fraud scheme
stories.Summary:
Seven people tied to a Providence community health worker agency were indicted by a Rhode Island grand jury over an alleged $2 million Medicaid fraud scheme. Prosecutors say the agency's owner and an employee used artificial intelligence to produce patient notes and treatment records months after the services supposedly occurred. Attorney General Peter Neronha announced a 51-count indictment on Oct. 22. The allegations have not been proven in court, and the defendants are presumed innocent.

The defendants are linked to U'Nique Diversity Innovations LLC, a provider on Branch Avenue in Providence that the state approved as a Medicaid community health worker provider in November 2024. Prosecutors allege that from then until June 2025, the owner billed for services never provided, services greatly overstated, services billed for family members, and services supposedly given to people who were incarcerated. They further allege that backdated training certificates were created and signed to make it appear staff had completed required training, and that none of the seven were certified as community health workers during that period. The indictment also describes cash bonuses for recruiting Medicaid members and alleged personal spending of Medicaid money. Charges vary by defendant and include Medicaid fraud, conspiracy, identity theft and racketeering.

Attorney General Neronha said that people who commit Medicaid fraud, as alleged here, are stealing public funds. The owner, Shanee Vega, 44, faces 48 of the counts and was released on $50,000 bail with surety after her arrest at home. The other six defendants turned themselves in over the following days. The investigation began in May 2025, when the state's Medicaid program integrity office referred the case to the attorney general's Medicaid Fraud Control Unit, and investigators searched the agency's offices in July 2025.

The case lands against a backdrop of concern about the community health worker program, which helps Medicaid members connect with doctors, food and housing support. Advocates have said these workers can prevent more costly care, while state officials said in 2025 that a crackdown with tighter billing rules was saving Medicaid nearly $2 million a month. The company has since closed. The records question matters beyond this case, since AI-generated notes can look complete on paper, so auditors may need to check records against appointment logs, phone records or member confirmations. Medicaid members who spot unfamiliar charges can call their health plan, and suspected fraud can be reported to the attorney general's unit or the HHS Office of Inspector General at 1-800-HHS-TIPS.

stories.Headline: Microsoft Pulls Out of Nscale’s UK AI Data Center Project Over Grid Delays
stories.Summary:
Microsoft has pulled out of the Loughton, Essex project that was to become the UK's largest AI data centre, according to reports published in mid-October 2026. The BBC understands that Microsoft, which had said it would fund a supercomputer at the site, has ended its involvement. The Telegraph first reported the grid problem on a Sunday, and the BBC's story followed on 18 October. Microsoft declined to comment, while the developer, Nscale, said it still intends to build the facility.

The site was part of a £2bn pledge Nscale announced in 2025, and it is expected to create 250 permanent jobs once it opens. The data centre was due to receive its power supply at the end of this year, but Nscale has now been told that will not happen until the 2030s. AI News reported that UK Power Networks, the network operator, told Nscale there would not be enough electricity until the early-to-mid 2030s. Microsoft had also said only last month that some of the $30bn (£22bn) it is investing in the UK would go toward the Loughton supercomputer. Nscale says it has cleared the scaffolding-yard site ready for construction.

Nscale said it remains committed to both the Loughton project and the UK, and is looking at alternative power sources for the site, along with other expansion sites in the country. The company described the situation as an "unfortunate London-wide grid issue" that does not affect its other contracts, and said its relationship with Microsoft stays strong and long-term. The two firms are still working together on projects in Norway, Portugal and the United States. AI News added that Nscale is also exploring a faster grid connection. Peter Griffiths, founder and executive chairman of Argyll Data Development, said electricity is the choke point and that ambition means nothing without the power to deliver it.

Griffiths used the episode to argue for faster grid access elsewhere in the country. He said Scotland has a clean-power pipeline of more than a thousand projects, yet those schemes are not reaching the grid on schedule, and that some 23 proposed hyperscale data centres are waiting in the same queue. In his view, Scotland's wind and hydro capacity could support them, and he called for fast-track connections for credible Scottish AI infrastructure or the investment and jobs would go elsewhere. He also pointed to a £600 million commitment on AI safety and security, which he called a meaningful down-payment, while saying sovereign AI infrastructure will cost billions. Nscale remains the developer at Loughton, and no new date for power has been given beyond the 2030s window.

stories.Headline: Daeryuk Aju, Lin sign AI compliance MOU with Deloitte Anjin
stories.Summary:
Three firms, Daeryuk Aju, Lin and Deloitte Anjin, signed a memorandum of understanding on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, at a conference room on the 20th floor of Donghun Tower on Teheran-ro in Gangnam-gu, Seoul. The agreement commits them to jointly support corporate AI compliance certification and the development of management frameworks for AI use. It was reported by Herald Business and Chosunbiz, both of which note that the signing took place in Seoul. The move responds to tightening rules at home and abroad, including the enforcement of Korea's Basic AI Act and the European Union's AI Act.

The cooperation covers a broad set of tasks. These include assessing AI compliance and governance frameworks, building certification criteria based on objective evaluation standards, and advising on domestic and international AI laws. It also covers AI risk diagnosis, stronger internal controls, and the creation of responsible AI policies and operating frameworks. The firms will additionally address privacy, security and intellectual property risks that come with AI use. They plan joint research on AI regulation and industry trends, along with joint seminars, and four seminars are set for November 11 to December 1 at Donghun Tower.

Lee Gyu-cheol, managing partner of Daeryuk Aju, said corporate responses to AI rules are moving beyond simple legal review toward organization-wide management systems. He expects the firm's legal expertise, combined with Deloitte Anjin's AI and risk management capabilities, to produce more practical compliance services. Lim Jin-seok, managing partner of Lin, said certification could become a new standard for earning trust from customers and the market, not just a tool for responding to regulators. Gil Gi-wan, CEO of Deloitte Anjin, said the collaboration aims to help companies use AI more safely and responsibly.

The three firms recently launched the AI Compliance Certification program, known as AICC, which examines corporate AI compliance and accredits companies that meet objective standards. Chosunbiz reports that the program will set evaluation criteria reflecting industry characteristics and levels of AI use. A Daeryuk Aju official said AICC is expected to help companies keep their AI systems stable, much as the firm's Serious Accidents Punishment Act certification has aided in preventing serious workplace accidents. The first seminars are scheduled to present the criteria to firms in finance, heavy industry, broadcasting, telecommunications, platforms and physical AI.

stories.Headline: Use of AI in filmmaking discussed at Artifex-2026
stories.Summary:
Artifex-2026, a two-day event on animation and filmmaking, opened on Wednesday at the Manipal Institute of Communication under Manipal Academy of Higher Education. The event was organised by the institute's Animation Department. At an interactive session, B. S. Srinivas, director and chairman of Arena Animation and Vedatma College of Design, Technology and Management in Bengaluru, looked at how AI is changing the filmmaking pipeline. He covered stages from pre-production and scene creation through visual effects, dubbing, colour grading and post-production.

The session stressed that AI-assisted tools can help smaller teams do work that once needed more time, money and staff. Srinivas also discussed AI in animation, virtual production and digital character creation. He raised concerns about copyright, consent, authenticity, employment and quality control. According to a release, the session concluded that AI can speed up workflows and widen creative options, but human imagination, empathy and storytelling remain central to filmmaking. A drawing competition on the theme of phone addiction was held during the event.

The other article covers a different gathering, the VST ECS CXO Tech Summit 2026, held October 20 to 23 at Shangri-La Boracay under the theme "Rethinking IT: Powering the AI-Driven Enterprise." Delegates from 14 academic institutions and education-related organisations attended, and the article says the academe's growing presence reflects rising interest in AI preparedness. On September 15, 2026, the Commission on Higher Education issued CHED Memorandum Order No. 21, series of 2026, which covers AI use in teaching, learning, research and institutional operations. The order sets safeguards for academic integrity, data privacy, human judgment and student welfare.

At the media briefing on October 22, representatives from HP, Fortinet and Nutanix addressed educator training, cybersecurity and student-facing technology. HP Philippines said it runs customised AI Academy programmes for teachers, including one with Ateneo de Naga University, and a similar programme for schools in Pasig City. Fortinet Philippines, through Bambi Escalante, described a cybersecurity skills gap of roughly one professional for every 2,000 to 3,000 employees, against an ideal of about one to 200. Nutanix's Daryush Ashjari said its platform lets students try different technology layers while IT teams manage them. The article concludes that moving from experimentation to responsible use will need coordinated investment in educator development, cybersecurity skills and student safeguards.

stories.Headline: Coco Robotics and Serve Robotics face Illinois lawsuits alleging delivery robots collected biometric data
stories.Summary:
Two class-action lawsuits filed in Cook County, Illinois, allege that delivery robots from Coco Robotics and Serve Robotics secretly scanned people's faces and hands and shared that data with artificial intelligence companies. The suits say the people involved never gave permission for this collection. One plaintiff, Mitchell Breidinger, says he ordered groceries through DoorDash in September 2025 and a Coco robot arrived even though he had not asked for a robot delivery. Another plaintiff, Barry Schain, says he received three Uber Eats deliveries by Serve robot without requesting one, and his suit was filed five days after an October 4 delivery in Lincoln Park. Both lawsuits were reported on October 27, 2026.

The lawsuits argue the companies violated Illinois' Biometric Information Privacy Act, which requires written notice before biometric data is collected, an explanation of how it will be used, and explicit permission first. Violations can carry fines of $1,000 to $5,000 each. Breidinger alleges the robot's cameras recorded his face, head and hands while LiDAR sensors captured the shape of his body parts. He further claims a remote operator watched the delivery live and that the data went to OpenAI and other companies.

Schain's suit alleges Serve collected video and sensor data and licensed it to third parties. Both companies deny the allegations. A Coco Robotics spokesperson called the lawsuit "frivolous" and said the company has not collected biometric data in Chicago. Serve Robotics told The Associated Press that it does not use its data to identify individuals and that its systems are not designed to identify people or create biometric profiles, and it has said its cameras and sensors are used only for navigation.

The cases come amid wider scrutiny of surveillance technology, including Flock Safety's automated license plate readers, which have sparked debate this year. Chicago residents have also complained about delivery robots blocking sidewalks and crashing into bus shelters. The city's robot delivery pilot program is set to end in May 2027 unless officials extend it. If the allegations prove true, the cases may prompt further investigation into how businesses inform people about data practices involving their devices.

stories.Headline: Amazon's anti-tokenmaxxing memo says engineers should be pickier about using AI
stories.Summary:
Amazon, on Tuesday, October 27, 2026, posted an internal memo on its website that sets out how software engineers and managers should use artificial intelligence tools. The memo, first circulated to staff in September, tells employees not to treat "tokenmaxxing," the practice of running AI as heavily as possible with little regard for results, as a sign of success. Amazon had earlier shut down an internal leaderboard in May after discovering that employees were inflating their token usage to climb the rankings. The company says it has not put caps on how many tokens employees may use.

The memo says that token usage, the rate of AI tool adoption, and counts of code changes or reviews are "deeply flawed" ways to measure AI use, since they can drive up costs and add complexity. It does not tell staff to ignore those figures entirely, however, and says they should be weighed "with care and judgment" alongside other data. Instead, Amazon says it prefers to measure teams by long-term outcomes. Marc Brooker, a vice president and distinguished engineer at Amazon Web Services, said the company has also looked at "feature velocity," meaning how many launches and successful production changes teams deliver.

The memo is credited to Terk Terkowitz, a vice president and distinguished engineer in Worldwide Amazon Stores, and it says that teams which have embraced AI have gained productivity while those that have not have fallen behind. It also says an engineer who finds that AI does not help their work should document why and share it, which the memo describes as showing sound judgment rather than failure. Terkowitz wrote that leaders must understand their teams' work and stay close to their products and businesses. Brooker added that the company accepts some wasted effort as the cost of experimentation, though it wants to avoid spending tokens on problems that do not matter.

The memo comes amid a wider industry reckoning over AI costs. Companies have been struggling with rising AI bills and with how to tell whether the tools produce real returns, and some have set limits on token use, switched to cheaper open-source models for certain tasks, or rethought their AI spending after what one report called "token shock." Amazon has moved quickly to fold AI into its operations under CEO Andy Jassy, who has predicted AI will change the scope and speed of work and could shrink corporate staffing over the next few years. The articles do not say what further steps Amazon plans beyond the guidelines in the memo.

stories.Headline: Fairbanks town hall to address data centers, AI development concerns
stories.Summary:
A town hall titled "Nobody Asked Us" is set for Thursday at 7 p.m. at the Taiga Center at Wedgewood Resort in Fairbanks, where local residents will look at data centers and artificial intelligence. The meeting comes as borough leaders weigh a temporary moratorium on data centers proposed by Fairbanks North Star Borough Mayor Grier Hopkins. The proposal would give the borough time to decide where data centers should go and to write rules covering electricity demand, noise and location. It still requires approval from the borough assembly.

A separate letter in the News-Miner, signed by Sarah Hollister of Fairbanks, invites residents to a town hall at 6:30 p.m. on October 29 at the same venue. The writer argues that federal land leases near Eielson Air Force Base would let developers avoid borough zoning and local taxes, and that public comment on those federal reviews comes too late. The organizers say they will hear community concerns and then deliver them to elected officials. The event is run with community residents, Alaskans for Data Center Accountability, the Northern Alaska Environmental Center and Families Over Billionaires.

Mayor Hopkins frames the pause as a way to give the borough room to think before commitments are made. The letter's author, by contrast, says that much of the planning for AI expansion in Alaska has happened at high levels and behind closed doors. The organizers say they want residents to see how close the Eielson lease parcels sit to homes, schools and neighborhoods in Salcha, North Pole and Eielson AFB. The articles do not say how the assembly will vote on the moratorium or whether the federal lease bids will proceed.

Data center development is a growing concern in many communities as demand for artificial intelligence and digital services rises. On November 3, voters in 11 states will consider 41 ballot measures on data centers, and most would place limits on development while some would ease construction. The Fairbanks discussion is one local part of that wider debate. The articles do not indicate what the borough assembly will do next.

stories.Headline: Opinion: Telcos have a role to play in AI
stories.Summary:
Two industry pieces this week look at where AI processing is heading, from telecom networks in one case and from Asian manufacturing in the other. Joe Madden, principal analyst at Mobile Experts, writes in a Fierce Network opinion column dated October 27, 2026, that his team has spent two years studying AI edge computing and released its first forecast, Telco Edge AI 2026, that week. He argues that the mobile edge computing push of earlier years failed because low latency alone did not persuade customers to pay, and that edge AI should be treated differently. In his view, the telco's real role is as a broker that decides which AI tasks run on a regional sovereign AI factory and which run locally for performance, privacy, or cost reasons. His colleague Sebastian Barros calls this function the "AI Control Plane."

According to the column, the telco's control plane would identify and authenticate the person, device, or AI agent starting a task, then route that task to the right model and compute location. It would also match connectivity to latency and reliability needs and govern each device or agent's use to prevent runaway token costs. Madden notes that many CFOs were surprised by token bills in 2025 and that employees often default to the most expensive model for every job. The forecast identifies four revenue sources: regional and sovereign AI services, telco edge and metro inference, managed services for private cellular networks running industrial AI, and support services for on-device AI models. Madden expects modest telco revenue for 2026 through 2030, but sees the control plane as strategic high ground by 2035.

Separately, a PR Newswire release published by The Manila Times on October 27, 2026, reports that Asia could take a larger role in physical AI, meaning intelligent machines deployed in real-world settings. The statement comes from a panel at Silicon to Scale: A Physical AI Summit, held during SF Tech Week and co-hosted by Startup Island TAIWAN Silicon Valley Hub and SparkLabs Taiwan. The summit drew more than 170 investors, industry leaders and founders, and featured five Taiwanese physical AI startups. Speakers said Taiwan's semiconductor and manufacturing strengths, Southeast Asia's chip assembly and testing operations, and Japan's flexible industrial lines all give the region advantages as robotics moves from prototype toward commercial use.

Investors on the panel, including Jeff Tao of Citi, Vandon Duong of DCVC, and Kosuke Yusa of Open Network Lab Fund, pointed to access to training data as the main obstacle. Tao said manufacturers are reluctant to share proprietary operational data, while Duong said developers will pay for well-annotated datasets but questioned how lasting advantages could be built as more firms enter the market. Panelists also flagged electricity availability as a growing bottleneck for AI infrastructure in the United States, creating openings for startups in power systems, cooling, and more efficient chip manufacturing. Tao cautioned that AI-driven productivity could displace workers in the short term. Speakers remained optimistic about long-term adoption, according to the release.

stories.Headline: Genie 4 introduces real-time interactive world simulation
stories.Summary:
Google DeepMind has announced Genie 4, a new world model that generates real-time interactive simulations with native audio and advanced physics. Announced on October 27, 2026, the model is described as natively multimodal, producing sound, ambient noise, and dialogue alongside the visuals. Gemini models supply the reasoning needed to keep a simulation coherent while it evolves. Genie 4 is currently in a research preview, so trusted testers are evaluating it before wider release. Users can steer a running simulation with natural language, changing the weather, moving the camera, or adding a person or object, and Gemini adapts each prompt to fit the surrounding scene.

The model also simulates physical interactions such as aerodynamics and collisions, and it generates characters who move naturally and respond to their surroundings. Its audio capabilities extend to ambient sound tied to each setting and to characters who speak and react to events in real time. Access begins with Google AI Ultra subscribers through Project Genie, followed by early partners using the Gemini API and Google AI Studio. Google DeepMind's researchers, named in the announcement as Raia Hadsell, Diego Rivas and Hang Qi, present the model as a step toward building artificial general intelligence. They argue that understanding and simulating the world matters for training robots and agents in safe, varied environments.

The company also frames it as a tool for creating new interactive experiences. TechGig's coverage adds that filmmakers, photojournalists, and game developers are already using it for rapid prototyping and scene simulation. TechGig reports that the model includes safety guardrails consistent with those of Google's other models, and that all generated content carries SynthID, a digital watermark for identifying AI-generated material. The articles also say Genie 4 remains an early experimental model with known limits, including difficulty maintaining consistency over long periods and accurately rendering complex physical interactions. Further testing and feedback from the trusted testers will shape its release to consumers and developers.

stories.Headline: Artificial intelligence transforms the workforce, regulations
stories.Summary:
Goldman Sachs estimates that 300 million jobs will be affected by artificial intelligence by 2030, and the technology is already reshaping industries day by day, transforming some jobs and erasing others. Nearly every sector has felt its effects, which has increased the call for oversight of how AI is used. Reporting from Gray DC on October 28, 2026, described the trend as one that is bringing a greater need for governance. The coverage focused on how quickly the changes are arriving.

Barry Jones, a vice president at X2X, an AI governance company, argued that human involvement must remain part of AI work and that current oversight is not sufficient. He gave the example of an AI assistant preparing financial reports, which could be useful but could also expose critical financial information if it operated outside a company's internal controls. Jones said self-governance by companies is not enough and that a third party, including government, should set out what AI systems may and may not do. He also pointed to private-sector job cuts, noting that Microsoft recently offered 60,000 employees buyouts because of AI.

Members of Congress gave differing views on the government's role. Representative Buddy Carter, a Georgia Republican, said he preferred less federal involvement but acknowledged that AI can be very useful while also carrying real concerns and dangers that must be addressed correctly. Senator Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, said the United States must deal with the serious risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems and that the American people, through their representatives, should make those decisions. Efforts to regulate AI have stalled on Capitol Hill, although the 120th Congress could take up the issue when it convenes in January.

For workers seeking a career change because of AI, Jones advised learning the technology and understanding how it applies to their profession. He stressed that judgment, experience, trust and accountability still matter, and that the goal should be to learn to use AI responsibly rather than to compete with the machine. The articles do not describe any specific regulation adopted so far. What happens next depends on whether Congress acts in January on the stalled proposals.

stories.Headline: House Democratic Committee Leaders Request Frontier AI Companies Report Misalignment & Safety Incidents to Congress Within 48 Hours
stories.Summary:
House Democratic leaders on three committees sent letters on October 28, 2026, to five leading frontier AI companies asking them to report misalignment and safety incidents to Congress. The lawmakers said the request follows a rise in reports of AI models taking unintended and potentially unsafe actions during testing. The letters went to Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI, and SpaceX, which the article lists as SpaceXSI. The letters were signed by Ranking Members Frank Pallone Jr. of New Jersey, Zoe Lofgren of California, and Jamie Raskin of Maryland. The lawmakers asked each company for a full accounting of identified incidents by November 11, 2026.

They also requested that companies notify the committees within 48 hours of discovering any new or previously unknown incident. For incidents that appear to involve critical infrastructure, the request is for notification within 24 hours. The Democrats framed these steps as a way to gather the best available information before Congress takes up AI governance. The Democratic leaders wrote that there are currently no mandatory reporting requirements or common guidelines about which incidents should be reported, to whom, in what detail, and at what intervals. They said companies have therefore set their own standards on a voluntary basis, and that the Trump Administration has relied on voluntary disclosures and self-regulation by the AI industry.

In their view, that approach depends too heavily on companies choosing to disclose incidents that could expose them to liability and reputational damage. They also said Congress must act to address gaps in AI governance. The three committees share jurisdiction over the development and deployment of AI as well as potential penalties for its misuse, according to the article. The article does not say whether the companies have responded to the letters or what steps Congress will take next.

stories.Headline: Fact Sheet: President Donald J. Trump Ended the Illegal and Discriminatory Practices of Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion
stories.Summary:
The White House published a fact sheet on October 28, 2026, saying that President Donald J. Trump has removed what it calls wasteful and unmeritocratic diversity, equity, and inclusion programs from government, education, and the private sector. The document claims that on his first day back in office, Trump rescinded orders from the previous administration and signed an executive order ending DEI programs and preferences in the federal government. It describes a long series of follow-on actions across 2025 and 2026, including orders targeting federal contracting, the armed forces, the Foreign Service, the Department of Education, the Smithsonian, higher education accreditation, school discipline, and disparate-impact liability. The fact sheet lists these as the administration's work, and the articles provided do not independently confirm the claimed results.

The fact sheet describes several specific measures and settlements. It cites a $221 million settlement with Columbia University in July 2025, a $50 million settlement with Brown University that same month, and a $60 million settlement with Cornell University and a $75 million settlement with Northwestern University in November 2025. It also says the administration paused $210 million in federal funding to Princeton and launched a review of $9 billion in federal funding for Harvard University. The document further reports that the Department of Health and Human Services froze over $100 million in funding to Duke University's medical school, and that the Small Business Administration ended race-based criteria in its 8(a) Business Development Program. Each of these is presented as an action taken by the administration, with the stated reasons attached.

The fact sheet is attributed to the White House, and its content is written from the administration's point of view. It states that the actions were taken to restore merit, fairness, and equal treatment under the law, and it characterizes DEI programs as illegal, discriminatory, or ideologically driven. Several universities, companies, and agencies are described as having changed their policies in response, including the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, which closed its DEI office, and about 90 percent of the top 400 S&P 500 companies, which cut at least some references to DEI through March 2025. The provided articles do not describe responses from the institutions named, nor do they include independent assessments of the claims or outcomes.

stories.Headline: Medical AI Competition in China Highlights Potential for ASEAN Health Care Cooperation
stories.Summary:
A national medical imaging AI competition took place on October 22 and 23, 2026, in Nanning, in China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. Researchers, clinicians and technology companies used it to test tools meant to help doctors spot disease and to explore health care cooperation between China and Southeast Asian nations. The 2026 National Healthcare Security Medical Imaging AI Recognition Competition drew 1,332 registered teams, including participants from ASEAN member states. Of those, 66 team entries advanced to the finals. The event covered eight categories, including lung cancer detection on CT scans, brain tumor analysis on MRI and breast cancer screening with mammography.

The competition reflects a practical problem: imaging technology now produces far more data for radiologists to review. A chest CT scan that once generated about 100 images can now produce thousands, which makes catching small abnormalities in time harder. One participating team from Shanghai, SenseLung, has built AI tools that flag suspicious lung nodules, analyze their features and produce structured reports, and its work also reaches disease screening and patient follow-up. Detection accuracy alone is not enough, because hospitals use different equipment and scanning protocols. For that reason the judges also measured how well algorithms handled images from varied sources, a point that matters even more across ASEAN, whose countries differ widely in health systems, digital development and access to medical resources.

The contest also showed the value of teamwork between clinicians and developers. In the mammography category, a team from Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region People's Hospital and a local technology company built a model to identify breast masses and tiny calcium deposits that can signal disease. Radiologists guided the engineers on clinical needs and helped refine the model, an approach the articles suggest could support joint research across borders. The competition was open to international participants and is part of efforts to link AI research with clinical testing and commercial use. Guangxi, which borders Vietnam, already serves as a gateway for China's exchanges with ASEAN, and institutions such as the China-ASEAN Artificial Intelligence Application Cooperation Center and the Fangchenggang International Medical Opening-up Pilot Zone add platforms for cooperation.

Under plans announced by Guangxi authorities, the region aims to work with ASEAN partners on cross-border clinical validation and demonstration projects to test how imaging AI can be adapted to different health care settings. The articles note that such work involves more than transferring software, since differences in equipment, procedures, patient data, privacy rules and regulation can determine whether AI can be safely used in practice. China is also developing medical imaging cloud infrastructure to share imaging records among institutions, and Zhang Huimao, director of radiology at the First Hospital of Jilin University and president-elect of the Chinese Society of Radiology, said such infrastructure could support AI development, testing and evaluation as well as clinical care. Strong competition results do not by themselves make a tool ready for hospitals, however, since models still need validation across institutions, equipment and patient groups, along with regulatory approval where required. Guangxi has introduced a three-year action plan covering product validation, industry development, clinical testing and cooperation with ASEAN partners, and the articles say AI is meant to support rather than replace physicians.

stories.Headline: Using artificial intelligence to step up the fight against doping
stories.Summary:
Officials from the World Anti-Doping Agency and representatives from 26 countries gathered in Santorini, Greece, for the 3rd Anti-Doping Summit of Central and Eastern European Countries, where the use of artificial intelligence in the fight against doping was a central topic. The event examined new technologies that could support data analysis, improve test planning and assist investigations. Some of these tools can process large volumes of information, which could benefit many competent organisations. However, participants also recognised that the same tools could be exploited by people trying to cheat. The discussions aimed to set out how these technologies might be used responsibly and effectively.

Sébastien Gillot, director of WADA's European Office, said that artificial intelligence gives anti-doping bodies a powerful means of spotting trends and patterns that offenders may be using. He noted that the technology could help improve testing in particular. He also warned that tools helpful to investigators could equally be used by those who cheat, so the sector needs to understand how to deploy them to its advantage. Dora Hegyi, a former Hungarian gymnastics champion and vice-chair of WADA's Athletes' Council, said the talks covered how athletes could become better informed and how national bodies could work more efficiently. She added that participants also discussed the legal questions and what athletes themselves think about the use of AI.

Penny Konitsioti, a lawyer and vice-chair of the Disciplinary Committee of Greece's National Anti-Doping Organisation, said that athletes must be told at the outset when a platform's search could later be used in legal proceedings. She argued that this warning should be clearly stated in the terms of use rather than buried in small print. She also stressed that artificial intelligence should support competent authorities, such as by helping gather evidence or assisting a sports judge, but should never replace established procedures or human judgement. Participants agreed that safeguards must accompany any technological progress, including human oversight of disciplinary cases.

Transparency and the protection of personal data were strongly emphasised, since modern digital systems create new opportunities but also demand careful handling of sensitive information. Hegyi argued that trust is needed, meaning AI systems should be developed with athletes rather than only for them, if future programmes are to succeed. Transparency, data security and human oversight were identified as essential to maintaining confidence in the testing system. Participants also discussed changes to therapeutic use exemptions and results management procedures. The summit reaffirmed that the global anti-doping community aims to apply reliable, consistent procedures while fully respecting international rules and athletes' rights.

stories.Headline: With Musk and Huang at odds on AI neoclouds, can China weather the storm?
stories.Summary:
Elon Musk and Nvidia chief Jensen Huang have publicly disagreed about whether the specialist cloud providers that rent out graphics processing unit capacity, known as neoclouds, can survive their mounting debts. Musk has warned of impending collapses and consolidation among the more than 200 such ventures, while Huang remains bullish and argues that strong market demand will unlock the capital the sector needs. The South China Morning Post reported the dispute on October 28, 2026, as investor anxiety over an artificial intelligence bubble grew. The article presents the split as a sign of liquidity pressure across AI infrastructure providers worldwide, including in China.

The piece places the debate within a broader pattern of heavy spending. Tech giants and specialised data-centre developers in China are committing tens of billions of dollars to build computing capacity before clear ways of earning money from it have emerged. Analysis published the same day on eu.36kr.com examines the position of Anthropic, an AI company whose prospectus describes commitments of roughly 6.37 trillion US dollars in computing power. Anthropic's annual recurring revenue stood at about 65 billion US dollars by July, which the report says is an order of magnitude below those commitments. The report also notes that Broadcom, SpaceX, Google and Amazon each have commitments reaching hundreds of billions of US dollars.

The analysis argues that Anthropic has in effect promised much of its future revenue to these large suppliers. It describes a "take-or-pay" arrangement in which a minimum payment is owed regardless of actual use, and says Anthropic's cash and equivalents stood at 112.4 billion US dollars at the end of the first half of the year. Against that, the report says the company needs financing to cover its procurement orders. It also reports that some investors have lowered their expected IPO valuation from 2 trillion to about 1.5 trillion US dollars, because sequential revenue growth slowed to roughly 43 percent in the third quarter.

The eu.36kr.com report also points to competition from China, saying the gap between top Chinese and American AI models had narrowed to about 3 percent in October. It notes that Chinese models such as DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Kimi K3.1 Pro are priced far below Anthropic's offerings, and that Anthropic has cut prices, including about 90 percent on its smallest model. The report expects Anthropic's growth rate to slow as its base grows larger. What happens next for the neocloud sector is not settled in the articles, which leave open whether demand will close the financing gap that Musk and Huang disagree about.

The headline reports that Anthropic's S-1 filing shows an 85% gross margin in the first half, drawn from running its models, a figure reported by Stephanie Palazzolo of The Information. That result runs against the view of skeptics who argued that pay-as-you-go model sales would not be profitable. The same week, markets were already reconsidering the AI boom, with shares of the large technology companies falling and the selling spreading to chipmakers and cloud providers. The articles place the figure in that context of doubt about whether AI revenue can support heavy spending.

The source articles describe a broader market pullback rather than any new requirement or rule. The Straits Times reports that the S&P 500, weighted toward Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Nvidia, was barely above its August peak. It also says the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 14% in the month to October 23, and that CoreWeave, the largest listed specialist AI cloud provider, lost more than 38%. The same piece notes that Treasury bonds rallied despite rising inflation, which usually pushes them lower.

It adds that the spending is increasingly funded by debt and circular deals. Markets are asking whether AI revenue can justify a build-out that the article describes as costing about a trillion dollars. The article recalls that Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella warned in 2025 that the company might end up with chips sitting in inventory that it could not plug in. That warning frames the concern about spending outpacing returns.

The articles do not assign responsibility for any wrongdoing, and the filing's margin figure is presented as evidence against the skeptics. The Straits Times piece says the initial euphoria over AI has hit a speed bump after three years in which investors treated AI spending as a down payment on the future. The articles do not say what will happen next or how the market will settle. They describe the Anthropic margin as a reality check that could shift the debate, but they leave open whether that view will hold.

stories.Headline: North Carolina Must Adapt to AI
stories.Summary:
The 2026 North Carolina midterms have put artificial intelligence on the ballot, and a recent political ad in the 11th Congressional District shows why. The ad, which targets Democratic nominee Jamie Ager, was almost entirely artificially generated and depicts a barn dance with drag queens that never happened. Reporting from The Daily Tar Heel, published October 27, 2026, raised questions about who will set the rules for AI and what it will mean for the political landscape. A Wesleyan Media Project estimate cited in the reporting puts spending on AI-generated ads in this midterm cycle at at least $137 million, with 88 percent coming from Republican-affiliated sponsors.

AI shapes campaigns in less obvious ways too, including targeted advertising, AI-generated search summaries, and unreliable candidate information. At present, no state or federal rule in North Carolina requires political ads to disclose that AI was used to create them, so the burden falls on voters to tell real content from artificial content. Scott Brennen of New York University's Center on Technology Policy told the paper that political ads rarely change voters' choices, though they can be effective at mobilization. Sourojit Ghosh, founder of UNC's UNSEEN Lab, warned that algorithms choose which messages users see based on what they seem to believe, which can subtly shape opinion.

AI is also a policy question on the ballot, since the outcome will help decide rules for data center development, surveillance, and AI use in elections, education, and government. Republican U.S. Senate nominee Michael Whatley has accepted funds from groups tied to CyrusOne, which runs a data center campus in Durham, and he supports tax breaks for data centers. Democratic nominee Roy Cooper has said local residents should have the final say on data centers, even if that means backing moratoriums, and he has called for federal guardrails and oversight. President Donald Trump has argued the United States must win the AI race against China, and Brennen said Trump appears to be opposing any regulation despite growing bipartisan interest in some.

Because federal action is limited, Michael Bitzer of Catawba College said data center questions are increasingly being settled at the local level, and the Orange County Commission plans to approve a new data center policy later this year. The entire North Carolina General Assembly is also up for reelection, and it is currently controlled by Republicans, who largely back AI development and limited regulation. Pending bills include S963, which would require a Department of Justice license before distributing a health-information chatbot, and House Bill 301, which would expand social media safety rules for minors and require school districts to adopt AI policies. Bitzer said the election will be an early test of how AI is used in campaigns, and he expects it to be used heavily in future elections.

stories.Headline: Human in the loop is not yet an AI agent recovery plan
stories.Summary:
Keeping a human in the loop is a common way enterprises govern what AI agents do, but a new study suggests that approval alone does not prepare organizations to recover when things go wrong. Krista Case, principal analyst and practice lead for cyber resilience and security at theCUBE Research, discussed the findings with Dave Vellante, co-founder and chief analyst at theCUBE Research, during a broadcast tied to the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit on October 28, 2026. The research examined how organizations are governing agent actions and preparing for incidents. Case said companies are still leaning heavily on human approval to secure AI actions while pushing to move faster at machine scale. The study drew on 25 enterprise technology and security leaders, 19 of whom had agents in production.

None of those 19 allowed agents to carry out high-risk actions without human involvement. Yet only four of the 25 had tested an AI or agent incident scenario. Vellante compared the gap to organizations that test failover in disaster recovery but never test failback. Case explained that restoring an agent does not reverse the records, transactions and downstream workflows it already touched, so recovery may require rebuilding the sequence of actions the agent took.

Eleven of the 25 practitioners said they lacked full ability to reconstruct agent actions across systems. Speed makes the problem harder, according to Case, because agents can take hundreds or thousands of actions a minute. The research also found a counterintuitive pattern: organizations that let agents perform low-risk actions on their own were more likely to invest in logging, monitoring and recovery infrastructure and to have tested agent incident scenarios. Case described this bounded autonomy as a sign of a more mature security program.

Twelve of the 25 respondents had not addressed, or did not plan to address, detecting anomalous agent behavior, and monitoring and reconstructing agent activity ranked as the least mature capabilities. Vellante said these are the capabilities needed if human-in-the-loop controls break down. Case expects the field to change quickly, saying it is very volatile and will likely look far more advanced within a year. The discussion was part of SiliconANGLE and theCUBE's coverage of the summit, and Dell Technologies sponsored that segment, though neither Dell nor other sponsors have editorial control over the content.
