stories.Headline: Deutsche Telekom Invests in Tandem Health's AI Healthcare Platform
stories.Summary:
Deutsche Telekom's strategic investment arm, T.Capital, has put money into Tandem Health, a Swedish company, as part of its Series B funding round. Tandem Health has built an AI-powered medical assistant that handles clinical documentation, coding and decision support on one platform. The system is already used at more than 10,000 healthcare facilities in 14 European countries, including Germany, and it is integrated into around 130 electronic health record systems. It holds a Class IIa medical device certification under the EU Medical Device Regulation. A second report puts the round at roughly $100 million (€90 million) and notes that the funding came last month.

The investment is meant to support Tandem Health's push toward an AI-native operating system for European healthcare providers. Beyond its current tools for documentation, coding and clinical decision support, the company is building applications for patient navigation, appointment management and administrative work. Deutsche Telekom presents the deal as part of its wider strategy to back artificial intelligence, digital platforms and sovereign cloud infrastructure in highly regulated industries. Staffing shortages and growing paperwork are putting heavy strain on European hospitals, and the companies argue that automating administrative tasks can help. Other backers of the round include the EU's Scaleup Europe Fund, managed by EQT, and LG Technology Ventures, alongside existing investors Kinnevik, Northzone, Amino Collective and Visionaries.

Lukas Saari, co-founder and CEO of Tandem Health, says the company wants to give Europe's healthcare professionals back one billion hours so that staff can spend less time on paperwork and more time with patients. Karine Peters, Managing Director at T.Capital, says AI will play a key role in addressing healthcare's challenges and that the firm sees Tandem Health as a fast-growing company that cuts administrative burden while meeting high standards for quality, safety and compliance. Gottfried Ludewig, Senior Vice President of the Health Industry and Head of Public Sector at T-Systems, says healthcare needs trustworthy, secure AI that can be deployed right away and that the partnership aims to speed up adoption of new care technologies. Saari has also said that Telekom, through T-Systems, which already works with hospitals across Germany, is the kind of European partner needed to help more professionals safely enter the AI era.

stories.Headline: AI is part of solution for climate change, COP31 pledge says
stories.Summary:
Turkey, which hosts this year's UN COP31 climate summit, has launched a voluntary pledge saying artificial intelligence can help tackle global warming even as data centers add to fossil-fuel pollution. The Antalya AI Pledge will be unveiled at the summit, which starts later this month in the coastal city of Antalya. It recognizes that AI carries environmental risks but could also be used to fight climate change. It is not yet clear which countries will sign up, and the United States, the biggest developer of data centers, is no longer part of the COP process. The pledge asks countries, NGOs and financial institutions to identify voluntary commitments, such as requiring AI providers to disclose their energy and environmental impact data.

It also calls for data centers to run on clean power sources and floats possible targets. Nations would return to next year's summit in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, to review progress. Data centers are emerging as a major new source of greenhouse gas emissions, particularly in the U.S., where big tech companies are building new gas-fired power stations to supply them. Their share of global energy use is expected to more than double by 2030, according to BloombergNEF.

Evan Tachovsky, chief data and AI officer at the World Resources Institute, a climate nonprofit, said the pledge sets the right direction but lacks accountability mechanisms to steer countries and tech companies toward better practice. The institute's statement adds that the pledge leaves out commitments to involve communities in data center decisions and safeguards for water and air quality. It urges strong guardrails, including clean power, full disclosure of energy and water use, and companies paying for their own grid upgrades. Simon Stiell, executive secretary of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, said last month that AI was energy guzzling and driving up fossil-fuel pollution.

European Union Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said the bloc was examining whether to sign up. The context is a series of UN warnings that the world is on course to overshoot the Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming to 1.5 Celsius above pre-industrial levels, which requires sharp emissions cuts this decade. The institute says the pledge's first stocktake at COP32 offers a chance to move from soft intentions to real accountability. Whether countries sign on, and whether the pledge gains enforceable targets, remains to be seen.

stories.Headline: Meta survey finds most Asia-Pacific small firms use AI
stories.Summary:
Meta has published research showing that most small business owners across Asia-Pacific already use artificial intelligence. The YouGov survey, covering almost 4,000 small business owners in Australia, Singapore, Vietnam, Indonesia, Taiwan, India, Thailand, Japan and Hong Kong, found that 84% use AI. Of those surveyed, 76% said it had a positive effect on productivity, and 71% said it had improved revenue or sales over the past 12 months. The findings, reported on 28 October 2026, point to wide uptake among smaller companies in the region.

The research also shows a gap between using AI and feeling confident about it. Eighty-six percent of owners said small businesses need more guidance to get the full benefits, and 51% named the cost of training as the main barrier. Respondents tied AI to the constraints smaller firms often face, with four in five saying it helps them compete with larger companies and the same share saying it makes starting a business easier. Another 83% said it lets small firms do things that once required much more money or resources. Among owners reporting higher productivity, 58% used the saved time to improve the quality of their existing work, half put it toward growth and planning, and 46% said it helped their current teams get more done.

Meta's survey says that day-to-day use remains centred on routine tasks. Among owners whose businesses used AI in the past year, 51% used it to create or edit content, 43% for local advertising and marketing, 38% for translation, and 37% for customer support and communications. Owners also said they want clearer information on costs, likely returns, and how to handle data privacy and security. Meta cited Husnul Khotimah, founder of the Indonesian modest fashion brand Zayya, as an example. She said she used Meta's Small Business Growth Academy and its advertising tools to expand into Malaysia on a daily budget of about USD $1.68, which Meta said generated 50 enquiries, cut response times from 30 to 60 minutes to under two minutes, and returned more than eight times the ad spend.

Meta is using the findings to promote demand for training. Its Small Business Growth Academy, launched across Asia-Pacific, offers courses on AI-enabled advertising, Reels, WhatsApp for Business and cross-border commerce, delivered through partnerships with governments, chambers of commerce and local programme groups. The report notes that technology companies are keen to present AI as a routine part of how smaller firms operate, not just a tool for large organisations with dedicated digital teams. The article concludes that AI is already part of many owners' everyday work, particularly in marketing and content, and that the harder question is whether businesses can move from basic use to more informed use without costs they cannot easily absorb.

stories.Headline: Google to report Q3 results as investors focus on AI growth, weigh Meta Muse AI risk
stories.Summary:
Alphabet's Google is scheduled to report its third-quarter earnings after the market closes on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, and Wall Street is bracing for detailed information about how its artificial intelligence business is performing. Investors have swung between worry and enthusiasm about whether the huge spending by large technology companies on AI will eventually pay off. That mood intensified last week, when shares of CoreWeave fell sharply over concerns about its heavy debt, pulling large parts of the market lower. The story is therefore less about any single company than about whether the AI trade can keep its momentum.

Analysts expect Google to post earnings of $3.01 per share on revenue of $127.8 billion, with revenue excluding traffic acquisition costs near $111.2 billion. Its advertising segment is projected to bring in about $83.5 billion, while its cloud unit could see revenue rise 91% to $28.9 billion. Google could also earn significant sums from selling its custom Tensor Processing Units to outside data centers, and Oracle said on Tuesday that it would be the first company to buy Google's AI processors for its own facilities. TD Cowen's John Blackledge estimates Google will generate $9.4 billion in TPU sales in the second half of 2026, a figure he expects to climb to $62.5 billion in 2027 and $138 billion in 2028. Google stock rose about 1% in premarket trading ahead of the release.

BofA Global Research analyst Justin Post has said near-term upside could come from TPU sales, a competitive agentic offering, and a broader launch of Gemini 4. The article also points to a rival threat from Meta, whose new Muse AI agent Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg says has been set up by 10 million people, mostly to shop. Post has said that if Muse grows its user base and gains ground in online sales, it could become a long-term threat to Google, particularly as Google works to move users to agentic search while keeping its monetization strong. Search usage and growth have therefore become a central focus for investors. The article notes that Meta's own third-quarter earnings will also test Wall Street's tolerance for AI spending.

stories.Headline: Opera launches local browser AI, testing enterprise privacy and AI PC strategies
stories.Summary:
Opera has begun rolling out AI models that run locally in its browser, and it introduced WebAI, a proposed web standard, as an opt-in early preview in its Opera One browser on October 27, 2026. The technology lets websites and browser extensions reach AI models running on the user's own device for tasks such as generating text and classifying content. The preview works on 64-bit Windows PCs with Intel or AMD processors and on Macs with Apple silicon, but not yet on Windows on Arm. Opera says the feature is optional, that models download only after users enable it, and that site-specific permissions control which websites can access them. Opera also says its implementation supports models including Google's Gemma and, on compatible Macs, Apple's on-device foundation model.

The company says the approach lets developers add AI features without running their own AI infrastructure or paying for every request, and it argues that users keep their data on their own device without needing an AI subscription. Opera has said Opera GX and Opera Neon will get the same capability soon, and it plans to add models optimized for different hardware over time. Local processing puts more demand on the computer, so performance depends on the device's hardware, and Opera does not specify a need for a dedicated neural processing unit. Analysts quoted by Computerworld see the change as a possible way to reduce enterprise privacy risk, although the benefit depends on how organizations control access to locally running models.

Pareekh Jain, CEO of Pareekh Consulting, said that processing sensitive information locally could reduce the need to send data to outside AI providers. He warned, however, that it can be harder for IT departments to monitor activity on individual laptops than network traffic. Jain also said malicious websites could try to manipulate local models through hidden prompts, and that rogue browser extensions could reach sensitive information shown on screen. Tulika Sheel, senior vice president at Kadence International, said enterprises would still need controls over which websites and extensions can use local models and how those models and permissions are managed. She also said lower usage costs do not automatically mean lower total costs, since model updates and system integration still carry expenses.

Jain said smaller models could handle tasks such as summarization and rewriting on existing PCs, which could delay some hardware upgrades, while complex workloads will still need dedicated hardware or cloud services. He expects a hybrid future in which browser AI handles simpler tasks and cloud AI supports advanced ones. Opera's move comes as privacy concerns grow about the personal data users hand to AI chatbots, and Opera has made digital privacy a central selling point for years. The articles do not say when WebAI might become a broader standard or how widely enterprises will adopt it.

stories.Headline: AI-generated models spark job fears and image rights battle in fashion world
stories.Summary:
AI-generated models are raising alarm across the fashion industry after a Reuters investigation found that brands are seeking broad rights over models' images. Reuters interviewed 15 modelling agency directors and reviewed more than a dozen confidential contracts from brands including Diesel, Calvin Klein and L'Oreal. The draft terms asked for permission to swap model faces using AI, to create digital clones without extra pay, and to use body images to train AI tools. Many of the agreements also contained broad legal wording that would give brands wide discretion over how the technology is used.

The shift matters because AI can cut production costs by more than 90 per cent compared with traditional photo shoots. Agencies report falling bookings and some studios have closed, with e-commerce work for fast-fashion platforms, a key source of income for models, under particular pressure. London-based model Adot Gak warned that the industry could soon be dominated by bots if models do not speak up. Fast-fashion brands such as Mango have already adopted computer-generated models at scale, while luxury houses have moved more cautiously. Moncler said it does not currently use AI-generated models on its website or in promotional material.

Several companies responded to the findings, though not all gave the same account. Diesel's parent company, OTB, said the casting sheet was drafted for one campaign and does not reflect its standard contracts. Calvin Klein said it is testing and learning in a fast-moving space and that its use of AI follows regulations and respects the rights of its models. L'Oreal did not comment directly on the clause about altering product appearance but said it uses standard AI tools in post-production that leave model likenesses unaffected. Reale Actives said it hires real talent and blamed the contract language on a third-party production partner.

Legal protections remain uneven, and the New York State Fashion Workers Act is described as a notable exception. From June 2025, that law bars companies from generating or modifying model replicas without explicit consent. Sara Ziff of the Model Alliance is pushing for similar protections in other US states and at the federal level. In Britain, the British Fashion Model Agents Association has issued an AI code of practice requiring explicit consent, but its head, John Horner, warned that without binding rules, models remain exposed. Industry voices say young models may not grasp how long signed AI rights could affect their careers.

stories.Headline: Google AI Privacy: How Personal Data Fuels Ads
stories.Summary:
Google's privacy policy, which took effect on October 16, 2026, now allows personal content from Gmail, Google Photos, and Google Drive to help shape personalized ads when users connect those apps to other Google services. The change sits alongside a new feature called Personal Intelligence, which lets AI Mode in Search and Gemini draw on a user's messages, inbox, and photos to answer questions. Android Authority first noticed the exception, and other outlets followed. Google's earlier policy had said it did not show personalized ads based on content from those services, and that statement remains, but it now carries an exception for users who opt in to share the data with other services.

The policy exception matters because Google's help documentation says that summaries, excerpts, generated media, and inferences drawn from connected emails and files may be used, and that the same inferences and summaries may be used to show advertisements. Google says the raw messages stay where they are, and that Gemini Apps chats are not currently used for ads, with users to be told if that changes. Turning off personalized ads in My Ad Center may not stop connected-app data from being processed for AI personalization, and disconnecting an app does not delete data already retained. Some connected data may also be read by human reviewers and used for product improvement, including AI training. Google's advertising business produced $82.3 billion in the fourth quarter of 2025, about 72 per cent of Alphabet's revenue for that period.

Google's public statements say the company does not sell users' information, and that advertisers do not get access to Gmail or Photos. The company's advertising policy also says it does not personalize ads around health, race, religion, or sexual orientation. Google has described the Personal Intelligence feature as opt-in, and its help pages present the connected-content features as separate from other Google AI services. Critics of the arrangement argue that a single consent click covers two different uses, and that the explanation sits in a policy most people never read. In 2017, Google stopped scanning consumer Gmail to personalize ads after years of criticism.

India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, requires consent to be free, specific, informed, and unconditional, and limited to the purpose stated. Parts of the Act are already in force, but the main obligations are scheduled to take effect on May 13, 2027, and the consent manager provisions on November 13, 2026. The Act places on the company the burden of proving valid consent for a new use of data, and it is for the Data Protection Board to decide whether one click can cover advertising. Ads in AI Mode for users with Personal Intelligence turned on are now being tested, and Google has said it expected ads to work this way for connected users later.

stories.Headline: Liquid AI Releases LFM3: 6 Open-Weight 2B-Class Multimodal Models
stories.Summary:
Liquid AI has released LFM3, a new generation of its Liquid Foundation Models, consisting of six open-weight models in the 2-billion-parameter class that share one backbone. The family covers text, vision, audio, omni, and decision tasks, and Liquid AI says every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU and then deployed on phones, laptops, private servers, or in the cloud. The two articles report the release on October 27, 2026, with the Hugging Face post presenting it as the starting point for specialized models. Both are written around the same family of models.

The family includes LFM3-1.7B, a text model with 1.73 billion parameters and a 256K context window that can run in about 1 GB of memory at 4-bit precision. LFM3-VL-2B is the first LFM vision model to accept video input, sampled at 2 frames per second, and LFM3-Audio-2B handles speech in and out across 18 languages with tool calling. LFM3-Omni-2B combines vision, audio, and language, and two decision models, d1-2B and d1-Omni-2B, answer many questions in one forward pass. According to Liquid AI's own evaluation, LFM3-1.7B averages 49.37 across 29 benchmarks, ahead of Qwen3.5-9B at 47.24, with strong results on IFEval and AutomationBench but weaker ones on Humanity's Last Exam without tools and RULER at 128K. Checkpoints in GGUF, MLX, ONNX, FP8, and NVFP4 formats ship with the release.

The architecture uses a tri-hybrid layer mix across 24 layers, made up of 13 gated short convolutions, 5 sliding-window attention layers with a 256-token window, and 6 global attention layers, with convolution kernels grown from 3 to 7. Liquid AI says it found this design through a hardware-in-the-loop architecture search covering 14 device and backend combinations, including a Raspberry Pi 5 and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU. Other changes include head-wise sigmoid gates, partial RoPE on global layers, and sandwich norm. The base model was trained on 22 trillion tokens, with the final 3.5 trillion focused on agent-heavy mid-training that extended context to 256K, and post-training ran in four stages.

Liquid AI reports that LFM3-1.7B beats its own LFM2.5-2.6B with 35% fewer parameters, and that it scores 38.42 on WebArena-Verified against 28.94 for Qwen3.5-9B. Its comparison table lists the LFM Open License v1.0, which carries a $10 million revenue threshold, while several rivals use Apache 2.0. The Hugging Face post, written by members of the Liquid AI team, presents LFM3 as a basis for fine-tuning on private data and deployment at the edge. Neither article describes further releases or timelines beyond the current family.

stories.Headline: DIDWW Partners with IdentityCall to Enhance AI Call Analytics
stories.Summary:
On October 28, 2026, DIDWW, a licensed global telecom operator connecting human and AI communications across more than 90 countries, announced a partnership with TechAI Solutions, a software provider building AI-powered business tools. The deal combines DIDWW's voice services with IdentityCall, TechAI Solutions' AI call analytics and quality management product. The announcement was published by GlobeNewswire from Dublin and carried by several outlets that day. Both companies framed the partnership as a way to make sure AI-analyzed phone calls connect reliably.

IdentityCall lets managers review every submitted call rather than the small sample most companies check. The tool transcribes, summarizes and categorizes calls, pulls out agreed actions, and scores each one against a company's own criteria. Its analysis looks at the content of a conversation instead of only keywords, and it can deliver results in a different language from the call itself. The product serves sales, support, dispatch and HR teams and is expanding into the Netherlands and the UK.

DIDWW's role is to carry the calls over its own geo-redundant network, with local numbers and SIP trunks that teams can connect to AI tools such as ElevenLabs, Retell, Vapi, LiveKit and IdentityCall. TechAI Solutions' CEO, Rima Vaskiene, said the company built IdentityCall so that no valuable insight from a customer call is lost, and she said DIDWW's local numbers suit clients who are growing into new markets because the call quality underpins the analysis. DIDWW's CEO, Karolis Jurys, said businesses are adding AI to every stage of the phone call and that DIDWW built its voice infrastructure for both people and AI so calls connect reliably in any market customers want to reach. He said the company was glad to support TechAI Solutions as it expands into the Netherlands, the UK and beyond.

The releases did not give financial terms or a timeline beyond those expansion plans. The announcement fits a broader push in which businesses use AI to answer, route and review customer conversations, and both firms describe their products as tools for that work. TechAI Solutions said it begins with a specific business problem and aims to make AI part of everyday work, and it pointed to earlier work with Laista and Wise Monks. The articles do not report customer results, pricing or any independent assessment of how the two products perform together.

stories.Headline: OpenAI now lets you text your Dot.
stories.Summary:
OpenAI has begun rolling out a feature that lets users text their Dot, its AI agent, through iMessage or RCS. The company said the feature is arriving in preview for US Pro users, after it had promised the capability for its AI agents. The Verge reported the news on October 28, 2026, noting that the feature is now available. The article itself is short and focused on the launch rather than on details about pricing or wider availability.

Separately, a Vocal Media piece published on October 28, 2026 reported that OpenAI is introducing an invisible watermark for text generated by ChatGPT and Codex. The system, called textGrain, slightly shifts word choices to embed a statistical pattern that is undetectable to readers but can be identified by a detector. It is set to apply by default only to users in the European Union, so a user in Munich would generate watermarked text while a user in Malaysia would not, unless a developer opts in through the API. The watermark does not identify the individual user, and it survives basic copying and pasting.

OpenAI itself acknowledged that the watermark is fragile, according to the article. In internal testing, replacing 10% of words in a 400-token passage with synonyms dropped detection accuracy from 92% to 66%, and swapping 25% of words reduced it to 17%. Detection is also weaker on short passages, math answers, and translated text, and OpenAI is limiting access to the detector to approved researchers and expert organizations for now. The company cautioned that a missing watermark does not prove human authorship, and a present watermark does not show how much human editing shaped the output.

The article places the move within a wider industry effort to establish AI provenance ahead of regulatory deadlines, including the EU AI Act's transparency rules that took effect on August 2. Google uses its SynthID watermark, Meta uses Content Seal, and Microsoft and Adobe back the C2PA standard, while Anthropic announced in August that it would watermark Claude text worldwide and faced user backlash. The article notes that open-source models can generate unwatermarked text and that each company's detector typically recognizes only its own mark. It concludes that text watermarking remains a probabilistic tool rather than definitive proof of authorship.

stories.Headline: States Don’t Have to Solve the AI Education Equation Alone. Tennessee Shows How
stories.Summary:
States across the country are taking different approaches to AI policy, with governors forming task forces, state education agencies issuing non-binding guidance, and legislatures requiring districts to adopt AI policies. A November 2025 survey found that 93% of 29 state education agency respondents had communicated or planned to communicate a vision for AI in K-12 education, but only 43% had assisted or planned to assist districts with implementation support. Among the 39 states and territories studied for a state early adopter database, just 11% had reached the "integrator" stage of moving past guidance into pilots, evaluation, procurement help, and implementation strategies. The authors, Bree Dusseault and Dana Harrison of the Center on Reinventing Public Education, argue that this gap leaves schools without the practical help they need. The authors say AI is a difficult policy area because both the technology and public opinion change quickly, so guidance and task forces alone fall short.

School and district leaders need state help with vetting products, generating evidence on what works, and building trust in how AI is used. States also need infrastructure that links policy to classroom practice and turns scattered local experiments into shared knowledge. The article notes that many state education agencies lack the funding or internal expertise to lead these efforts. Intermediary organizations, the authors write, can fill that role, and a majority of participants in their study reported pursuing partnerships for strategy development, implementation, or both.

The article uses Tennessee's State Collaborative on Reforming Education, known as SCORE, as its main example. SCORE is a statewide nonprofit without formal authority over district decisions, and its influence comes from long-standing relationships with state leaders, districts, colleges, funders, and technology providers. After Tennessee required districts to adopt AI policies covering safety, academic integrity, and risk mitigation, SCORE convened a working group that met regularly for roughly 18 months, and its recommendations were reflected in the state's Action Plan. SCORE also helps districts evaluate tools without endorsing products, and it helped fund a larger rollout of Coursemojo, an AI-enabled literacy tool, across seven districts, 20 schools, and more than 4,000 students in 2025-26.

The authors say participating leaders and teachers reported positive results, and districts later renewed the work, often with their own funds. The authors stress that the Tennessee model need not be copied exactly, since an intermediary could be a nonprofit, a university, a technical service provider, or a research group, as long as it has trust, staying power, and the ability to connect people who do not normally work together. They warn that without such coordinated support, better-resourced districts may experiment while smaller and higher-need systems struggle to evaluate tools, set safeguards, and provide training, which could widen existing inequities. They conclude that the next phase of state AI leadership will depend less on publishing guidance than on building infrastructure for continuous learning, so that policies set direction and partnerships provide the capacity to follow it.

stories.Headline: SAP, NTT to Advance Sovereign Cloud and Business AI Capabilities
stories.Summary:
SAP SE and NTT announced on October 28, 2026 that they intend to cooperate on SAP Sovereign Cloud and SAP Business AI, with the initial focus on combining SAP Sovereign Cloud On-Site with NTT-managed infrastructure and operations in key markets. The planned collaboration would join SAP's enterprise applications and AI capabilities with NTT's global infrastructure, integrated operations, industry AI expertise and customer reach. The stated goal is to let customers adopt cloud and AI while keeping control of sensitive data, operations, technology and security. The companies describe the effort as a way to advance secure, resilient and sovereign digital transformation for regulated industries.

The offering centers on SAP Sovereign Cloud On-Site, a deployment option for customers with strict sovereignty, regulatory and compliance demands. It allows SAP-managed cloud solutions to run in a data center that the customer owns or selects. According to the announcement, this gives organizations strong local physical control, data residency and operational assurance while helping them meet applicable local legal and regulatory rules. NTT would contribute its experience in advising, designing, delivering and operating secure infrastructure. The capabilities are aimed at governments, defense organizations, defense industry companies, critical infrastructure operators and other regulated enterprises that need to modernize critical processes without giving up control.

SAP and NTT presented the collaboration as a first step toward wider work with governments, critical infrastructure operators and highly regulated industries. They intend to explore how to modernize mission-critical processes and adopt AI in a manner that is secure, responsible and sovereign. Dominik Asam, member of the Executive Board and Chief Financial Officer of SAP SE, said the cooperation aims to give customers a practical path to cloud and AI innovation while preserving the control, governance and trust they require. He added that for public sector and regulated organizations, sovereignty is a basis for resilience, competitiveness and responsible AI adoption, not merely a compliance matter.

Yutaka Sasaki, Representative Member of the Board, Senior Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of NTT, said customers want practical ways to use AI for real business problems. He said that pairing SAP's business applications and AI with NTT's understanding of industry needs and mission-critical operations is intended to help organizations change how they work, make better decisions and speed business results. The announcement was issued from Tokyo, and the companies said the press release was prepared with the help of artificial intelligence and reviewed by the editorial team. The articles do not give a timeline for launch or the specific markets involved beyond saying "key markets."

stories.Headline: [PRNewswire] Guidewire Delivers Core Platform for Agentic Insurance
stories.Summary:
Guidewire, the insurance software company listed on the NYSE as GWRE, launched a new platform approach to agentic insurance on October 28, 2026, at its Connections conference in Las Vegas. The company says the platform gives insurers an open, secure, and complete foundation for using AI across the insurance lifecycle. It brings together applications, data, workflows, and controls so that insurers can move from isolated AI experiments to governed agents that improve the speed and precision of decisions. Guidewire presents this as a practical model for doing so.

The platform places agents on the same system that runs the company's core applications, so they can work with an insurer's current data and workflows. Controls define what each agent can know and do, with consistent security and an audit trail that stays current through ongoing updates. Guidewire describes its growing portfolio across underwriting, claims, and technical infrastructure, including Advanced Product Designer, PricingCenter, Risk Accumulation App, UnderwritingCenter, ProNavigator, Concierge, and Kaleidoscope. Several features, marked as early access or roadmap items, are available only to certain customers, and the company notes that some release features may not be available in all regions.

Mike Rosenbaum, Guidewire's chief executive officer, said that insurance is a business of decisions made in context and that embedding agents in core operations gives them the context and controls they need. Diego Devalle, the company's chief product development officer, said the scalability and observability that support the core now support agents as well, which lets insurers put them to work on live claims and policies. Amy Mollin, vice president of product management, said agents built into ClaimCenter capture losses, summarize files, and flag risk so adjusters have more time for important conversations. Karlyn Carnahan of Celent said the next challenge for insurers is making these capabilities work within existing systems. Tatjana Lalkovic, chief technology officer at Definity, said Guidewire's Developer Assistants help her company's teams move from idea to implementation faster.

The announcement comes as insurers face pressure from competitors to become more agile with products and pricing, and as many have moved past early AI experiments. Guidewire says it is also using AI in its own professional services, where it reports materially shorter migration and implementation timelines. The company is demonstrating the platform at Connections, where more than 3,000 insurers and partners from 36 countries are gathered for its annual customer conference. Guidewire will continue to expand its portfolio of agents, though the announcement itself does not specify a timeline for further releases.

stories.Headline: Oracle Cloud to Offer Google TPUs and New AI Chips
stories.Summary:
Oracle announced on October 27, 2026, at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas that it will broaden the AI chips available through Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI). The company said it plans to deploy Google's Tensor Processing Units, and it described itself as the first hyperscaler to offer TPUs outside Google Cloud. The move also includes inference chips from OpenAI, Cerebras, SambaNova, and Positron AI, and it came alongside an expanded partnership with Nvidia. Together these additions give OCI customers more choice beyond the Nvidia GPUs that the cloud has relied on most heavily.

Oracle said Google TPUs for training and inference will become available on OCI in 2027, with adoption ramping over several years. It also plans to deploy the Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine for fast AI inference in 2027, and Positron AI's Positron Atlas inference chip is already generally available on OCI. Oracle said it will deploy OpenAI's Jalapeño inference accelerators, built with Broadcom, though it did not give a date, while OpenAI and Broadcom had expected initial deployment by the end of 2026. SambaNova said it is working with Oracle to bring its SN50 inference chip to OCI, without naming an availability date. On the Nvidia side, Oracle said the Vera Rubin NVL72 systems and Vera CPUs are now generally available and that it plans to scale OCI Superclusters to multi-gigawatt levels with them.

Analysts quoted in the coverage said the expansion reflects an industry shift toward heterogeneous computing, in which different chips suit different workloads. Brendan Burke of Futurum Group said Oracle must prove the new accelerators are competitive with Nvidia-based offerings and show a long-term commitment to them. Matt Kimball of Moor Insights & Strategy described Oracle's aim as becoming an open silicon cloud. Google's decision to make TPUs available on OCI appears tied to the value of the chips and to strong demand for AI compute, with Burke suggesting there is more value in offering capacity externally than keeping it all for internal teams. Kimball said the arrangement lets customers use TPUs without moving their data to Google Cloud, which matters because much enterprise data already sits in Oracle databases.

Google's own announcement at the same event describes related work to connect Oracle AI Database@Google Cloud with its data and AI tools. It said a Remote MCP Server with a governed ExecuteSQL Data API is now generally available, letting AI agents securely run SQL against Oracle databases without custom middleware. A Knowledge Catalog integration and a Gemini connector for Oracle data are in preview, allowing users to query Oracle data in natural language within the Gemini app while respecting access permissions. The coverage presents these as steps toward agentic workflows built on existing enterprise data, and the articles do not say what comes next beyond the stated availability timelines.

stories.Headline: AI and the quiet erosion of human judgment
stories.Summary:
Winnipeg Free Press columnist Rod Lastra, in an opinion piece posted on October 28, 2026, argues that the quiet loss of human judgment is a more pressing concern than the predictions surrounding artificial intelligence. He opens by recalling Paul Simon's 1986 song The Boy in the Bubble, using its image of a world more technologically capable but not necessarily wiser as a frame for the present. Lastra notes that predictions about AI have multiplied since ChatGPT's release in November 2022, and that tech leaders have talked up approaching superintelligence and futures ranging from flourishing to catastrophe. He says these predictions often carry more confidence than evidence.

The column's central concern is whether people can still understand, question and oversee AI outputs as systems grow more capable and take on more complex work. Lastra explains that AI is not a single technology, that fluency does not guarantee accuracy, and that agentic systems can carry out sequences of actions on people's behalf. He describes a paradox in which delegating work to gain efficiency can produce so much output that meaningful human review becomes difficult. He also points to Manitoba's Bill 51, the Public Sector Artificial Intelligence and Cybersecurity Governance Act, which recognizes human oversight as part of responsible AI governance, while asking whether that capacity could be lost anyway. Signing off on a result, he writes, is not the same as understanding it.

Lastra's thought experiment describes an organization in which one AI analyzes thousands of records, a second summarizes the findings, and a manager approves the recommendation, leaving the question of what was actually reviewed. He warns of oversight fatigue, in which approval becomes routine once recommendations arrive faster than people can examine them, and he cites automated financial trading as an earlier example of transactions outpacing human intervention. The more work is delegated, he argues, the fewer chances people have to practise the judgment needed to supervise it, so dependence can reinforce itself. He says the aim is not to reject AI but to adopt it deliberately, defining its purpose, testing it under real conditions, keeping the ability to intervene and allowing time for review. He adds that AI literacy must mean more than writing prompts.

A separate opinion piece on UPI.com, published October 27, 2026 by Carlos Cantero Ojeda, raises a parallel concern for Latin America. It notes that the fourth Latin American Artificial Intelligence Index, released October 20, 2026 by Chile's National Center for Artificial Intelligence and the U.N. Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean, ranks 20 countries, with Chile first, followed by Brazil and Uruguay. Cantero Ojeda argues that technological readiness differs from human agency, which he describes as the capacity to act intentionally, reflect on choices and accept responsibility for them. He draws on the work of Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela to argue that AI systems are designed and sustained from outside themselves, so they cannot carry the ethical judgment and moral responsibility that people bear. He describes the weakening of attention and deliberation as "agency starvation," which he attributes partly to platform designs that narrow what people see and make reasoning harder to follow.

stories.Headline: Korea should not sacrifice AI boom over chip dependence fears: IDB economist
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday, October 27, 2026, Laura Alfaro, chief economist and economic counselor at the Inter-American Development Bank, told a press conference in Seoul that Korea should keep pursuing the artificial intelligence boom rather than slow growth out of worry about its heavy reliance on semiconductors. She made the remarks at the Global Financial Stability Conference 2026, hosted by the Ministry of Finance and Economy and the Korea Development Institute. Her position was that the country should instead cushion itself against swings through stabilization funds and greater structural flexibility. The comments were reported by the Korea Times and the JoongAng Daily, the latter with a wire contribution from Yonhap.

Alfaro compared Korea's exposure to chips with the "resource curse" that has affected Latin America, where economies dependent on minerals and oil suffer when commodity prices fluctuate sharply. To manage such cycles, she recommended a stabilization fund that would set aside part of the gains made during boom periods and draw on them during downturns. Such a fund could also limit excessive appreciation of the domestic currency and soften the effects of large, rapid capital inflows. She also called for more flexibility in labor markets and government spending, saying the core problem in boom-and-bust cycles is an inability to adjust in downturns. The JoongAng Daily reported that Korea has proposed a Future Fund, drawing on sources including windfall tax revenue from chipmakers, with a general account and four program accounts covering youth, growth engines, regional development, and education and talent development.

Alfaro said she was not familiar with the details of the government's proposed Future Response Fund but supported its underlying rationale, and the JoongAng Daily quoted her as saying the "spirit" of the Future Fund sounds like what needs to be done. Asked whether debt repayment should take priority over building assets, she said neither approach was necessarily superior, since both amount to saving. She also described herself as "AI positive" and argued that concern over volatility should not deter investment in the technology, since productivity gains from AI offer a route to growth in a region facing shrinking birth rates. Separately, she said Latin America's green energy and mineral resources, such as copper, could support mutually beneficial exchange with Korea in AI, given how energy-intensive the technology is. The reports do not indicate any formal government response to these remarks or what steps will follow.

stories.Headline: Asia stocks rally as SK Hynix earnings boost AI trade; Fed decision ahead
stories.Summary:
Asian stock markets rallied on Wednesday, led by South Korea after chipmaker SK Hynix reported a sharp jump in quarterly profit that fed optimism about demand for artificial intelligence. South Korea's KOSPI ended 6.6% higher, reaching its highest level in two weeks. SK Hynix shares closed nearly 11% higher after the company reported a 631% rise in third-quarter operating profit, supported by strong demand for memory chips used in AI applications. The company also announced an additional 60 trillion won in shareholder returns, which added to investor enthusiasm. Samsung Electronics, another major memory chip supplier, rose 9%.

The gains followed an advance on Wall Street overnight, where technology shares led the market higher. Japan's Nikkei 225 rose 1.5%, with chipmakers leading, as Kioxia Holdings jumped 13.8% and Taiyo Yuden gained more than 7%. China's Shanghai Composite and CSI 300 each rose 0.9%, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng edged up 0.2%. Elsewhere, moves were subdued as investors waited for the U.S. Federal Reserve's policy announcement later in the day, with interest rates widely expected to stay unchanged. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 finished largely flat, and India's Nifty 50 fell 0.4%.

Investors were also focused on quarterly results from Alphabet and Microsoft, due after the U.S. market close, for evidence that heavy spending on AI infrastructure is producing lasting revenue growth. The rally in AI-related shares has been reinforced by a series of funding announcements and by Anthropic's filing for an initial public offering. Earlier concerns about the cost of building data centres and the long-term sustainability of AI investment had weighed on sentiment. Markets will also look for guidance from Fed policymakers on the outlook for borrowing costs, since persistent inflation and elevated oil prices complicate the picture.

Oil prices also rose, with Brent crude trading above $115 a barrel, which adds to concerns that energy costs could keep inflation under pressure and limit central banks' room to cut rates. Australian data showed underlying inflation accelerating more than expected in the third quarter, strengthening the case for a Reserve Bank of Australia rate hike next week. New Zealand's central bank unexpectedly kept rates unchanged, and New Zealand's NZX 50 edged 0.1% higher. In India, Jio Platforms shares surged more than 20% in their Mumbai market debut after the country's largest-ever initial public offering.

stories.Headline: Azerbaijan to establish Artificial Intelligence Observatory
stories.Summary:
On 27 October 2026, the Ministry of Economy of Azerbaijan and IE University of Spain signed a framework cooperation agreement to establish and develop an Artificial Intelligence Observatory focused on competitiveness and economic transformation. Deputy Minister of Economy Samad Bashirli announced the deal at the opening ceremony of IE University's Leadership and Innovation Center, which was set up with the backing of the Ministries of Economy and Science and Education. One report describes the agreement as part of the AI Hub initiative, and names the university partner as the University of Artificial Intelligence, which differs from the IE University named in the other report. The announcement came the same day as the ceremony, and the reports were published that afternoon and evening.

The observatory is meant to bring together academics, government bodies and business representatives to produce knowledge on Azerbaijan's economic development and to inform policy decisions. Its work will centre on applied research into economic diversification, productivity, competitiveness and international comparisons. The reports say the goal is to turn research findings into practical policy recommendations, and one adds that discussions will be held to support this. The articles do not give a budget, a timetable, staffing numbers or a launch date for the observatory.

Bashirli said the centre would help build human capital, strengthen the country's economic competitiveness and raise its innovation potential. He stated that the aim is to link international knowledge with national economic priorities and to turn investment in people into higher productivity and concrete economic results. He also said that Azerbaijani startups and entrepreneurs would be connected with international innovation networks, investors and experts, and that startups, investors, and technology park residents and operators would be able to benefit from tax incentives lasting up to 20 years, along with incentives for research and development, entrepreneurship investment and hiring international specialists. One report includes a letter from Mikayil Jabbarov that stresses developing human capital and modern technology as priorities.

The reports attribute the announcement to the government, with Bashirli speaking on its behalf, and the framework agreement is between the ministry and the university. The articles offer no comment from other parties or critics. They place the observatory within the country's wider push to diversify its economy and build innovation, and they note the support mechanisms already in place for startups. Beyond the stated plan to carry out the research and hold discussions, the articles do not say what will happen next.

stories.Headline: Nvidia vs TSMC: Here’s Which One May Be the Biggest AI Winner.
stories.Summary:
TSMC is reportedly weighing a price increase of as much as 20% for its Chip on Wafer on Substrate (CoWoS) advanced packaging technology, according to a Trendforce report cited by Tom's Hardware on October 27, 2026. The report relies on supply chain sources and local media, and it ties the possible increase to strained capacity as AI demand grows and delivery times for chipmaking tools get longer. Equipment lead times have stretched to eight months. Pressure from Nvidia's Blackwell and Rubin chips is putting extra strain on packaging capacity, and CoWoS is already described as one of the tightest links in the supply chain. The price rise has not been confirmed by TSMC.

A separate Motley Fool piece by Adria Cimino, published October 28, 2026, compares Nvidia and TSMC as AI investments. It says Nvidia designs the graphics processing units central to major AI tasks while TSMC manufactures the chips, and that Nvidia's stock has gained more than 400% over three years against more than 300% for TSMC. In Nvidia's most recent quarter, revenue jumped 106% to $96 billion, and its gross margin has consistently topped 70%. TSMC reported its sixth straight quarter of record profit, with revenue of $46 billion for the period, and both revenue and net income beat analysts' estimates.

On who is behind these developments, the CoWoS pricing story rests on Trendforce, which attributes its information to supply chain sources and local media, so no TSMC executive is quoted on the matter. The Motley Fool article gives the author's view that both companies are well placed in the AI boom, but that Nvidia may score the bigger win. She argues that Nvidia's market leadership, annual product updates, CUDA platform and full range of products let it charge premium prices and earn strong margins. TSMC, she says, benefits whichever chip designer succeeds, since it holds more than 70% of the pure foundry market according to Counterpoint Research, and she calls it a relatively safe AI stock. She adds that TSMC carries heavy manufacturing overhead for facilities and expensive equipment, costs that Nvidia does not face.

As for context, the article notes that TSMC makes chips for most major players, from Advanced Micro Devices to Broadcom. As of October 27, TSMC shares closed at $436.87, up 2.95%, with a market value of $2.27 trillion, while Nvidia closed at $217.94, up 0.90%, with a market value of $5.25 trillion. Cimino expects revenue gains at both companies to continue for some time because AI is only beginning to enter real-world use. The articles do not say when TSMC might decide on the CoWoS price increase.

stories.Headline: [PRNewswire] Ozelle to Spotlight Scalable AI-Assisted Hematology
stories.Summary:
Ozelle, a company founded in Silicon Valley in 2014, announced on October 28, 2026 that it will showcase its O-Cyte 1 automated hematology analyzer at MEDICA 2026. The company says that as AI-assisted morphology becomes part of routine hematology, laboratories need more than automatic cell classification, since cell images must remain available for professional review while analyzers also meet daily testing and maintenance needs. The O-Cyte 1 combines complete blood count testing and 7-part white blood cell differentiation with high-resolution cell imaging and AI-assisted classification in one instrument. Its cell images are linked to numerical results so that laboratory staff can examine visual evidence when needed. The announcement was prompted in part by the International Council for Standardization in Haematology, which approved a new digital morphology standardization project at its October 14 to 15 General Assembly.

The analyzer is built for changing workloads and routine service. A standalone unit delivers up to 60 tests per hour, while a six-unit cascade reaches up to 360 tests per hour. Its integrated reagent kit and key fluid-contact components are housed in consumables, which the company says simplifies reagent handling and reduces routine maintenance. Built-in self-checks and replaceable modules are intended to make faults easier to identify and service. Ozelle also says scalable configurations can serve laboratories with different testing volumes and give distributors a path for future capacity expansion.

Ozelle is the company responsible for the product and the announcement, and it describes the O-Cyte 1 as part of its vision for the fourth generation of hematology analysis. The company says this approach aims to make morphology intelligence more consistent, reviewable and scalable across routine workflows. Ozelle will also feature the EHBT-75, which combines 7-diff hematology with cell imaging and morphology analysis, and the EHBT-50, which integrates hematology, immunoassay and dry biochemistry in a compact platform. Visitors can also see Open Dx, its AI Workbench for AI-assisted report review and result sharing. The company will exhibit at MEDICA 2026 from November 16 to 19 in Hall 1, Booth D63, at Messe Düsseldorf in Germany, where it plans to discuss distribution opportunities.

stories.Headline: Behind-the-Meter Power Draws $700 Million Bet as AI Demand Surges
stories.Summary:
Neuberger Specialty Finance, the financing arm of the private investment firm Neuberger, announced earlier this month a $700 million financing facility for Crusoe, an AI infrastructure developer. The money is meant to buy power infrastructure that will directly energize AI factories that Crusoe builds and owns. The article describes this as a potentially risky bet that behind-the-meter power projects, and possibly microgrids, will spread as demand for energy-hungry AI facilities grows. Rod Walton, the managing editor of Microgrid Knowledge, wrote the piece, which was published on October 28, 2026.

The deal fits a wider pattern in which private equity firms are funding dedicated power for data centers because the public grid is constrained. Blackstone, KKR, Brookfield and ArcLight Capital Partners have each announced larger commitments to dedicated energy infrastructure. Crusoe is planning more than six gigawatts of AI infrastructure and wants off-grid power to avoid long waits in grid interconnection queues. stories.Headline: Montana State scientist part of team working to improve weather forecasting with artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Colorado State University scientists are building a forecasting system that uses artificial intelligence to detect destructive hailstorms earlier and more accurately, according to a report dated October 26, 2026. The project is led by atmospheric and radar scientists at the university, including Kristen Rasmussen, an associate professor of atmospheric science. Current forecasts often give hail warnings with less than 30 minutes of notice, while the team hopes to predict hail several hours or even days ahead in Colorado and Wyoming. The effort is funded by the National Science Foundation and combines a short-term nowcasting model developed with NVIDIA and a machine learning model for longer-range storm prediction.

The project is part of the ASCEND Engine, which works with researchers, start-ups, and public and private partners in both states to develop technologies for regional challenges such as severe weather. The engine launched in 2023 and carries a total 10-year federal award of up to $160 million. The system is meant to merge regional radar data with nine years of historic weather observations from across the country. Researchers say the work matters because hail damages crops, roofs and vehicles, and rising homeowners insurance costs in part reflect those risks. The article notes that the window for large hail events is expanding into earlier spring and later fall months.

Chandrasekar, a University Distinguished Professor who manages the regional radar systems, led work with NVIDIA on a model called Hail-StormScope that produces hailstorm forecasts with a two- to three-hour lead time. Russ Schumacher, a professor in the Department of Atmospheric Science, leads the other half of the project, which uses machine learning to assess storm conditions across the country over one- to eight-day windows. His model, called Colorado State University-Machine Learning Probabilities, compares past storm conditions with simulated environments and human forecasts. Schumacher said the team must decide whether to merge the short-term and long-term approaches into one system or keep them separate. Rasmussen said the initial results have been encouraging.

The next step is scheduled for spring 2027, when the team plans to install RM60 sensors from Vaisala near the CSU-CHIVO radar in Greeley to gather ground data for validating the new forecasts. Rasmussen said the models already offer resolution of about 1.3 kilometers and better represent storm interactions around the state's mountains. The article reports that the sensors have not yet been widely used to assess hail. Researchers say the project should improve forecasting and build trust with human forecasters who want to understand how the system reaches its conclusions. The team plans to continue the work with the National Science Foundation and other partners.

stories.Headline: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe and Granary v2: Intelligent Multilingual Transcription You Can Prompt and Adapt
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA released Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe, an open-weight, promptable speech model, on October 28, 2026, through Hugging Face and ModelScope, alongside Granary v2, an expanded open multilingual speech dataset and curation pipeline. The model combines transcription, speaker attribution, translation, and audio question answering in a single checkpoint. It transcribes 40 languages, translates 31 of them to or from English, and attributes speakers in 13, handling recordings up to an hour long with up to eight speakers. Developers can steer its output with natural language prompts, choose where audio is processed, and adapt it to domain vocabulary and accents. The model is a 30-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts system with about 4 billion parameters active per token, so it can run on hardware ranging from a Jetson AGX Thor or DGX Spark to Blackwell data-center GPUs.

Quantized versions are described as coming soon, and local deployment through NeMo-Speech.cpp is also forthcoming. Granary v2 covers 463,062 hours across 48 languages and 16 source corpora, up from 25 languages in the first version, and generates three transcript styles per recording. Transcribe is built for recorded audio rather than live streaming. The company also says NeMo Speech fine-tuning tools let developers adapt the model further, and in one medical case study fine-tuning cut word error rate on held-out speakers by 45.8% relative to the best prompt. NVIDIA is the company behind the release, and its materials make the performance claims.

On the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard, Transcribe ranks first among open-weight models for English at 5.33% average word error rate. Artificial Analysis places it at 2.8% AA-WER, tied for first among open-weight models. On David AI's multilingual diarization benchmark across 21 languages, it posts the lowest diarization error rate of the 14 systems tested, and on VoiceArena's English full-session benchmark it has the lowest concatenated error rate. Agora has also shown a classroom demo that pairs word-level timestamps with replay recordings. These results come from the company and third-party leaderboards, and the articles note that developers should still spot-check names, speaker changes, and answers against the original recording.

stories.Headline: Businesses increasingly adopt AI for cybersecurity while individuals expand privacy protections
stories.Summary:
Businesses across the OECD are turning to artificial intelligence to defend against cyber threats, while individuals are using privacy tools to take more control of their personal data, according to new OECD data released in late October 2026. In 2023, 17.7% of enterprises in the OECD experienced ICT security incidents, a rise of 28.2% from 2018. In 2025, 5.3% of enterprises used AI for ICT security, roughly one quarter of all enterprises using AI. Uses include machine learning systems that detect and prevent attacks and AI-based user authentication. Adoption in 2025 was 23.2% higher than in 2024, 68.6% higher than in 2023, and more than double the 2021 level.

Use of AI for security depends heavily on company size and sector. In 2025, 26.7% of large enterprises used AI for ICT security, compared with 9.6% of medium-sized enterprises and 3.7% of small ones. Among industries, 18.1% of firms in information and communication reported using it, well ahead of professional, scientific and technical activities at 8.9%. Adoption in the ICT sector was about nine times higher than in accommodation and food services, at 2.1%. The OECD suggests these tools spread most in information-intensive sectors, where cyber risks and reliance on digital systems are greatest.

Individuals are also acting more on their own data. Between 2020 and 2025, the share changing browser settings to limit cookies rose by 26.8%, while those refusing personal data use for advertising rose by 17.2% and those restricting access to their location rose by 14.0%. Smaller increases were seen for limiting social media profile access (11.3%) and using anti-tracking software (7.0%). The OECD links these trends to more privacy controls in browsers, operating systems and online platforms, and to greater awareness of data protection. By 2025, more than half of individuals had either restricted location access or refused personal data use for advertising, while the share reading privacy policies before sharing data fell by about 8.4%.

Concern about privacy is rarely the reason people avoid generative AI, with only 4.5% of OECD individuals citing it as their main reason in 2025. Older adults aged 55 to 74 were more likely than those aged 16 to 24 to avoid AI over such concerns, at 5.8% against 1.9%, and less likely to take active privacy steps. Younger people reported fewer worries about AI but frequently used privacy controls and anti-tracking tools. Education also shapes privacy behaviour: individuals with higher attainment were far more likely to refuse personal data use for advertising (68.1% against 39.5%) and to restrict location access (65.8% against 38.9%) than those with low attainment, although concern about generative AI was similar across both groups.

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence is killing jobs but also creating new roles.
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is affecting nearly every industry, according to a report from Gray DC published on October 28, 2026. Goldman Sachs estimates that 300 million jobs will be affected by the technology by 2030. Some roles are being transformed while others are being eliminated outright. Those changes are also raising demand for oversight of how AI is used.

Barry Jones, a vice president at X2X, an AI governance company, argued that human involvement must remain part of AI work. He said current oversight is not sufficient. Using the example of an AI assistant preparing financial reports, he warned that such a tool could expose critical information if it operated outside a company's internal controls. Jones added that self-governance alone is not enough and that a third party, including possibly the government, should set limits on what AI can and cannot do. He also said private oversight is creating new roles.

Several members of Congress have stated their positions on regulation. Representative Buddy Carter, a Georgia Republican, said he would prefer the federal government stay out of it where possible, but that the technology must be handled correctly because it has real dangers. Senator Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, said the United States must address the risks of increasingly powerful AI systems and that the American people, through their representatives, should make those decisions. The report notes that efforts to regulate AI are stalled on Capitol Hill.

The report also points to job losses already under way, noting that Microsoft recently offered 60,000 employees buyouts because of AI. Jones advised workers seeking a career change to learn AI, understand how it applies to their profession, and recognize that judgment, experience, trust and accountability still matter. He said the aim should be to use the technology responsibly rather than compete with it. The article says the 120th Congress could take up the rapidly evolving technology when it convenes in January.

stories.Headline: Nvidia backs Simplismart in $14 million funding for AI efficiency
stories.Summary:
On October 27 and 28, 2026, reports described how Bengaluru-based AI infrastructure startup Simplismart raised $14 million in a Series B round led by Dallas Venture Capital, with Nvidia investing alongside Accel, Shastra VC and Micromax. The four-year-old company, founded in 2022 by Amritanshu Jain and Devansh Ghatak, is now valued at about $100 million including the new money. Its software sits between AI models and computing hardware, automating how models are deployed and managed so that customers can tune response speed, request handling and computing consumption. Simplismart employs 58 people.

The funding is aimed at reducing dependence on GPUs, the specialized chips used to run AI models, by helping companies get more out of the hardware they already have. The company plans to use the money to expand its presence in the United States and North America, grow its team, and further develop its inference platform. It also intends to build partnerships with cloud providers and sovereign AI players. Simplismart has also been developing a dynamic GPU scheduling layer intended to match workloads with available capacity across regions and time zones, which would help cloud providers improve utilization. The company does not own computing infrastructure itself, instead supplying the software layer that lets providers offer AI services on their own hardware.

Jain and Ghatak said the advantage in AI now lies in how models are run rather than simply having access to them, pointing to cost per interaction, response speed and reliability as demand grows. Dayakar Puskoor, managing partner at Dallas Venture Capital, said inferencing is becoming one of the biggest factors in AI economics. Jain also said Nvidia has collaborated with Simplismart on technical integrations, including its Dynamo inference software, and has introduced the startup to potential customers and partners. The company has said its software helped video-generation platform InVideo cut GPU serving costs by 56 per cent.

The context is a shift among enterprises toward controlling what it costs to run AI applications in production, as open-weight models offer alternatives to proprietary models accessed through paid interfaces. Simplismart's annualised revenue run rate grew 14-fold over six months to an eight-figure sum, and more than half of its revenue comes from the U.S., even though it has more customers in India. Its clients include HeyGen, Higgsfield, InVideo, Shiprocket, Apna and Ema, and Indian cloud provider Yotta uses its technology to power the serverless inference layer of Shakti Studio. Simplismart competes with Nvidia itself, major cloud providers and numerous other startups building tools for faster and cheaper AI operations. Jain said the company wins where clients have strict service-level agreements and total cost of ownership requirements.

Cielo, a talent solutions firm based in Milwaukee, introduced Cosm by Cielo on October 27, 2026. The company describes it as an AI-native operating model meant to turn workforce demand into business outcomes faster than traditional recruiting models. It is powered by Cielo Lumis, which Cielo calls its system of action, and it links talent expertise, governance, AI-enabled workflows and real-time intelligence. The launch follows faster shifts in business priorities, skills demand and talent availability across employers.

Cielo cited its own Talent Benchmark research, which found that 87% of organizations increased talent acquisition technology investment over the past 12 months, yet many still struggle to turn that spending into greater hiring agility. It also referred to McKinsey research showing that organizations getting the most value from AI are redesigning how work gets done. Cosm starts with the business outcome and then determines the workflows, systems, decisions and human touchpoints needed to reach it. Rather than optimizing isolated hiring steps, it treats talent acquisition as a connected business capability.

Cielo says this moves hiring beyond faster task execution toward better decisions and quicker responses to shifting demand. Cielo reported results from early Cosm-enabled deployments, compared with prior performance: up to 5x higher candidate submissions, a 10% productivity improvement, a 15% lower cost per hire, and 20% fewer aged requisitions. Cielo's chief executive, Marissa Geist, said companies need a better way to turn work priorities into action rather than more disconnected recruiting tools. Cielo Lumis, the company says, connects workforce, talent and market signals to workflows and recruiter actions, and it works across applicant tracking and human capital management systems that organizations already use.

Cielo's chief operating officer, Molly Thiel, said the platform is meant to reduce friction so recruiters can spend more time advising the business and making accountable decisions. Cielo says Cosm operates within governed workflows and human oversight, with built-in transparency, accountability and clear limits on autonomous action. The company states that its AI governance framework is supported by ISO/IEC 42001 certification for AI management systems and ISO/IEC 27001 certification for information security management systems. stories.Summary:
Vera Health, a company that offers an AI search platform for clinicians, announced on October 27, 2026 that it had secured $28.5 million in Series A funding, bringing its total raised to $32 million. Threshold Ventures led the round, with participation from Mantis VC and SV Angel, and existing investors Y Combinator and Gradient also put more money in. Fierce Healthcare reported that Optum Ventures took part as well. The platform is free for licensed clinicians and medical trainees, who can ask questions about diagnoses, medication dosing, guidelines and treatment and receive summaries linked to their sources.

The company plans to use the new capital to improve its platform, scale into more healthcare markets and expand partnerships with medical societies, publishers and health systems. It also intends to keep investing in locally relevant clinical guidance and in tools that let healthcare institutions add their own medical knowledge to the platform through its Vera Spaces offering. Fierce Healthcare reported that the platform scans more than 60 million peer-reviewed publications, clinical guidelines, consensus statements and drug labels, and that it is used by more than 800,000 clinicians in 190 countries, up from a few thousand a year earlier. The company also said it doubled its team from six to 12 people and is now hiring internationally.

Taieb Bennani, a cofounder of Vera Health, has described the company's focus on clinicians and its emphasis on evidence. He said clinicians make decisions in seconds and that the team, which includes clinicians or their relatives, builds the product around that need. Threshold Ventures co-founder and managing partner Emily Melton said in a statement that the platform starts with evidence rather than just an answer, which helps clinicians assess the research behind a decision. Bennani also told Fierce Healthcare that the company's approach rests on honesty, traceability, transparency and context, and that the tool searches for evidence before writing an answer.

The funding comes amid growing competition in clinical AI search. MobiHealthNews noted that OpenEvidence secured $250 million in Series D funding in January, doubling its valuation to $12 billion, and that Doximity recently partnered with Wolters Kluwer Health to bring UpToDate content into its Ask tool. Fierce Healthcare added that established reference companies such as Elsevier's ClinicalKey and Wolters Kluwer's UpToDate are competing with AI-native tools as well as consumer technology firms like OpenAI and Anthropic. The articles do not say what Vera Health will do next beyond the plans already described.

stories.Headline: Expert Judgement Can Be Easily Hacked by AI, Anthropic Study Finds
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI model, published a study in late October 2026 finding that people who rely on AI for decisions tend to adopt its conclusions without realizing it. In the experiment, 50 professional analysts were asked to advise a fictional farming cooperative on whether to expand or end a paid advisory program. The researchers secretly set each participant's Claude assistant to favor one option on each of four choices, using a coin flip to decide which way it leaned. Participants then made their final recommendation after working through those choices with the assistant.

The participants matched the AI's preferred option 86 percent of the time, well above the 50 percent rate that would be expected if the assistant had no effect. When a participant had already formed a view and the assistant disagreed, that person changed their mind in 60 percent of cases. In a follow-up survey, 77 percent of analysts used the assistant's arguments to explain their choices, sometimes word for word, but only 15 percent credited the AI as an influence. The study had limitations, including that it covered a single task and used assistants deliberately set to have a preference.

The researchers, Amaç Herdagdelen, Hailey Joren, and Alex Tamkin, said this deference may be hard for experts to notice in themselves. They warned that if people hand key judgment calls to AI systems whose underlying assumptions are arbitrary or misaligned, those assumptions could shape scientific and policy outcomes without anyone choosing them. They argued that oversight should track how decisions are made, surfacing key decision points as work proceeds and helping experts state the assumptions and values they would otherwise leave unspoken. Their paper framed this as a way to keep human judgment a meaningful check.

The findings arrive as AI companies face intense public debate over the risks of advanced systems. Anthropic is preparing for an initial public offering valued at up to $2 trillion, and supporters of the technology expect large productivity gains, while critics point to possible job losses and cyberattacks. Commentators quoted in coverage called the study important work on how humans and AI interact. The study itself did not say what policy changes, if any, would follow from it.
