stories.Headline: Biometric information on tourists necessary
stories.Summary:
Home Affairs Director General Mkhuseli Apleni has said it is necessary to take fingerprints from all tourists and travellers visiting South Africa, a position he set out at a Pretoria meeting attended by key tourism and immigration stakeholders. He argued that fingerprints help identify a person, particularly when a crime has been committed. The meeting, which the article dates to 7 December 2016, was held to discuss developments in the immigration regulations. Apleni stressed that taking fingerprints of everyone entering the country was important.

The Department of Home Affairs had introduced a biometric system the previous April that captures travellers' fingerprints at South Africa's international airports. The department said the system would be rolled out to six of the country's busiest land ports of entry. The system is currently used at OR Tambo International Airport and is expected to reach other major airports. Apleni said the department was working on ways to avoid delays there, particularly at OR Tambo, and that people do not have to wait long to have their fingerprints taken. He also expressed hope that other countries would adopt the same biometric system to reduce delays at ports of entry.

Aneme Malan, Deputy Director-General at the Department of Tourism, said her department was working closely with Home Affairs on visa regulations. She noted that the number of tourists arriving in the country had increased, but said the sector had not yet reached its potential and that some areas needed further engagement. The article also covers rules on children, which Apleni and the stakeholders emphasised. Since June 2015, stricter requirements have applied to anyone under 18 travelling to or from South Africa, whether a citizen or a foreigner. A Parental Consent Affidavit must accompany an unabridged birth certificate or equivalent document when a parent is not travelling with the child.

Parents travelling with their children can apply at any Home Affairs office for a fee of R75, bringing their identity documents and the child's abridged birth certificate, while South Africans abroad can apply at their nearest embassy. The article says the law is aimed at curbing child trafficking. According to Home Affairs, 132 353 children were processed in June 2015 across arrivals and departures, of whom 1 878 did not meet the requirements, leaving compliance at 98%. Foreign children numbered about 57 436 on arrival and 74 917 on departure that month.

He added that the company would act as a reliable partner for long-term investment. Market expectations for continued memory industry growth are tied to the spread of artificial intelligence, and analysts see the upturn continuing. Investors are also looking ahead to the third-quarter earnings reports from SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics. The inflows suggest individual investors are spreading money across the global memory value chain rather than a single theme. stories.Headline: Apple adds AI tools to Creator Studio in major update
stories.Summary:
Apple has added new artificial intelligence features and editing tools to its Apple Creator Studio suite, updating Final Cut Pro, Logic Pro, Pixelmator Pro, Keynote, Pages and Numbers. The update was announced on October 27, 2026, alongside new iMacs and a 14-inch MacBook Pro powered by the M6 chip. It will be a free App Store update for existing subscribers in November. The package brings MotionVFX content into Final Cut Pro, a new image-editing tool in Pixelmator Pro, video assets in the Content Hub, and beta assistants in Logic Pro and the productivity apps.

In Final Cut Pro for Mac, editors can now reach templates, graphics, titles, transitions and tools such as rotoscoping, tracking and colour grading without leaving the app. Apple has also added its Content Hub, which offers stock video, photos and backgrounds it curates. Pixelmator Pro gains Generate Fill, which changes selected parts of an image based on a text prompt and matches lighting, perspective and texture. Logic Pro receives a redesigned Browser, an expanded Stem Splitter that can separate drums, and a beta assistant built on Apple models and OpenAI technology. Keynote, Pages and Numbers get beta assistants that understand document context, along with Model Context Protocol support that lets external AI tools act inside those apps.

Apple's Brent Chiu-Watson, senior director of worldwide product marketing for apps and iCloud, called it the company's most exciting update since the suite launched and said the MotionVFX content gives subscribers rapid access to professional video effects. He also said the assistants in Logic Pro, Keynote, Pages and Numbers would change how people interact with and learn those apps. Apple has not announced an exact launch date for the new features beyond saying November. The new assistants will arrive in beta, in U.S. English only, on supported Apple Intelligence devices. stories.Headline: SK hynix reports 632% surge in Q3 profit due to AI-driven demand for memory chips - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
SK hynix, the South Korean memory chipmaker, reported on Wednesday that its operating profit for the July to September quarter rose 632 percent from a year earlier. The company said the increase was driven largely by the artificial intelligence industry's strong demand for its advanced memory chips. Operating profit for the period reached 83.33 trillion won, or about $62.8 billion. Net profit climbed 215.7 percent to 39.77 trillion won, and sales reached 104.61 trillion won. The firm said this marked record revenue and operating profit for six straight quarters.

The results fell short of market expectations, as analysts had estimated net profit at 59.67 trillion won, according to South Korea's Yonhap news agency citing its own data. SK hynix also announced an additional plan to return 60 trillion won to shareholders, following completion of a 40 trillion-won shareholder return programme. The company's shares have been under pressure since June, when they retreated from record highs, and have fallen nearly 60 percent from that peak according to one professor cited in the reporting. Investors have pushed for more cash returns through dividends or buybacks.

SK hynix supplies high-bandwidth memory chips to Nvidia and is a pillar of South Korea's tech-led economy. The company's statement attributed its growth to a cycle in which AI-driven productivity gains and new revenue in software development, customer service and search lead to greater AI adoption. Market research analyst MS Hwang of Counterpoint said long-term agreements with major customers signal another phase of price increases across conventional DRAM, NAND and HBM. Hwang added that quarterly earnings have not yet peaked and that the upward trend will likely continue at least through 2027.

Not all observers are as optimistic about the outlook. Hwang warned that weaker AI spending, increased competition and the company's own capacity expansion could drive price volatility heading into 2027, and named a pullback in cloud providers' orders as the most severe threat. Kim Dae-jong, a business professor at Sejong University, said investors appear to be pricing in concern that current earnings levels may not be sustainable one or two years out. The reporting notes that the global race to build AI data centres has transformed the company's fortunes, even as worries grow that the sector may be overvalued.

stories.Headline: Autonomous machine learning
stories.Summary:
Two sources cover very different things, so I will treat them separately. The first is a research article titled "Autonomous machine learning," published in Science China Information Sciences on 28 October 2026 by Wenwu Zhu, Xin Wang and Zhiqiang Xu. The article itself is only partly visible here: it lists a set of references on self-supervised learning, active learning, AutoML, meta-learning and self-directed learning, and notes funding from the Beijing National Research Center for Information Science and Technology under Grant No. BNR2026TD03005. The authors are affiliated with Tsinghua University in Beijing and Xi'an Jiaotong University. The visible text does not state the paper's findings, so no claims about its results can be drawn from it.

The second source, published on 27 October 2026, describes geoscientists in China who used high-resolution 3D seismic imaging together with machine learning to map fault networks in the deep Tarim Basin. Earlier surveys relied on seismic data gathered from widely spaced grids, which could not detect smaller fracture lines. The researchers instead ran 3D reflection surveys in the Shunbei central region and applied machine learning classifiers to millions of seismic data points, which found many low-order branch connections between major fault fragments automatically. The article says this speeded up fault mapping and reduced human bias, though it reports no specific figures for the speedup. Physical sandbox experiments using sand and silicone were also used to model deep basement faulting, and they suggested that large regional faults absorb tectonic strain early on, leaving secondary faults inactive.

The article attributes the work to geoscientists focusing on China and does not name individual researchers. It presents the findings as relevant to understanding continental deformation, planning oil and geothermal extraction in desert environments, and avoiding dangerous drilling problems. It also says that revised fault maps at different scales could help connect plate tectonic theory with reservoir engineering and guide future drilling projects. The articles do not describe any further steps or timelines beyond these general aims.

stories.Headline: When artificial intelligence wears a famous face
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Iowa State University, working with colleagues at Indiana University and the University of Sydney, studied how customers respond when a customer service agent is a digital twin of a celebrity. The study, published in the Journal of Management Information Systems in October 2026, examined a trend called "Celebrity-as-a-Service," in which companies use AI-powered or human-operated replicas of famous people to talk with customers. In the experiments, the team built a prototype that placed actor Hugh Jackman's face onto a digital representative, doing so under U.S. fair use rules for research. Lingyao (Ivy) Yuan, an associate professor of information systems and business analytics, led the work. Her team chose Jackman because he is widely recognized and has a largely positive public image.

The researchers ran two controlled experiments in which participants dealt with either the celebrity version or a non-celebrity version of the same representative, which gave identical help. Participants rated the celebrity agent more favorably on whether it seemed capable, benevolent and honest, even though the service itself never changed. In a second experiment, the team introduced common errors such as mishearing a name or misunderstanding an address. Participants using the celebrity version were more forgiving of these mistakes and less angry about them. The study also found no sign of "algorithm aversion," meaning people were not harsher toward an AI-controlled avatar than toward a human-controlled one.

Yuan explained that people often carry positive feelings about a well-liked person over to whatever that person is associated with, a pattern she described as a halo effect. She said participants seemed to transfer those feelings to the service itself. She argued that the technology is becoming more common and that the key question is how people respond to it and how those responses shape their decisions. The study suggests companies could tailor virtual representatives to a customer's age, language or preferences, which Yuan presented as a possibility rather than a current practice.

Yuan stressed that transparency and ethical guidelines will matter more as the technology develops, so customers always know when they are dealing with AI rather than a real person. She said the technology can offer real value when used in a regulated and ethical way. Her summary was that a familiar face may not change how well a service works, but it can change how people feel about using it. The articles do not describe any specific regulations or further studies that are planned.

stories.Headline: Teens often turn to AI when feeling distressed; report flags mental health risks
stories.Summary:
A new report from The Jed Foundation, a youth mental health organization, links some uses of artificial intelligence with poorer mental health among teenagers. The group surveyed thousands of middle and high school students and found that more than 80% use AI in some capacity. It did not find a link between overall AI use and worse mental health, but it did find associations among students who used AI for schoolwork, problem-solving advice, companionship, or help when they were emotionally struggling. The report was published this week as a follow-up to a Capitol Hill briefing the researchers held over the summer.

Students who used AI for schoolwork reported higher levels of loneliness and a greater lifetime history of suicidal thoughts. Those who turned to AI for relationship or problem-solving advice showed greater symptoms of anxiety and depression, more loneliness, and higher suicidal risk. Students who used AI for friendship or companionship, or who sought help from it when emotionally struggling, had greater anxiety and depression symptoms, more loneliness, and a history of suicidal thoughts and attempts. They also reported lower resilience and flourishing. Most students, 58%, said they use AI for schoolwork, while 12% said they use it for friendship or companionship.

The report's author, Kayla Anderson, JED's vice president of research and evaluation, said the way adults talk with young people about AI matters a great deal. She noted that 57% of students said they use AI when they feel sad, stressed, lonely or overwhelmed, though only 8% said they specifically sought help with their feelings from it. Anderson said AI should never replace human counsel and connection for young people. She also cautioned that the study found an association rather than a cause, and that it is still unclear how much AI itself drives worse outcomes. She said it is plausible that already struggling kids lean on AI more, and that such use could also worsen their problems.

Anderson said the issue needs to be addressed at the systems level, with tools designed specifically for safety. For parents, she said the first advice is not to let young people use AI as a friend or companion, since AI companions are associated with worse mental health in teens. She added that families should have early and frequent conversations about what young people use AI for, so that they do not hand too much of their thinking and relationship work to the technology. Anderson stressed that such work should stay in human spaces.

stories.Headline: MP Spurious Liquor Case: Accused Used AI to Learn Brewing Methods
stories.Summary:
Police in Madhya Pradesh's Dewas district say an arrested man used artificial intelligence to learn how to brew liquor at home by mixing chemicals and water. The fake liquor was blended with real alcohol and poured into empty licensed bottles bought from scrap dealers, then sold mostly in rural areas. Police arrested 10 people on Monday, October 27, and seized six cartons of country liquor, according to Dewas Kotwali Police Station in-charge Shashikant Chaurasia. Police said the arrested man, Ajay Rathore, had been using AI since September to look up home-brewing methods. Reports also say he ordered chemicals through a private firm in Indore, though the officials did not name the chemicals.

Investigators say Rathore collected empty licensed bottles from scrap dealers between October 2 and 7 and prepared the fake liquor with help from other accused. Among those arrested are two managers and two salesmen from three licensed liquor shops in Dewas and Indore districts, who allegedly supplied alcohol illegally. Police say the adulterated liquor was sold to local residents between October 6 and 12. The Indore warehouse of the private firm that supplied the chemicals has been sealed, and relevant provisions of the Excise Act have been added to the FIR. Viscera samples from the two deceased, along with the recovered liquor, have gone to the Forensic Science Laboratory, and the cause of death will be confirmed once the report arrives.

Police say two other employees of a licensed liquor shop are also involved, and a search for them is underway. Villagers in Chandana, Binjana and nearby areas of Dewas claim at least 10 people died after drinking poisonous liquor between September 27 and October 16. State Congress President Jitu Patwari alleges that 22 people died and at least 40 lost their eyesight over the past month. The district administration first dismissed the death claims. After the controversy grew, the state government formed a five-member high-level investigation team to probe the matter.

The reports note that the death toll claims remain under investigation and that the forensic findings are still awaited. Police have not confirmed how many of the deaths were linked to the adulterated liquor. Each account is based on statements from police officials and local claims as reported by PTI. The next step is the forensic report, which will determine the cause of the deaths, along with the work of the state investigation team.

stories.Headline: Bond investors have gotten picky about AI
stories.Summary:
Bond investors have grown more selective about which AI-linked borrowers they will finance, even as AI borrowing keeps rising. The shift follows a sell-off in early October, when yields on bonds issued by CoreWeave, a heavily indebted AI company, climbed sharply, meaning its bond prices fell. Since then the broader corporate bond market has calmed, and enthusiasm around Anthropic and Meta has helped restore confidence in the AI trade that supports stock prices. Axios reporter Matt Phillips, writing on October 28, 2026, says that calm hides lingering caution toward the more leveraged players.

The price moves have spread beyond CoreWeave itself. Bonds that finance data centers leased to CoreWeave, including those issued by Edged Compute, Core Scientific and Applied Digital, saw their yields creep higher after CoreWeave's bonds fell, with CoreWeave's own unsecured bonds reaching yields of around 16 percent. Data center debt tied to Oracle has moved in step with Oracle's own bonds. Roughly $14 billion of bonds maturing in 2045, issued to build a large data center campus in Saline Township, Michigan, wobbled along with Oracle's over the past couple of weeks. Ratings agencies say Oracle's signed 17-year lease for that campus is a major support for those bonds.

Citigroup's high-yield debt analysts said in a note last week that tenant-specific risk was exposed during the October pullback, with CoreWeave and similar neocloud and data center companies bearing most of the selloff. They warned that data center bonds are not immune to tenant default and can reprice quickly as that risk rises. Axios reports that the same pattern is visible among safer investment-grade bonds, where investors now distinguish sharply between borrowers rather than treating AI-related debt as largely interchangeable. The articles do not say how these conditions will evolve.

Its advanced packaging business drove nearly all of that growth, while its semiconductor solutions segment, which sells front-end manufacturing gear, came in just short of analyst expectations. The company guided fourth-quarter revenue to between $670 million and $730 million. The split result points to packaging, rather than front-end chipmaking tools, as the current bottleneck in AI hardware. Advanced packaging is now growing faster than the equipment that makes the chips themselves.

Thermo-compression bonding equipment, used to stack high-bandwidth memory onto AI accelerators, is the fastest-growing piece. ASMPT's advanced packaging unit posted record first-half revenue of $339 million in 2026, up 17% year over year. Thermo-compression bonding revenue grew 146% in the most recent period covered by the company's disclosures. The company has said the addressable market for its bonding tools alone could top $1.6 billion by 2028. ASMPT's legacy business trails well behind that growth.

The constraint now lies in packaging capacity rather than wafer output. TSMC's CoWoS capacity, the process that binds compute dies to memory stacks, is reportedly booked through 2027. Nvidia alone is expected to need about 1.2 million CoWoS wafers that year, while AMD's needs are projected to rise roughly 308%, from about 130,000 wafers in 2026 to 530,000 in 2027. AMD has reportedly routed about half its packaging orders to ASE, SPIL and Amkor. SK Hynix, which along with Samsung and Micron controls nearly all HBM supply, has committed roughly $12.85 billion to a new packaging facility in Cheongju, South Korea.

ASM International, a separate Dutch equipment maker often confused with ASMPT, reported its own record quarter the same day, with revenue of €1.159 billion, up 44% at constant currencies. It now expects to reach €5.7 billion in 2027 revenue, a target it had originally set for 2030. Similar AI-driven beats have come from SK Hynix and TSMC this year. Companies selling into advanced packaging and HBM are beating guidance, while those in legacy chipmaking equipment are relying on a recovery in the mainstream market.

The first body is a State Level Steering Committee headed by the chief secretary, which will give strategic direction and oversee implementation of the policy. It will include senior officials from the finance, industries, planning, higher and technical education, revenue, energy, and skills and employment departments.

This committee must meet at least once every six months. The second is an Executive Committee led by the secretary of the electronics, information technology and artificial intelligence department, which will approve proposals for incentives and subsidies. It will also coordinate multi-department AI projects, help build partnerships with AI companies and research institutions, and review progress quarterly. The third body, a Technical Committee, will check proposals for technical compliance and eligibility and recommend suitable cases to the Executive Committee. It will also monitor projects once they have been approved.

The government also plans an online portal to help carry out the Maharashtra AI Policy. The policy itself was announced on May 6, and it aims to promote the use of AI technology and encourage AI-based initiatives across government departments. They also do not give a timeline for when the online portal will go live. stories.Headline: Army taps AWS and WWT to boost AI-enabled cybersecurity initiative
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Army has selected Amazon Web Services and World Wide Technology to support Project Griffin, a pilot effort to build an AI-enabled cybersecurity capability, the service announced in late October 2026. The pilot has a combined value of $2.6 million and falls under the Army Rapid Development of Cyber Defense Systems program, which is driven by the project manager for cyber warfare under the portfolio management executive for intelligence and spectrum warfare. Army Cyber Command is also involved in the initiative. The selections followed a solicitation released in August for agentic AI solutions for an Intelligent Response and Orchestration Node capability, and the Army received more than 100 industry submissions before choosing two vendors.

The Army is seeking an agentic, autonomous AI platform that can help cyber defenders neutralize threats faster than human operators can. The goal is to reduce vulnerabilities that arise when network protection depends on manual data review and human action. The system is meant to draw on information from the Army's network sensors and take defensive measures against potential threats. Project Griffin is one of the first efforts under Project ARDS, which uses rapid industry sprints to speed the adoption of AI-enabled cyber defense tools. The pilot is one of three fast-tracked efforts under that initiative.

Brandon Pugh, the secretary of the Army's principal cyber advisor, leads the ARDS work and said the selections let the service move at the speed of business needed to deliver the capability. He said the Army will quickly deploy tools that detect, divert and deceive threat actors, and adopt agentic AI to scale network defense securely. Col. David Bergmann, project manager for cyber warfare, said partnering with commercial industry is a national security imperative because private firms drive rapid innovation in AI, cloud architecture and cyber operations. Officials at AWS and WWT did not immediately respond to requests for comment, though a WWT executive publicly highlighted the selection on LinkedIn.

The pilot comes after other recent Army cybersecurity moves, including the naming of eight companies in May to compete for work under a potential $49 million contract backing the Next-Gen Commercial Operations in Defended Enclaves pilot for small defense suppliers. The Army also enlisted Keysight to test zero trust security on its unified network. Defense officials are increasingly focused on the threat of AI-enabled digital attacks against their systems, and Project Griffin is intended to answer that threat with commercial tools. The articles do not say when the pilot will conclude or when its capabilities will be fielded across the Army's networks.

Roughly 250 people attended the opening, which the organization called the largest capital project in its history. The warehouse was built to serve up to a million people a year, and the group hopes to eventually triple its current reach beyond the more than 350,000 New Yorkers it serves annually.

The facility uses advanced cold storage, automation and artificial intelligence to manage inventory and distribute food more efficiently. It supports the Met Council's network of more than 200 food pantry partners across the five boroughs, along with year-round kosher and halal distributions. It also helps the group provide medically tailored meals and groceries to eligible Medicaid recipients through New York's Social Care Network program. Officials described the project as a major step in expanding the group's ability to feed hungry New Yorkers. The building was reported to have taken about five years to develop.

David Greenfield, the Met Council's chief executive, said the organization was building infrastructure to fight poverty on a much larger scale, and he called the project a labor of love. He told attendees that anyone who is hungry in the city is welcome at the building, regardless of background or language. Joseph Allerhand, the group's co-president, said the facility shows its commitment to feeding those who need help most, including working-class and middle-class families. Speakers at the event, including New York City Comptroller Mark Levine and state Comptroller Thomas DiNapoli, praised the use of technology to reduce waste and serve more people.

The project sits within growing demand for food assistance across the city, and speakers linked the work to public safety and community strength. stories.Headline: AI is changing our world. First, let's understand what it is.
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence has been around for decades, but generative AI has made it feel suddenly everywhere. A Pew Research Center survey from June found nearly half of U.S. adults use AI chatbots such as ChatGPT, and one in four of them use one every day. About a third of American homes have devices with AI built in, such as doorbells, thermostats or smart speakers. Use is growing even as many people remain skeptical, with more adults expecting a negative rather than positive impact on them and on society.

Generative AI differs from older tools such as the iPhone's Siri, which worked with limited data inside preexisting code. Newer systems learn from enormous quantities of data and produce original text, images, audio, video and computer code in response to user prompts. The field changed quickly after a 2017 Google paper on the "Transformer" framework, and by late 2022 OpenAI had released GPT-3 to the public. Companies including Google, OpenAI and Anthropic have since raced to build more advanced models, and many are now described as agents that can act on their own without a human prompt. Gerol C. Petruzella, an academic technology consultant at Williams College, argues that this shift means society must figure out new rules for a world where humans are no longer the only entities able to act independently.

The article was written by Ben Niewoehner and introduces a three-part series by Petruzella in The Berkshire Eagle, which will examine AI's effects on local businesses and systems, daily life, and what separates the technology from profit-driven hype. Petruzella defines AI broadly as any technology that does things that would traditionally have required human cognition. He says AI is already part of the digital tools and apps people use, and it is becoming part of the environment in which people work and live. The series is meant to explore how the technology will affect Berkshire County in the coming months and years.

stories.Headline: AI Emergency Alerts Are Coming. Humans Might Not Be Ready
stories.Summary:
Earlier this month, after Hurricane Isaias made landfall on the Gulf Coast as a Category 3 hurricane, a meteorologist in Alabama called emergency management expert Laura Myers about a problem. A local emergency manager had published a graphic warning that the storm might bring a "sting jet" of high winds to the Alabama coast, but he had made the graphic with an AI chatbot, and it was not meteorologically accurate. Myers, who directs the University of Alabama's Center for Advanced Public Safety, said the official had asked the tool to help him draw attention to local risk, and it produced what he asked for rather than what the weather data supported. Most emergency management agencies do not allow staff to use generative AI, yet the experts interviewed agree that it is likely already widespread in state and local disaster departments. Hundreds of companies are selling AI tools to emergency managers, and public communication is among the areas where officials and startups show the most interest.

Public alerts are a natural target for these tools because emergency managers often struggle to communicate clearly. They tend to use jargon, leave out information they assume people already know, and include details that distract from urgent instructions. Jeannette Sutton, a disaster researcher at the University of Albany who built a dashboard of alert templates, said many agencies have too few staff and little time, so they treat communication as a priority only after a failure reveals its importance. Emergency managers at the state and local level form the first line of defense after an extreme weather event, and they often say that trust is their currency, which they build or lose through what they tell the public. Poor communication has already caused harm in past disasters.

In 2016 adjacent California counties issued a "voluntary" and a "mandatory" evacuation for the same wildfire, and in 2019 Australian officials used a "Watch and Act" phrase that the government later admitted caused significant confusion. The most serious case cited is Montecito, California, after the 2017 Thomas Fire, when a heavy rainstorm weeks later produced a deadly mudslide. Santa Barbara County sent alerts to residents in the voluntary evacuation zone, telling them to stay alert and be prepared to leave immediately, and many people treated the notice as optional, while others had no wish to leave a second time in a month. The mudslide killed 23 people and injured more than 160 others. Sutton describes this pattern as warning fatigue, and she warns that governments issuing poor warnings risk losing the public's trust.

Advocates of AI argue that large language models could help here, since they can review large volumes of alerts and research in minutes and then revise a draft in seconds. Rob Dale, who runs emergency management in Ingham County, Michigan, said an inexperienced official facing a chemical plume could likely do better with AI help than with memory of training taken years earlier, though he would still want to control when an alert is sent. Some companies say the technology is already good enough, and the startup EM1 says its in-house model can match or exceed most human emergency managers on benchmark tests. When Sutton ran a flood alert from a New Mexico county through the model, it produced a much clearer message that named the sender, specified the location, told residents what to do, and pointed them to updates, though it still needed human review.

EM1 has contracts with about a hundred agencies and school districts, but none uses it to automate extreme weather alerts yet. Experts believe many officials are already using personal or free chatbot accounts to draft messages, even if they do not say so. Still, researchers warn that AI-generated content can seem inauthentic to a skeptical public, and that faster alerts could add to warning fatigue. For now, the experts say, the software is only as good as the person using it, and it has not yet reached the point of working without a human expert involved.

stories.Summary:
Korea's Kyunghyang Shinmun published an opinion piece on October 28, 2026, arguing that the country should stop looking abroad for models of artificial intelligence policy and build its own framework. The author begins with the sharp split in public debate, where one camp expects AI to boost growth and offset the demographic decline, while the other warns that falling behind will doom the nation. Both camps, the piece argues, treat AI as an unstoppable force and society as something that must simply adapt. The author claims this framing hides the real question of where society should be heading.

The piece makes the case that technology takes its shape from the institutions it meets, using Korea's COVID-19 epidemiological tracking system as an example. The capability to map large datasets existed by 2014, but the system only emerged after the MERS outbreak prompted legal revisions, the removal of barriers between ministries, standardized data formats, and privacy safeguards. The author describes AI as a mirror that reflects existing prejudices and structural problems and a megaphone that amplifies them. The piece then sketches three phases of modern Korean society, a closed hierarchical era, an open liberal era after 1987, and a fractured winner-takes-all society after the 1998 currency crisis. It says this fracture has produced what the author calls a three-no society marked by distrust, discontent, and anxiety, which AI could accelerate.

The author places much of the responsibility on institutions and on the people who design and run them, arguing that opacity has moved from personal networks into algorithms that set platform fees, welfare screening, and credit scores. The piece also cites the Seongsu Bridge collapse, the Sampoong Department Store collapse, and the Sewol ferry disaster as examples of slow-building disasters rooted in past growth-at-all-costs policies. The author warns of three waves of change, one affecting personal cognition as people outsource thinking, one hitting organizations as automated agents replace the routine tasks through which newcomers learn, and one from physical AI reaching care, logistics, construction, and manufacturing. The piece says Korea cannot simply copy the American market model, the Chinese state model, or the European regulatory model, and proposes "dignity" as the goal, built on safety, cohesion, inclusion, and capability. The excerpt ends before the author details the specific measures, so the articles provided do not include the full set of proposed changes or numbers beyond the dates above.

stories.Headline: Dartmouth Provost Resigns Over AI Use
stories.Summary:
Dartmouth University Provost Santiago Schnell resigned on a Wednesday after a faculty-led review committee concluded that he used artificial intelligence to meaningfully alter his writing and fell short of the university's academic integrity standards. The controversy began in August, when Semafor reported that the AI detector Pangram flagged an editorial Schnell wrote for The Washington Post as at least 80 percent AI generated. The Dartmouth student newspaper later applied the same tool to nine professional articles he published this year and found them to be 96 percent AI written, including the Post essay and two academic papers on mathematics. Schnell acknowledged using AI to help with his writing, but he said it did not substitute for his research, intellectual judgment or authorship.

President Sian Leah Beilock convened an independent advisory committee of faculty and alumni to examine his AI use, whether he met publishers' disclosure requirements, whether he was honest about that use, and whether it violated university policy. The committee's eight-page report, delivered to Beilock on Tuesday, did not rely on AI detectors, which it did not use, and instead examined articles written for publishers that barred or required disclosure of AI use, along with records from Schnell's university Claude account. According to the report, he used the university's enterprise version of Claude to substantially edit a manuscript published in ChemSystemsChem last month, troubleshoot code and generate figures after peer reviewers requested major revisions. The committee also found that the publisher had required disclosure of such use since at least 2023, while Schnell had said the requirement began in 2025. It further concluded that his disclosures and public statements understated how he had used AI, and that he had not provided logs from personal AI accounts when asked.

Beilock wrote in a memo to students, faculty and staff that she expects senior leaders to hold themselves to the highest standards, and she said Schnell resigned out of respect for his colleagues and the institution. The resignation came less than two weeks before faculty leaders were set to hold a no-confidence vote against him. In the same message, Beilock said Dartmouth, which calls itself the birthplace of AI, would continue to keep pace with the technology while modeling transparency and human judgment. Matthew Delmont, a history professor and associate dean of faculty for international and interdisciplinary studies, will serve as interim provost through June 2028.

stories.Headline: Acts of God Meet Acts of AI in Private Equity’s New Debt Play
stories.Summary:
Private equity firms are adding force majeure-style clauses to new buyout loans that would let borrowers pause the consequences of defaults they attribute to artificial intelligence disruption. H.I.G. Capital secured such language in a €470 million ($524 million) loan backing its majority stake in Terras Group, a German-headquartered provider of infrastructure engineering and construction services, according to people familiar with the deal. Several creditors said the language goes further than usual and has appeared in at least two leveraged buyout financings since September. One lender-side lawyer, Jeremy Duffy, a partner and chair of European leveraged finance at Cahill Gordon & Reindel LLP, said lenders and investors are closely reviewing such proposals.

Traditionally, force majeure clauses cover catastrophes such as hurricanes, earthquakes, the Covid pandemic or the 9/11 attacks. In the Terras deal, H.I.G. adapted that language so the clock stops on a default if AI disrupts the company, alongside other triggers including Covid-19 or another pandemic, a substantial rise in energy or resource prices, and war or terrorism. Lenders normally allow a grace period, typically 30 days, before a missed interest payment becomes a default that lets them demand repayment. The new provisions are framed as extending that grace period, but AI disruption has no clear end date the way a pandemic might. According to one person familiar with the deal, the clause would let Terras defer the consequences of unpaid interest for as long as it feels AI's impact, although the company still owes the interest.

Some creditors argue the provisions undermine the basic expectation that lenders will recover their money even when things go wrong. Lenders succeeded in having similar language struck from Bain Capital's €4.7 billion-equivalent ($5.3 billion) leveraged loan for its acquisition of a controlling stake in Volkswagen AG's heavy diesel-engine unit Everllence, according to the same people. The market's approach to investor protections has become split, with sponsors pressing for looser terms where they expect deals to perform well and reinserting covenants in troubled sectors like software. Software-as-a-service firms are seen as especially exposed to AI disruption, and buyout firms have large bets on them. H.I.G. was advised by Paul, Weiss lawyers including Neel Sachdev, while representatives at H.I.G. and Bain declined to comment and Sachdev did not reply to a request for comment.

stories.Headline: Could next-gen artificial intelligence help map out future space outposts?
stories.Summary:
Researchers at The Ohio State University have built an artificial intelligence framework that could help plan future trips to the moon. Developed by Gokce Inal, a PhD candidate in civil, environmental and geodetic engineering, the system is meant to help scientists judge possible lunar landing sites, flag hazards that future crews could face, and search new areas for valuable geologic features. The work was presented this month at the 58th Annual Meeting of the Division for Planetary Sciences of the American Astronomical Society. Inal said the findings were shared as part of a broader effort to bring together artificial intelligence and planetary science.

The system, called LUMINA, is an extension of an earlier lunar model known as LLaVA-LE, which could describe lunar terrain and answer science questions. LUMINA adds the ability to plan and carry out multistep analyses, evaluate candidate landing sites, and explain the evidence behind its recommendations. Early results show it can make complex lunar observations and produce meaningful commentary on landing sites, which could help planners find areas rich in water ice and other resources. Inal designed the tool as a decision-support system rather than a semi-autonomous machine, so that it works alongside mission planners who make the final calls.

She described the goal as an active scientific assistant rather than a passive tool that only answers questions. Alper Yilmaz, a co-author and professor in the same department at Ohio State, said the approach could also apply to other planetary bodies, including Earth, Mars and some asteroids. He noted that few GPT-like map models currently exist for space exploration, and that the team aims to make its model generalizable to other surfaces. Yilmaz added that as datasets grow more advanced, efficient tools will be needed to sort through them, since finding the best landing spots would otherwise be like searching for a needle in a haystack.

He also said such a system could act as another set of eyes to verify and question findings in a harsh environment. The team plans to test LUMINA on new high-quality lunar data and to further evaluate how well it supports mission planning as the system develops. Inal noted that NASA's Artemis program creates important opportunities for this research, and that new lunar data could improve systems like hers. Reporting on the work came from Ohio State News and Newswise, which both credited the research to the university.

The companies are developing the technology together, and Otto Group will evaluate a wider rollout across its logistics network if the second phase succeeds.

The robots run on Cortex, Sereact's Physical AI model, which can handle items it has never seen before without product-specific training or a fixed catalog. Returns are difficult because items arrive folded, crumpled or repackaged, and the product mix of a multi-category retailer keeps changing. Cortex decides in real time how to grasp each item, assess its condition and route it. Sereact trains and validates the model with NVIDIA Isaac Sim, NVIDIA Isaac Lab and NVIDIA Cosmos, turning real picks into simulated variants so that fixes can reach the robots within days rather than weeks.

Sereact operates and maintains the systems under a Robotics-as-a-Service model. The robots will be introduced in stages, and each stage will produce operational feedback that the partners will use to improve the systems. The companies say this process will show whether the technology meets the reliability, flexibility and quality standards needed for broader use.

Martin Umland, Group Vice President Supply Chain Management at Otto Group, said the project will show at real scale how far Physical AI can go in making returns faster and the supply chain more flexible. Sereact CEO and co-founder Dr. Ralf Gulde said a robot that knows only yesterday's catalog is of little use in a returns center and that each handled return improves the model. The partnership is part of Otto Group's medium-term commitment to invest €350 million in technology and AI, and it follows the group's earlier robotics investments across its logistics operations. stories.Headline: AI Is Thriving at Capital One | Thomas H. Davenport and Randy Bean - MIT Sloan Management Review
stories.Summary:
Capital One, the U.S. bank, has been using data and analytics for decades, and according to a column by Thomas H. Davenport and Randy Bean published in MIT Sloan Management Review on October 28, 2026, it is now expanding its use of artificial intelligence across several areas of the business. The authors say the bank, founded in 1994 as a spinout from the credit card business of Signet Bank, is the eighth-largest U.S. bank by assets as of September 2026 and ranks second among global banks in AI capabilities in the 2025 Evident AI Index, behind only JPMorgan Chase. The column is based on interviews with Prem Natarajan, the bank's chief enterprise AI officer and chief scientist, and Amy Lenander, its chief data officer. Neither the authors nor the executives describe a single new rule or law, so the piece is better understood as a profile of current practice than as an announcement of a discrete change.

The articles report several concrete uses of AI at the bank. In customer service, generative AI helps human agents find accurate answers faster, and agentic AI produces call summaries, which several hundred agents now use, with the summaries added to customer records. In risk and compliance, the bank built an intelligent assistant for auditors that Natarajan said reduced quality errors by 85 percent and saved an estimated 5,000 hours across 30 auditors in a few months, with one audit task falling from five hours to three minutes. Lenander said the bank analyzes call transcripts and clickstream data with generative AI to spot near-real-time trends, and it manages data as "data products" owned by the teams closest to them. The bank has also begun marketing Databolt, a data tokenization tool built internally to protect sensitive information in AI workflows, through Capital One Software, its second product after Slingshot, a cloud spending tool.

Natarajan argued that measuring AI purely by quarterly return on investment is premature and shortsighted, saying, "You can't achieve transformation if you're focused on quarterly ROI," and that "the ultimate ROI is a happy customer." Lenander framed the bank's current work as an extension of its long history of automated decisioning, moving from regression to machine learning to generative AI, and she said that proprietary, unified data gives the bank a competitive advantage. The authors conclude that the company remains a leader in data-driven and AI-driven enterprise practice, and they describe this as a trait deeply embedded in its culture. stories.Headline: Using AI to improve lives: UTulsa students advance prosthetic research - The University of Tulsa

Students at The University of Tulsa are using artificial intelligence to study how prosthetic limbs affect the comfort and confidence of people who wear them. The work takes place in the biomechanics laboratory of John M. Henshaw, department head of mechanical engineering and Harry H. Rogers Endowed Chair in Mechanical Engineering. Students combine engineering, healthcare and machine learning to find out why one prosthetic device may feel more comfortable than another. The article reports that the project brings students from several disciplines together.

Maddie Fulk, a master's student in mechanical engineering, and fellow student researcher Maura Wahl analyzed data collected from people with below-the-knee amputations as they walked with different prosthetic devices. Motion sensors placed across the body recorded hundreds of measurements tied to gait, balance and movement. Using machine-learning techniques, the students looked for the measurements that best separated one device from another. The article says the model consistently flagged movement near the pelvis as one of the strongest indicators, which suggests changes near the body's center of mass may reveal how users experience different prosthetics.

Henshaw described the model as very successful and said it revealed patterns that would have been hard to find with traditional methods alone. Wahl said many people may not know that a better option exists, and that some wear prosthetics that do not work well with their bodies. The team is now investigating whether sensors in smartphones could eventually gather similar movement data during everyday activities. The article notes that such an approach could make prosthetic evaluation more accessible and scalable.

Andreas Polycarpou, dean of the College of Engineering & Computer Science, said the project reflects the kind of hands-on experience that sets a UTulsa education apart. He said students are working with faculty mentors on real-world problems using technologies such as AI. The article adds that the experience is shaping career plans, with Fulk aiming for medicine and Wahl considering graduate study in prosthetics and biomedical engineering.
