This summer, Engineering Summer Bridge added weekly Critical AI Literacy Lunch and Learns, lectures on the development and deployment of AI systems. The lectures drew on research from the AI Institute for Societal Decision Making, an initiative led by Carnegie Mellon University with collaborators including Penn State. Students used the lunch sessions to plan solutions for disaster response and recovery, starting from the communities they wanted to help rather than forcing AI into their designs.

The lunchtime format was chosen to keep the setting low stakes so students could engage without becoming overwhelmed. The sessions also cover cognitive and social sciences, parts of the humanities, and human-AI interaction, which the program presents as a foundation for future coursework and careers. MEPO's design competition has used a custom chatbot since 2024, developed with Penn State's Human in Computing and Cognition Lab. The chatbot is trained to guide students through each year's challenge, improve factual accuracy, and avoid suggesting complete solutions. Students described using it to test their understanding of their scenarios, and one team worked on helping hazmat crews contain dangerous gases in a skyscraper.

Christopher Dancy, an associate professor at Penn State who directs the lab and is a principal investigator in the AI institute, led the Lunch and Learn design and said the aim was to give students a solid base before they take on AI-heavy coursework. Lauren Griggs, director of the Multicultural Engineering Program that runs both programs, said students from underrepresented groups who took part in either program were more likely to stay in the College of Engineering than similar students who did not. She framed the programs as a way to keep human connection central as AI systems become more common. The article names sponsors for both programs and notes that the AI institute work is supported by National Science Foundation grant IIS 2229881, with the MEPO work supported under award 2144887. It does not describe any further changes planned for next summer.

Articles.Title: Incoming first-year students build AI literacy in summer engineering programs

stories.Headline: Elon Drone Day to explore AI, emerging drone applications on Friday, Oct. 30
stories.Summary:
Elon University's School of Communications will host its annual Elon Drone Day on Friday, Oct. 30, featuring presentations, demonstrations and networking in Turner Theater and the Snow Family Grand Atrium. The free event is organized with the North Carolina chapter of the Association for Uncrewed Vehicle Systems International and is open to the public, though attendees must register. Recreational and commercial pilots, industry professionals, educators and students are expected to take part. This year's program puts particular emphasis on artificial intelligence and emerging drone applications. Last year's event drew a record 185 attendees, vendors and volunteers.

The keynote will be delivered by Sambit Bhattacharya, a professor at Fayetteville State University, under the title "Preflight Checks for Intelligent Machines: What Drones Can Teach Us About Trustworthy AI." His talk will argue that aviation's focus on safety, testing and accountability can guide the development of reliable AI systems. Drawing on research from Fayetteville State's Intelligent Systems Lab, he will examine how autonomous drones make decisions and the difficulties of deploying AI in real-world settings. Bhattacharya's research team was recently awarded a $10 million grant to expand its work on AI and unmanned aerial systems. Beyond the keynote, the program covers agriculture, disaster response, invasive species management and flight planning software.

Randy Piland, a teaching professor of visual communication who organizes the event, said the keynote reflects both the growing role of AI in drones and Elon's wider effort to broaden conversations about AI across its programs. He noted that many new autonomous drones depend on AI to function. Piland's stated aim is to give local drone enthusiasts and professionals a place to exchange knowledge, network and find solutions to their problems. The schedule opens with a drone soccer demonstration by Asheboro City Schools and a vendor showcase. Flight demonstrations take place in the afternoon in the parking area behind the Schar Center.

Elon Drone Day was established in 2021 and has grown into an annual gathering for people interested in the evolving drone industry. Its mission has stayed the same even as the technology has changed quickly. Organizers describe the event as a practical outlet for people working to improve their drone operations. The 2026 gathering will carry that purpose forward with its focus on AI and new applications. Registration is required for the free public event.

Articles.Title: Elon Drone Day to explore AI, emerging drone applications on Friday, Oct. 30

stories.Headline: Learner collaborates with MIT peers to develop book of AI insights
stories.Summary:
Prabha Jha, a Verizon leader, and 20 peers from an MIT Open Learning course for senior executives released "The AI Anthology," a collection of essays on how artificial intelligence has affected industries and society. The book came about one year after Jha's cohort finished the AI for Senior Executives program offered through MIT xPRO. Jha had taken the course, which included an in-person component, to deepen her understanding of AI. The MIT News article reports the release as occurring in late October 2026.

The book is meant to support other leaders facing similar challenges with AI and to capture perspectives that go beyond operational efficiency and revenue growth. Jha's idea grew out of a gathering at the home of Manolis Kellis, a professor in MIT's Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, where a peer shared how her interest in AI stemmed from work on her mother's Alzheimer's disease and dementia. The article also describes an interruption in Jha's studies, when a severe infection kept her in the hospital for two weeks and led her to join the next cohort with MIT staff help. She described the extra five days on campus as a valuable part of her learning, since she met peers from diverse backgrounds face-to-face.

Jha argues that many leaders remain stuck on traditional measures of success such as revenue, cost-cutting, and time saved, and says leaders must think differently to find more empowerment through AI. She believes AI adoption is not optional for businesses and sees it as a transformation that can help people overcome insecurity and grow. Jha also said that Verizon's role in providing critical infrastructure to groups such as first responders and children gives the company an obligation that AI can help it meet. She is currently working on an initiative to help small and medium-sized businesses understand which AI tools they need, how AI fits their operations, and how to measure success.

Articles.Title: Learner collaborates with MIT peers to develop book of AI insights

stories.Headline: The 5 forces creating urgency around ethical AI adoption
stories.Summary:
Jeffrey Saviano, a senior lecturer at the MIT Sloan School of Management and a former EY executive, has argued that organizations face five pressures that make adopting ethical AI urgent. His view appears in an excerpt from his new book, "Boundaries of Tolerance: A Foundational Model for Ethical AI Strategy and Governance," published by Wiley, with the excerpt released on October 28, 2026. According to the piece, artificial intelligence is driving innovation across industries while also creating risks and ethical consequences that traditional enterprise risk frameworks no longer handle well. Saviano frames AI governance as a leadership question that reaches the boardroom and senior executive teams, not only technologists or regulators. The article describes the human cost of governance gaps.

A patient's diagnosis can be compromised by a model trained on incomplete or biased clinical data, and a job candidate can be rejected by an automated hiring system shaped by outdated employment patterns. Small input errors can cascade into outcomes that reinforce inequality and erode stakeholder trust. Saviano prefers the term "ethical AI" over "responsible AI" because it stresses the role of leadership judgment in designing and deploying these systems. He also argues that ethical AI strategy has become a leadership necessity as AI moves into core operations across nearly every industry. Saviano identifies five forces behind this urgency.

Competitive pressure pushes companies to deploy AI quickly, often before leaders have clarified how it should be governed. AI also changes how risk behaves, since minor problems can escalate rapidly once systems spread through an organization. Investors and markets are beginning to ask who oversees AI risk, in ways that resemble earlier scrutiny of cybersecurity. Employees across functions are raising ethical questions about data, deployment, and responsibility, and when decision authority is unclear, those concerns either go unvoiced or are settled informally. Finally, public expectations about fairness and human dignity are rising, shaped by civil society groups and scholars, and compliance alone no longer answers them.

Saviano concludes that these forces have changed what leadership must do. Ethical AI strategy is no longer a discretionary add-on, and leaders must decide what their organizations will tolerate from intelligent systems when regulatory guidance is incomplete. He argues that this responsibility cannot be delegated to regulators, which explains why ethical AI governance now belongs in the boardroom and C-suite. The excerpt does not describe specific regulatory deadlines or enforcement steps beyond these points.

Articles.Title: The 5 forces creating urgency around ethical AI adoption

stories.Headline: Body Sensors and AI May Lead to New Kinds of Learning
stories.Summary:
Researchers at NJIT have proposed a concept called Minds and Machines: A Neuro-Adaptive AI Learning Companion, which combines physiological sensors, AI and extended reality to help students stay on track in their studies. The idea was reported on October 28, 2026, by NJIT News, with Evan Koblentz as the writer. Under the concept, students would wear a wrist device or headset that detects bodily signs of distress, such as overloaded brain waves measured by electroencephalogram, during lectures or other lessons. The article presents this as a way to spot students who may be falling behind or who are highly engaged and ready for harder material. The project is funded by a $50,000 university grant.

When those signs appear, an AI system would choose a different way to present the topic, drawing on preprogrammed knowledge of educational best practices and student motivation. The new material could be delivered in real time or later, and it could use augmented or virtual reality to make concepts more vivid. The approach could also extend beyond classrooms into hands-on settings such as NJIT's makerspace. Jessica Simon, a neuroscientist and pedagogical and instructional innovation specialist at the Center for Educational and Innovation and Excellence, is joint principal investigator with Zhifeng Kou, associate chair of biomedical engineering. Simon said personalized teaching has been shown to raise performance by at least two standard deviations, though the article notes the field of neuroscience-informed education is still young.

Kou said his interest grew from years of using AI for biomedical imaging analysis, and that when large language models emerged, he saw a way to help students learn. The team now faces the main hurdle of making the parts work together in a live classroom rather than only in a laboratory. They must separate useful body signals from background electrical noise and handle several signals while customizing instruction in real time. The researchers must also decide whether students are comfortable sharing body data and make sure that data stays private. Once the technical problems are solved, they plan to turn the research into a product that could be shared with other universities.

Several other faculty members are co-principal investigators on the project: Nicole Bosca, Elisa Kallioniemi, Bryan Pfister, Mengjia Xu and Lin Zhao. Kou emphasized that the goal is to build something practical and impactful, not only scientific. The article does not give a timeline for when the product might reach students or describe any results from testing with students. It frames the work as an early-stage effort in a growing field that combines education and neuroscience.

Articles.Title: Body Sensors and AI May Lead to New Kinds of Learning

stories.Headline: Coping with AI in our Communities
stories.Summary:
A four-part public forum series titled "Coping with AI in our Communities" is being held at College of the Atlantic, a college in Maine, running from October 25 through November 15. The series, announced on the college's website on October 28, 2026, is organized around current research on the problems people face in coping with advanced AI systems. The organizers say these systems increasingly behave less like obedient tools and more like insubordinate employees, independent agents, threatening competitors, and manipulators. Speakers will examine local and global challenges along with strategies for responding in individual lives and communities.

The series is free and open to all, though pre-registration is required for those who want to attend online. Sessions take place on Sundays at 6 p.m. in Room 102 of the Center for Human Ecology and are streamed live over Zoom. The dates and themes are October 25, on challenges and strategies for coping with AI in peaceful, ecological and spiritual ways; November 1, on negotiating futures with AI through a peace studies approach; November 8, on reclaiming digital commons in Maine through human-ecological approaches to community empowerment; and November 15, on spiritual approaches to AI drawing on Catholic, Quaker and Buddhist perspectives. Questions can be directed to the listed email address or to the phone number 207-460-1163.

The forums are presented by College of the Atlantic, and the announcement frames them as an alternative to approaches taken by researchers and companies, which the announcement says have been trying to engineer control over AI machines while also making them more capable at engineering than humans. The forum instead draws on peace studies, human ecology, and diverse spiritual and faith traditions. The organizers pose the central questions of how people can benefit from helpful AI while safeguarding families, companies and communities, and how they can keep their futures human. A recording of highlights from the first forum in the series is already available, according to the announcement.

Articles.Title: Coping with AI in our Communities

stories.Headline: $20M grant renews UH role in AI research to improve engineering design
stories.Summary:
The University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa will keep helping develop artificial intelligence tools that could make it faster and less expensive to design and test products such as airplanes and wind turbines, following a new $20 million federal grant. Three Mānoa faculty members, Assistant Professors Chrisy Xiyu Du and Andrei A. Klishin of the Department of Mechanical Engineering and Associate Professor June Zhang of the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, will serve as senior personnel in the National Science Foundation AI Institute in Dynamic Systems. The five-year award renews the institute's work, which the NSF first funded for 2021 through 2026, and it will cover its next phase of research from 2026 through 2031. The award supports a collaboration among several universities that uses AI to understand and predict how complex physical systems behave.

The institute focuses on AI that learns from physical data and the laws of science, rather than general-purpose tools that mainly handle text and images. Engineers could use these methods to test ideas more efficiently, reduce the need for costly computer simulations and improve designs before building expensive prototypes. The funding also gives participating faculty flexibility to pursue research questions over several years, support graduate students and postdoctoral researchers, and work with experts at other universities. The article describes Klishin's 2025 study, which developed a method to help AI identify the underlying rules behind noisy, real-world data, and Zhang's work on teaching AI systems to train themselves when data is limited.

Klishin said that AI can help engineers go beyond predicting how a system will behave and explore how to make it work better, adding that combining AI with an understanding of physics can help researchers test more ideas and improve designs. The article also points to HydroGym, an open-source platform developed through the institute that lets researchers test AI methods for predicting and controlling fluid flows. Such tools matter for designing aircraft, ships and wind turbines, and the platform aims to make simulation tools more accessible so researchers can build on one another's work. The institute is led by the University of Washington, with Mānoa as a participating campus alongside Harvard, Columbia, the University of Michigan and Caltech.

Articles.Title: $20M grant renews UH role in AI research to improve engineering design

stories.Headline: Networked State Capital in China’s AI Ecosystem
stories.Summary:
This is an event announcement rather than breaking news, and the articles do not describe any incident, so I cannot write it as a breaking story with the required structure. What the page does give is a talk scheduled for November 3, 2026, from 12:20 to 1:20 pm, at Harvard Law School, where Curtis J. Milhaupt of Stanford Law School will present "Networked State Capital in China's AI Ecosystem." The talk is part of the East Asian Legal Studies series and is co-sponsored by the Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society. Milhaupt is joined by Liwen Lin of the University of British Columbia's Allard School of Law on the underlying joint project. Registration is not required but is appreciated, and a Harvard ID is needed to enter the buildings.

The research addresses a puzzle about China's artificial intelligence sector. Self-reliance and technological resilience in AI are described as national priorities of the Chinese party-state, yet most major players, including firms the government has designated as part of an "AI National Team" and AI unicorns, remain privately controlled at the top of their corporate groups. The authors ask why leading players are not subject to the apex-level state ownership and hierarchical administrative control usually associated with Chinese state capitalism. Using corporate registry data, the project maps where state-affiliated capital enters private technology groups, finding it positioned at multiple points within ownership, investment, and deployment networks, typically in subsidiaries below the apex. The authors argue that these positions can create durable channels for coordinating technology development, pilot projects, standard setting, and deployment with policy goals.

Based on the article, the analysis reframes China's approach to state capitalism in AI as a networked system of state capital and institutionalized state-private interaction, rather than a simple split between state-owned and private firms. Milhaupt is described as an internationally recognized expert on comparative corporate governance, East Asian legal systems (particularly Japanese law), and state capitalism. The page does not indicate any findings beyond the framing above, nor any follow-up publication date. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Networked State Capital in China’s AI Ecosystem

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Neurosurgery: Balancing Innovation with Responsibility
stories.Summary:
This is an opinion and commentary piece rather than a breaking news report, so the instructions to write the story in the requested structure apply. The article, published by Stanford Medicine on October 28, 2026, argues that artificial intelligence is entering neurosurgery as a growing set of routine tools, including documentation platforms, inbox management, radiographic analysis, scheduling, patient communication, and early decision support. The authors say the field should focus less on whether AI will affect practice and more on how it is implemented so that patient trust, professional accountability, and the specialty's ethical standards are preserved. They cite a 2025 systematic review of AI in neurosurgery, along with a Coalition for Health AI guidance document, a 2023 review of medical liability, a pending lawsuit, and a 2023 Nature paper on a speech neuroprosthesis as supporting sources.

The authors identify several requirements and concerns. They say patients deserve meaningful transparency when AI is listening to, summarizing, recommending, or otherwise influencing their care, and they point to a recent lawsuit, Washington et al v Sutter Health et al, filed in the Northern District of California on April 7, 2026, which alleges that patient conversations were recorded and processed by AI note-taking tools without adequate consent. They also warn of automation bias, the tendency to defer to polished, confident AI outputs even when they are wrong. They argue that models should be validated locally, monitored after deployment, and governed by institutional policies, since neurosurgical datasets are often small and clinical situations highly context dependent. Health systems should involve clinicians, data scientists, administrators, legal experts, ethicists, and, where possible, patient representatives in governance.

The authors state that physicians remain legally and ethically responsible for medical decisions, and that AI may assist but does not replace professional judgment or liability. They describe the Coalition for Health AI's guidance, which emphasizes local validation, monitoring, and adaptable governance, as an encouraging step. The piece is written by Stanford neurosurgery authors and is framed as a call for the specialty to help define the rules rather than remain passive. It also weighs potential benefits, including reduced documentation burden, more precise risk prediction, operative video feedback for training, and outreach to vulnerable patients at risk of being lost to follow-up. The authors conclude that thoughtful implementation could strengthen the physician-patient relationship, while careless deployment could erode the trust on which clinical care depends.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Neurosurgery: Balancing Innovation with Responsibility

stories.Headline: Optimizing AI energy consumption throughout its entire lifecycle
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the University of Michigan Engineering, working with colleagues at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and defense contractor BAE Systems, have launched a project aimed at cutting the energy that AI requires by up to half. The work is funded by a $1.83 million contract from the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, DARPA, and is titled "E-CALC: Energy Calculus for ML Lifecycle Optimization." The article was published on October 27, 2026. The project is set to run for two years.

The proposed system would let developers estimate energy use at every stage of an AI workflow, from data processing and model training to real-world deployment, instead of relying on costly trial-and-error testing across thousands of hardware and software setups. The team plans to build high-precision energy measurement tools that combine physical sensors with software analysis, and to release them as open-source documentation and software. The mathematical framework behind these tools is called "energy calculus." The article notes that data center energy consumption is expected to more than double by 2030 from roughly 420 terawatt-hours in 2024, with AI driving much of that growth.

The project is led by Mosharaf Chowdhury, an associate professor of computer science and engineering at the University of Michigan and the principal investigator. Nishil Talati, an assistant professor of electrical and computer engineering at UIUC, and David Nicholson, a principal research engineer at BAE Systems, are the co-principal investigators. Chowdhury said that AI's rapidly growing electricity use could raise costs, strain power infrastructure, and make advanced AI harder to deploy, and that the project asks how the broad benefits of AI can be obtained with minimal energy. The article also states that the DARPA funding covers the project's work, while the views expressed are those of the authors and not necessarily of DARPA.

The effort builds on earlier tools from the same team, including Zeus, which automatically adjusts settings such as batch size and power limits to reduce energy use during AI model training, and ML.ENERGY, a public leaderboard that compares energy consumption across open-weight AI models and open-source software frameworks. The article says misalignments between software and hardware can waste as much as 30 percent of electricity during AI model training alone. Lower energy demand would reduce the cost of AI and extend battery life for AI-enabled devices, which the article describes as especially important for national defense equipment that runs complex AI under strict power limits. A related October 12, 2026 report notes that NVIDIA is evaluating how to add the energy-saving software to its open-source training platform.

Articles.Title: Optimizing AI energy consumption throughout its entire lifecycle

stories.Headline: MATRIX AI director joins World Economic Forum council on next-generation computing
stories.Summary:
Dhireesha Kudithipudi, founding director of the MATRIX AI Consortium at UT San Antonio, has been named a member of the World Economic Forum's Global Future Council on Next-Generation Computing. She is one of only 19 global experts selected to advise global leaders on emerging computing technologies. The appointment, reported by the university in late October 2026, recognizes her leadership in transdisciplinary research. The university says the role positions MATRIX as a contributor to international discussions on the next era of technology.

The Forum's Global Future Councils form a knowledge network of 37 thematic groups with more than 700 experts. Kudithipudi will serve alongside figures from IBM Research, SandboxAQ, Hewlett Packard Enterprise, UC Berkeley, the University of Toronto, Australia's Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation and the European Space Agency. The council's work feeds into its Next-Generation Computing Framework, released in October 2026 with the Forum, which guides governments and organizations on the technologies and strategic priorities shaping computing. Kudithipudi also received a special invitation to attend the Forum's Quantum Economy Day in Geneva, Switzerland, in October.

Kudithipudi's own research focuses on neuromorphic AI, artificial intelligence modeled on the brain, with an emphasis on reducing energy use. The article explains that conventional computing separates memory and processing, which contributes to the high energy demands of many AI models, while neuromorphic systems aim to learn and adapt at much lower energy cost. In January 2025 she was lead author of a review in Nature that brought together international experts to examine how neuromorphic computing might scale. She has said her work aligns with the council's concern that computing grow more powerful while staying sustainable and centered on human needs.

MATRIX has grown under her leadership into a network of nearly 90 scientists across three organizations, with expertise in engineering, neuroscience, ethics, medicine and computing. The consortium works on healthcare, energy, cybersecurity and smart cities, and Kudithipudi leads national research efforts. She serves as institutional lead for two Centers of Excellence and contributes to six in total. The university also launched THOR: The Neuromorphic Commons this year, which the article describes as the nation's first open-access hub for brain-inspired computing, funded by the National Science Foundation. The university says the appointment will expand its role in international discussions and create new collaborations.

Articles.Title: MATRIX AI director joins World Economic Forum council on next-generation computing

stories.Headline: UWF to host Leadership in the Age of AI conference with special Veterans Day observance - University of West Florida
stories.Summary:
The University of West Florida's Office of Military Services announced that it will host the second annual Leadership in the Age of AI conference, followed by a UWF Veterans Day Observance, on Friday, Nov. 6, in the UWF Conference Center. The office is working with the Aylstock, Witkin, Kreis & Overholtz Center for Leadership and the Center for Cybersecurity and AI on the event. The free conference is sponsored by PenAir Credit Union and will examine how artificial intelligence is changing modern leadership. The program also includes a special observance honoring those who have served.

The event is open to students, faculty, staff, military service members and their families, veterans and the wider Pensacola community. Attendees can expect networking and breakfast beginning at 8 a.m., followed by opening remarks and a keynote from Patrick Rooney, director of entrepreneurial development at Co:Lab Pensacola. A leadership panel moderated by Christian Hendrick, a retired U.S. Air Force Special Operations veteran and systems integration subject matter expert at Booz Allen Hamilton, will look at practical uses of AI across industries. Panelists include Joshua Turner, Joshua Hartigan and Jay Wells, who will discuss AI's influence on leadership, entrepreneurship, decision-making and workforce development.

The conference is intended to encourage dialogue among academia, industry and the military about emerging technologies. After the panel, the program shifts to the Veterans Day observance, which will feature Lieutenant Colonel Keith Nelson and recognize military service and sacrifice. Dr. Andrew Del Gaudio, executive director of the Office of Military Services, said the event is meant to broaden perspectives and give participants new ideas for navigating a changing professional landscape. He also said the observance gives the university a chance to honor those who have served the nation.

Del Gaudio described the office's commitment to serving those who serve and strengthening ties between the military community and the university. The university presents the event as a way to link conversations about the future of leadership with the principles of service and responsibility that veterans embody. Those who want more information or wish to register can visit uwf.edu/AgeofAI, while details about the Office of Military Services, the Aylstock, Witkin, Kreis & Overholtz Center and the Center for Cybersecurity and AI are available at uwf.edu/militaryservices, uwf.edu/awko and uwf.edu/cyberai. The announcement was published on Oct. 27, 2026, and reaffirms the university's support for veterans, service members and military-affiliated individuals.

Articles.Title: UWF to host Leadership in the Age of AI conference with special Veterans Day observance - University of West Florida

stories.Headline: Taxing artificial intelligence: What’s on the table, and what’s at stake
stories.Summary:
The Brookings commentary by Elena Patel and Aparna Mathur, published October 27, 2026, examines proposals to tax artificial intelligence and what is at stake for federal revenue. The authors start from the premise that AI could raise productivity while also replacing some workers, and that the answer to how many and how fast remains uncertain. Because individual income and payroll taxes generate roughly 85% of federal tax receipts, a shift of income from wages to business profits and other capital income could lower effective tax rates and erode revenue at the same time that demand for programs helping displaced workers grows. Lawmakers have responded with AI-specific tax proposals aimed at different goals, including maintaining revenue, funding displaced workers, covering the power and water costs of AI facilities, and slowing AI growth.

The authors lay out the main arguments for taxing AI, each resting on a different scenario. One holds that AI could shrink the tax base, leaving income and payroll tax receipts falling before any offsetting gains from profits arrive, if they arrive at all. A second concerns the costs AI infrastructure imposes on nearby communities, since data centers consume large amounts of electricity and water, and two-thirds of data centers built since 2022 sit in regions already short on water. A third holds that firms may be overspending on AI in pursuit of market share, which a tax could curb, though the authors note this is hard to verify.

They also argue that AI-specific taxes are easy to explain politically but are not required to reach these goals, since reforming capital income taxation, adopting a value-added tax, a carbon tax, or a corporate cash-flow tax could address some of the same concerns. The piece adds that such taxes could conflict with international tax and domestic investment strategies and shape where AI infrastructure is built, with implications for national security. The commentary then weighs the leading designs, which target different points in the AI production process. A training compute tax would charge developers for computing power used in training runs, offering timely revenue and a narrow set of taxpayers, but it would depend on self-reported data and be hard to predict in yield.

A data center electricity tax could be verified through existing utility meters, though separating AI use from other computing use would again require self-reporting, and a related approach would have data centers pay for grid upgrades instead of passing costs to other ratepayers. A usage tax on tokens would be broader and less well targeted, falling on both labor-displacing and productivity-enhancing applications, and tokens vary in length and computing demand across models. A windfall profit tax, discussed last, would reach profits rather than activity. The authors caution that these designs differ in timing, revenue potential, economic cost, and ease of administration, and that each involves trade-offs.

Articles.Title: Taxing artificial intelligence: What’s on the table, and what’s at stake

stories.Headline: AI Doesn’t Have To Be an Empire. It Can Be a Bicycle.
stories.Summary:
Karen Hao, an award-winning journalist and author of Empire of AI, gave a talk at Lorimer Chapel at Colby College as part of the Davis Institute for Artificial Intelligence's Distinguished Lecture Series. In the talk she compared today's largest AI companies to historic empires and argued that ordinary people can push back against them. The audience, which included students from Bowdoin College, gave her a standing ovation when she finished. Stacy Doore, Clare Booth Luce Associate Professor of Computer Science, introduced her. Doore called Hao a powerful ally for advocates of ethical AI.

Hao said that companies such as OpenAI are pursuing a scale-at-all-costs approach that consolidates economic and political power. She drew parallels with past empires, saying these companies claim resources that are not theirs, exploit large amounts of labor, monopolize knowledge production, and justify their actions with a moral and existential imperative. She warned that training ever-larger models risks eroding intellectual property and requires data centers that use large amounts of energy, freshwater, and minerals for computer chips. Her alternative was to build smaller, task-specific systems, which she likened to bicycles rather than rockets. She cited AlphaFold by DeepMind, which predicts protein structures, as an example of a tool trained on a curated dataset that does not need supercomputers to run.

Hao pointed to grassroots resistance as proof that the trend is not inevitable. She described Tucson, Arizona, where Amazon proposed a $3.6-billion data center called Project Blue, and where residents formed the No Desert Data Center Coalition to fight it. She said the coalition packed city hall on a day when temperatures reached 114 degrees Fahrenheit, and the council voted 7-0 to stop the project in its current form. Her message to the audience was that individuals can resist the idea that giant AI companies are all-powerful. She summed up her view by saying that when people rise, empires fall.

Articles.Title: AI Doesn’t Have To Be an Empire. It Can Be a Bicycle.

stories.Headline: Kempner hosts Mass AI Hub grant award celebration
stories.Summary:
Massachusetts leaders gathered at Harvard University's Kempner Institute for the Study of Natural and Artificial Intelligence to celebrate five recipients of the Mass AI Hub's 2026 Applied AI Models Innovation Challenge, which awards nearly $3.3 million to projects tackling challenges across key industries. The event was reported by news.harvard.edu on October 27, 2026. Massachusetts Secretary of Economic Development Eric Paley attended along with leaders from the Massachusetts Technology Collaborative and Mass AI Hub, and Harvard Senior Vice Provost for Research John Shaw. The gathering marked the recognition of the selected projects and the work behind them. One grant recipient is Yulin Du, an assistant professor of computer science at Harvard and an investigator at the Kempner Institute, whose team is building large video generation models for industrial robotics.

The models are meant to produce detailed visual descriptions that let robots learn industrial tasks from video demonstrations and adapt without manual programming. The technology is intended to make automation more flexible and affordable for small and midsize businesses in manufacturing, logistics and recycling. Du said in his award video that the team plans to open source the model and provide inference code so others can connect it to any robotics platform. Paley said that Massachusetts is committed to responsible AI that addresses challenges facing industries across the state. He said the challenge supports projects that will strengthen the economy, advance strategic sectors and reinforce the state's position as a hub for applied AI.

Shaw said that sustained commitment to innovation allows the institutions to have a positive impact, recruit top talent and secure resources for innovative work. He stressed that this success is not limited to Harvard or the Kempner Institute, but depends on the broader ecosystem of partner universities, affiliated hospitals and the private sector in the region. The other recipients include the Atlantic Resiliency Innovation Institute, which is developing an AI-driven coastal resilience platform for hyperlocal flood-risk predictions for energy infrastructure, and Boston University, whose PandemIQ Llama tool supports real-time global disease surveillance and automated epidemiological reporting. Bristol Community College plans an AI system to assess workers' skills against industry frameworks, while UMass Lowell Applied Research Corporation is developing a platform to coordinate multiple sensor systems in counter-drone operations. The articles do not say when the projects will be completed.

stories.Headline: Quantum, fusion and AI stand out during DOE leader’s campus visit - UW–Madison News
stories.Summary:
On Monday, October 26, 2026, Under Secretary for Science Darío Gil of the U.S. Department of Energy spent a daylong visit touring laboratories and research spaces at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. Hosted by Vice Chancellor for Research Dorota Brzezinska, the visit showcased the university's work in quantum science, fusion energy, national security, critical minerals and biotechnology. Gil also toured the Proteus autonomous laboratory at the Wisconsin Energy Institute, along with the Great Lakes Bioenergy Research Center and the Wisconsin Crop Innovation Center. Discussions centered on the growing role of artificial intelligence in research and teaching, which one campus leader said has changed everything about the classroom.

The visit also tied into the university's part in the Department of Energy's Genesis Mission, under which UW–Madison recently received five Round 1 awards. Those awards support projects in artificial intelligence, fusion energy, critical mineral recovery and advanced computing. According to the article, the university earned more Genesis awards than any public university in the nation, tying Stanford University and trailing only the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Gil urged participants to become an integral part of the Genesis platform and to align campus strengths with national scientific priorities.

Participants also stressed the university's longstanding leadership in Department of Energy-supported bioenergy research. A session with early-career faculty, graduate students and postdoctoral researchers explored how federal investment and AI, machine learning and advanced computing are being used to tackle research challenges. Rose Cersonsky, a chemical and biological engineering professor, said AI has changed the faculty's responsibility in preparing students for the world beyond campus. A fusion energy roundtable highlighted a plan to build a fusion innovation hub based on the university's plasma physics expertise and its WHAM prototype device, which operates with Realta.

Participants called for collaboration among universities, industry, government agencies and national laboratories. Gil challenged attendees to think boldly about where their research could stand in five to 10 years. Brzezinska said the work is about more than university growth, describing it as a way to build a statewide, regional and national ecosystem for translating research, strengthening supply chains, developing workforce and expanding manufacturing. The article does not describe any next steps beyond the visit itself.

stories.Headline: Before the storm: Doctoral student earns international recognition for AI research on cognitive decline
stories.Summary:
Marquette University doctoral student Karen Wurzel has received the Best PhysioNet Challenge Oral Presentation award for her artificial intelligence research on cognitive decline. The award was presented at the 53rd Computing in Cardiology Conference in Madrid, Spain. Wurzel, who studies electrical and computer engineering, used AI to analyze sleep study data and look for patterns linked to future cognitive impairment, including dementia and Alzheimer's disease. Her work focuses on a single night of sleep, and the goal is to predict decline one to six years before a diagnosis.

The recognition came from the George B. Moody PhysioNet Challenge, an annual international competition co-organized by PhysioNet and Computing in Cardiology. The competition was established in 2000 and brings together researchers from different disciplines to address unresolved medical problems. This year's challenge asked participants to use data from sleep studies to predict future diagnoses of cognitive impairment. Wurzel's win places her work among computational approaches the challenge has used to evaluate emerging methods in biomedical research.

The article presents the award as a sign that the approach shows promise, though it does not describe the results in detail. Wurzel's research adviser, Dr. Richard Povinelli, praised her as an outstanding scientist with insight, rigor, and enthusiasm for discovery. Wurzel said that her adviser encourages her to pursue projects she cares about and serves as a sounding board when her work stalls. She also said that presenting technical work clearly has been a skill she worked to build, and that the award confirmed her effort.

Beyond prediction, Wurzel hopes her research will eventually help protect brain health, not only forecast its decline. The article describes Wurzel's path at Marquette, where she stood out in Povinelli's Introduction to Artificial Intelligence course in fall 2024 and began lab research during her first year as a Ph.D. student. The award has also raised the visibility of her work and brought new professional contacts, including conversations with researchers at the conference. The article does not say what comes next in her research timeline or whether the approach will be tested in clinical settings.

stories.Headline: Collaborative Collision: FSU researchers explore the future of artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Florida State University brought researchers from many fields together during its Discovery Days to explore how artificial intelligence can advance research and address complex challenges. The Office of Research hosted an event called "Collaborative Collision: The Future of Intelligence," which gave faculty a forum to discuss AI, connect across disciplines, and build partnerships. Attendees joined breakout sessions on how AI intersects with different fields, including human health, smart cities, and robotics. The day was designed to spark new ideas and collaborations that could lead to scientific discovery. The article was published on October 27, 2026.

Paul Marty, associate vice provost for academic innovation, said the conversations stressed keeping humanity at the center of the university's work on AI in society, health, education, science, and the workforce. Mike Wolfe, director of AI research solutions, said bringing different perspectives into one room was meant to encourage cross-domain discussions that could produce new project ideas. The discussions pushed researchers to look past their own work, find shared interests, and consider how their expertise could combine to address scientific and societal problems. Wolfe's group hopes these exchanges will lead directly to new partnerships. The event also highlighted the range of research at FSU, from autonomous security systems to the social aspects of AI integration and artistic creativity.

The Research Development team introduced Collaborative Collision LaunchPad Funding, which lets researchers turn their cross-departmental connections into joint projects. Participants were encouraged to form interdisciplinary teams and write proposals that could compete for up to $25,000 in seed funding. Jared Parmer, research development coordinator, said the event reflects the Office of Research's commitment to cutting-edge scholarship across all disciplines. He said the LaunchPad grants are meant to catalyze new research teams and seed new projects. In a dedicated resource room, attendees also met representatives from Information Technology Services, FSU Libraries, and the Research Computing Center to learn about tools and technical support.

Parmer and the other organizers framed the event as a step toward building a future that the university community can look forward to. The article directs readers who want more information on research development opportunities at FSU to the university's FSU Research Development site. The coverage presents the event as a starting point rather than a final outcome, with new teams and proposals expected to follow from the connections made that day. stories.Headline: Wall St banks, Blackstone line up $63 billion to finance Broadcom AI chips for Anthropic
stories.Summary:
Bank of America, Blackstone, Citi and Morgan Stanley announced on Oct. 26 local time a $63 billion transaction to provide AI computing capacity to Anthropic. Broadcom arranged the deal, which uses a newly created special purpose vehicle, or SPV. The SPV will buy Broadcom's XPU-based AI accelerators along with networking equipment, then lease them to Anthropic. The four financial institutions will lend to the SPV, with the Broadcom products it buys serving as collateral.

Equipment deliveries are set to begin in 2027. Bank of America, Citi and Morgan Stanley will hold first-priority security interests, which gives them the first claim on proceeds from any asset sales if the SPV runs into financial trouble. Blackstone will be the only holder of a second-priority interest. Lenders in that second position typically earn higher interest rates than first-lien lenders, in exchange for being repaid later. Broadcom will also guarantee the residual value of the collateralized equipment, up to the amount of the first-lien loans.

That guarantee means that if the resale value of the accelerators falls and the SPV cannot fully repay its first-lien debt, Broadcom will cover the shortfall. The structure is meant to lower the risk of losses for the first-lien lenders. Hock Tan, Broadcom's president and chief executive officer, commented on the deal, saying it shows the standing of advanced technology and strong confidence in the AI ecosystem. He added that demand for AI computing is growing at a tremendous pace and that enough capital exists to support that growth.

The financing was announced as Anthropic filed to go public. According to Techmeme's summary of coverage, the company filed a registration statement on Form S-1 with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission for a Nasdaq listing under the symbol ANT, with the number of shares and the price range still to be determined. Bloomberg reported that the filing shows an $80.7 billion net loss on revenue of $16.3 billion in the first half of 2026, compared with a $13 billion net loss on revenue of $1.2 billion in the first half of 2025. Anthropic's own posts and commentary cited in the roundup say it had raised $141.1 billion in total capital as of June 30, 2026. The articles do not say when the IPO might price or whether the leasing structure will be repeated.

stories.Headline: AI governance starts with your data: Building the evidence the EU AI Act and new U.S. rules expect
stories.Summary:
The EU AI Act and new U.S. state rules are pushing organizations to show, with evidence, what data sits behind their AI systems. The European Union has moved its high-risk AI obligations to December 2027, while Colorado repealed its AI Act and replaced it with a narrower law effective January 1, 2027, the same day California's rules on automated decision making technology begin to apply. A federal effort to preempt state AI laws continues, but those state laws remain enforceable. The article argues that the deadlines have shifted but the underlying data work has not. It is framed around a sponsored IAPP web conference scheduled for December 8, 2026, co-hosted with Exterro.

The EU AI Act requires providers of high-risk systems to govern their training, validation, and testing data, including where that data came from and whether it is relevant, representative, and as free of errors as possible. California requires risk assessments before a business processes sensitive personal information or uses automated decision making technology for significant decisions. The article says neither obligation can be met without knowing what data an organization holds, where it lives, and what sensitive information it contains. It adds that many organizations rely on a data inventory that went stale years ago. The session promises to show how Exterro OptiX360 maps, classifies, and governs enterprise data in place.

The session is presented by Fahad Diwan, director of product marketing and management at Exterro, who holds several privacy credentials. According to the article, the speaker will cover where the EU AI Act and U.S. state rules now stand, which data questions regulators and review committees are likely to ask, and how to build an AI-ready data foundation. That foundation includes inventory, sensitive data classification, and defensible disposition of data that should no longer be kept. The page also lists eligible continuing professional education credits and explains how registration information is shared with the IAPP and the sponsor.

The context here is a separate piece from Lexpert on Canada, which describes a similar pattern of delay and uncertainty. Canada's Artificial Intelligence and Data Act died when Bill C-27 expired on the order paper in January 2025 without becoming law. Canadian businesses currently rely on existing rules such as PIPEDA and Québec's Law 25, while two new federal bills tabled in June 2026 were still at second reading as of October 2026. The article notes that Canada's approach to AI regulation remains unsettled.

stories.Headline: ADLC compliance: Mapping agentic development to NIST SSDF, the OWASP LLM Top 10, and the EU AI Act
stories.Summary:
Endor Labs published a blog post on October 28, 2026, titled as a guide to ADLC compliance, which maps agentic software development to three frameworks: NIST's Secure Software Development Framework, the OWASP risk lists for large language models and agents, and the EU AI Act. The post says ADLC compliance covers two surfaces: the code an AI coding agent produces, and the actions the agent takes while working, such as running shell commands, reading and writing files, calling tool servers and installing packages. It also states that no official crosswalk exists between these frameworks, so the mapping is the company's own interpretation rather than legal advice. Existing controls such as static analysis, dependency scanning, secrets detection and release signing still apply, while new work centers on agent inventory, permission scoping, real-time action policy and audit logs.

The post argues that most published crosswalks cover only the code surface and miss the action surface, where an agent could read a malicious file, run a risky install command or access credentials before any code reaches a pull request. It recommends treating models, tool servers, skills and plugins as supply chain components with provenance and inventory records. It ties this to the NIST practice of reusing well-secured software and to the OWASP supply chain risk entries. It also says that using coding agents internally mainly triggers AI literacy duties under Article 4 of the EU AI Act, and that obligations for high-risk systems listed in Annex III apply from December 2, 2027. The post warns that a written rule in a system prompt does not count as a control, and that an agent reporting passing tests is not evidence, favoring deterministic policy and independent tool output.

On the NIST side, the post uses SP 800-218, SSDF Version 1.1, as its reference and notes that a revision was released as a draft in December 2025 and should be checked before citing practice identifiers in an audit. It also notes that SP 800-218A, a companion profile for generative AI, is mainly relevant to teams that train or fine-tune models, while most teams using coding agents will use it to evaluate vendors. On the OWASP side, it distinguishes the 2025 LLM Top 10 from the Agentic Top 10 released in December 2025, and it suggests reading each list from the angle of the coding agent itself and from the angle of AI features shipped to customers. The post recommends applying a principle of least agency, granting agents only the autonomy and tool access a task needs. Further sections of the post, which the excerpt does not fully include, cover the EU AI Act in more detail and the remaining OWASP mappings.

stories.Headline: 2026 State Privacy Law Trends: Consumer Data Protection Updates
stories.Summary:
Four states enacted comprehensive consumer privacy laws in 2026, according to a MultiState analysis published October 28, 2026, bringing the total to 24 states with such protections. Alabama, Louisiana, Oklahoma, and Vermont joined the group this year, with Alabama's law covering businesses that process more than 25,000 consumers' personal data or earn at least 25 percent of gross revenue from selling it. The article notes that Florida's law, which applies to a narrow set of businesses, may or may not be counted in that total. Massachusetts could become the next state to join, since each chamber has passed a version of its privacy bill and a conference committee is working on differences this fall.

Several states also amended existing laws in 2026, including Connecticut, Delaware, Kentucky, Maryland, New Hampshire, and New Jersey. The changes follow five trends identified by the article: broader coverage, limits that go beyond consent, expanded consumer rights, closer scrutiny of data use, and more data broker registration. Delaware lowered its coverage threshold from 35,000 consumers to 10,000, while Connecticut and Virginia now ban sales of precise geolocation information regardless of consent. New Jersey prohibits the sale of sensitive data even with consumer consent, and Connecticut and New Jersey joined California, Oregon, Texas, and Vermont in requiring data brokers to register.

The article attributes these developments to state lawmakers and governors, with the absence of congressional action cited as a reason states have continued to act. California Gov. Gavin Newsom vetoed a bill that would have banned selling or sharing sensitive data with third parties, citing potential unintended consequences and enforcement costs in his veto message. Newsom's veto is presented as an exception to the broader trend. The article also notes that many of the strongest proposals have come from Democratic-led states, so the outcome of November's elections could affect whether stalled proposals are revived.

Looking ahead, the article says lawmakers are likely to focus on whether conversation logs from AI chatbots can be used for targeted advertising, and children's privacy remains a major concern with many state attorneys general filing actions against businesses. Colorado's revised AI law will begin regulating automated technology that materially influences consequential decisions in 2027. Connecticut has directed the creation of a universal deletion mechanism by 2028, and Vermont approved a feasibility study on a similar tool. The article suggests the next debate may focus less on establishing privacy rights than on making them easier to exercise.

stories.Headline: Pennsylvania Enacts an AI Ad Disclosure Law: What Companies Need to Know Before December 21
stories.Summary:
Governor Josh Shapiro signed Pennsylvania's Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act, known as SB 806, into law in late October 2026. The law takes effect December 21, 2026. Under it, an advertiser may not run an ad that uses synthetic content in a way that creates a false consumer perception about the nature, origin, or authenticity of what is being sold, unless the ad carries a clear disclosure. Synthetic content covers any image, video, audio, or text that AI has significantly modified or generated.

The disclosure must say that the ad contains content modified or generated using artificial intelligence, though the law does not require any particular wording. It must be easy to notice and understand given its size, contrast, duration, and volume, it must appear in the consumer's language, and it must show the first time the content appears and in the same medium. Where technically feasible, it must be permanent or very hard to remove. The law exempts content that is evidently fictional, parody, satire, commentary, criticism, and text-only content. The Attorney General or a district attorney may seek an injunction or sue, and courts may award damages, fines of up to $3,000, and attorney fees and costs, but there is no private right of action.

The law applies to advertisers who create and disseminate an ad or cause it to be created and disseminated, and earlier drafts limiting it to knowing, reckless, or willful conduct were removed. Because it covers all advertising shown in Pennsylvania, it reaches commercials made in other states or countries as well. Commentators have noted that terms such as "significantly modified" are subjective, and the broad exemptions for parody and commentary may leave advertisers room to maneuver. Unlike California and New York laws aimed at synthetic performers, this law appears to focus more on consumer protection.

Companies will need to decide when a disclosure is needed. A strict reading suggests none is required unless AI use creates a false consumer perception, but regulators have not yet said how they will enforce that standard. Some companies may therefore adopt a conservative approach and disclose more broadly. Observers expect that Pennsylvania's law is part of a wider trend of states regulating AI in advertising.

The articles cover a North Carolina political ad story rather than a new Pennsylvania law, so I'm writing the story as the reporting supports it. A drag queen featured in an allegedly AI-generated ad in North Carolina's 11th Congressional District race has sent a cease-and-desist letter to Republican candidate Jennifer Balkcom and the North Carolina GOP, saying her image was used without permission and asking that the ad be taken down. The ad was reportedly produced by the National Republican Congressional Committee in the final days before the midterms and targets Democrat Jamie Ager, whose campaign features square dancing. Spectrum News 1 reported the story on October 26, 2026.

The reporting notes that AI use in campaigns is growing, with Wesleyan University tracking more than $137 million in spending on AI ads this year by campaigns and political action committees. A September survey by Catawba College and YouGov of 1,200 people, with a margin of error of 3.6 percentage points, found that 68 percent were very or somewhat concerned about AI's use in this year's midterms. Fifty-two percent said they were very or somewhat confident they could tell real political content from AI-generated content, while 39 percent were not very or not at all confident. The National Conference of State Legislatures says 31 states regulate deepfakes in political messages, and North Carolina is not among them, so the articles say the state does not appear to require disclosure of AI use in political ads.

The National Republican Congressional Committee stands by the ad and did not answer whether it disclosed the use of AI, saying the ad raises issues voters need answered. Balkcom's campaign referred questions to the committee. Ager's campaign manager, Grayson Barnette, called the ads fake and AI-generated, accusing the opponent of lying and saying the campaign wants to do politics better. Michael Bitzer, a political science professor at Catawba College, said AI has raised doubts about whether voters can trust campaign information, and that AI can be used to twist facts, present things out of context, and mimic people's voices. The articles do not say whether the cease-and-desist letters will lead to the ad being removed or to any legal action.

stories.Headline: Digital Personal Data Protection Act does not infringe on press freedom: Ashwini Vaishnaw
stories.Summary:
Information Technology Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, that the Digital Personal Data Protection Act does not infringe on press freedom. Speaking to reporters in New Delhi, he insisted that the Constitution guarantees journalistic independence and that the government has no intention of affecting it. He invited editors and media professionals to take part in an open dialogue with the government about their concerns over the law. The remarks came after news publishers warned that the statute, lacking a specific exemption for journalism, could make investigative reporting harder.

Publishers argued that the law could affect reporting on matters of public interest, particularly investigations involving personal information gathered without consent. They also raised concerns about retaining information needed for investigative work and about protecting confidential sources. According to sources cited in the report, the government is open to amending the law to explicitly protect journalistic activity if needed. One senior source said that the intent is clear and that any confusion could be settled through an amendment in Parliament. The government's willingness to discuss the matter has been framed as a route to resolving the disagreement.

Vaishnaw said the Act was brought in after a Supreme Court judgment recognised the right to privacy as a fundamental right. He noted that the law was drafted after more than a year of consultations with stakeholders, including newspapers, television channels, media representatives, and the information technology industry. He said the government had made clear that the Act's provisions do not infringe on freedom of the press, journalism, or media. Publishers, however, remain concerned that the absence of an explicit exemption leaves room for doubt. The debate is therefore likely to continue through any consultations or proposed amendments.

stories.Headline: At ADE 2026, a Top Music Lawyer Talks AI, Independence & What the Biz Can Learn From Radiohead
stories.Summary:
At the Amsterdam Dance Event in October 2026, UK lawyer and music industry analyst Cliff Fluet, co-head of media and entertainment at Lewis Silkin LLP, gave a talk titled "The State Of Things" on Friday, October 23, about where power in the music industry is moving. He used Radiohead's 2007 release of In Rainbows, which invited fans to pay what they wanted, as the starting point. Fluet argued that the decision was less about the price of recorded music than about who owns the relationship with the fan. The talk was part of ADE Pro, the event's industry programme, which hosted 148 panels, 25 mixers and other sessions.

Fluet's main points were that electronic music already shows how direct monetisation, independent infrastructure and community building can work, and that the rest of the industry could learn from it. He described the global dance industry as a $15 billion scene, up 7 per cent in 2025, with catalogues younger on average than other genres. He said independence is no longer about company size but about who controls rights, data and fans, and whether an artist can take those with them when they leave. He also pointed to the Curve royalty platform, which the European Commission required UMG to sell when approving its purchase of Downtown in February, and which Merlin and Jaimy Capital bought together in August. On data, he said ticketing and fan information could become the most valuable data set in music, since a single ticket purchase often serves four to six people while the industry records only one buyer.

Fluet also argued that managers are becoming custodians of artist trust as voice and likeness turn into licensable assets, noting that Lionel Richie has moved to trademark his voice. He observed that the industry is now buying systems, not just catalogues, citing Downtown going to UMG for more than $700 million, Kobalt selling to Primary Wave, and DistroKid being acquired by CVC Capital Partners. He said companies that own the royalty and data infrastructure now hold significant value. He cited Live Nation's record 49 million fans in a single quarter and more than 143 million tickets sold by mid-July, while saying the industry has been slow to use that information to understand its fans. Fluet's remarks, as reported, offer his own views on where the industry is heading rather than any announced rule or regulatory change.

stories.Headline: AI Diversion Theories Emerge as New Securities Lawsuit Risk Zone
stories.Summary:
Securities plaintiffs are filing a new kind of lawsuit tied to artificial intelligence, according to a Fried Frank analysis published by Bloomberg Law on October 28, 2026. Cornerstone counted 15 AI-related securities cases in the first half of 2026, against 16 for all of last year, putting this year on pace for nearly double. The authors describe a growing category of claims that companies concealed how shifting toward AI pulls resources and customers away from their core businesses. They call this the "AI diversion" theory.

The article walks through three recent complaints that illustrate the theory. In In re Microsoft Corporation Securities Litigation, the plaintiff alleges Microsoft diverted computing capacity from its Azure cloud business to Copilot development without telling investors. The complaint says capital expenditures reached $72.4 billion for the first half of fiscal 2026, largely from AI infrastructure and Copilot costs, without producing the expected Copilot subscribers. In Tejada v.

ZoomInfo Technologies, the plaintiff alleges customers shifted spending from ZoomInfo's seat-based software toward in-house AI tools, cutting into core license revenue. In Potter v. monday.com, the complaint says Google's "AI Overviews" and chatbot use reduced clicks to the company's website, eroding its paid search acquisition channel, and that executives described the effect as temporary or minor. The authors say the courts have not yet settled how to handle motions to dismiss these claims.

They point to In re Sprinklr Securities Litigation, where earlier this year the court dismissed a similar complaint after finding Sprinklr had adequately disclosed its resource realignment toward an AI-powered product line. The court also found the complaint relied on hindsight rather than particularized facts. The authors note that the Microsoft, ZoomInfo, and monday.com cases have not yet been decided on those motions. If they survive the pleadings stage, the authors expect many more complaints pleading AI diversion claims against other companies.

Articles.Title: AI Diversion Theories Emerge as New Securities Lawsuit Risk Zone

stories.Headline: Del. idea for AI-run companies draws eye of powerful congressional committee
stories.Summary:
Rep. James Comer, a Kentucky Republican who chairs the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, has asked Delaware's governor for documents about a proposed plan to create a new legal entity for companies run by artificial intelligence agents. The letter, which concerns Delaware's Artificial Intelligence Company initiative, suggests Congress may be looking at limits on state AI rules. Comer wrote that he worried the proposal could protect powerful AI firms and their investors from responsibility for harmful actions. Gov. Matt Meyer's office said it is reviewing the letter. The initiative was announced in July by Secretary of State Charuni Patibanda-Sanchez and John Nay, founder and CEO of Norm AI, in Fortune magazine.

A draft by John Mark Zeberkiewicz, a lawyer at Richards, Layton & Finger, would let an AI agent act as a company with legal personhood, able to own assets, file lawsuits and serve as a liability shield. A single member, either a person or an entity, would have to keep the company adequately capitalized and would be shielded from its debts unless it failed in that duty or used the company to break the law or commit fraud. The company must keep a log of its activities and may pursue any lawful purpose except banking. If the bill passes, organizations would have 30 months to apply to a regulatory sandbox for AI-run companies, and the bill would create a sandbox committee and an administrator. State lawmakers are expected to take up the idea next year.

Comer's letter cites a WHYY News article from September that noted Patibanda-Sanchez declined to answer questions about the relationship between Norm AI and the Meyer administration. Comer said Delaware officials praise transparency in AI decision-making, yet the public-private partnership lacks it, and he also raised concern about regulatory capture by hidden interests. The Richards Layton & Finger firm said attorneys have long helped shape the state's corporate statutes and that lawmakers weigh that input. Nay did not respond to a request for comment, and a spokesperson for Patibanda-Sanchez referred questions to Meyer's office.

The debate has drawn both criticism and support. Corporate law professors have questioned who would be accountable if an AI-run company caused harm, and one University of Pennsylvania professor called the idea a solution in search of a problem. Lawrence Cunningham of the University of Delaware's John L. Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance argued that Delaware, a leading home for business formation, would be irresponsible to ignore the idea. The committee wants documents and communications dating back to January 1, 2025, including internal AI chat logs, and Delaware's response is due November 9.

Articles.Title: Del. idea for AI-run companies draws eye of powerful congressional committee - WHYY

stories.Headline: Inside YES Bank’s AI playbook: Turning experimentation into enterprise-wide transformation - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
Muqbil Ahmar of ETCIO published an exclusive interview on October 28, 2026, with Mahesh Ramamoorthy, Chief Information Officer at YES Bank, about how the bank is moving from AI experiments to bank-wide transformation. The piece frames AI integration and automation as top strategic priorities for CIOs across the banking, financial services and insurance sector. Recently, YES Bank hosted an "AI Fest" at its Mumbai office to explore the next phase of AI-led change. The event brought together more than 29 technology partners and focused on real-world AI applications and scalable implementation strategies.

Ramamoorthy argued that AI adoption is becoming unavoidable, but that financial institutions should advance cautiously because trust is their central asset. He described AI as probabilistic rather than deterministic, which means firms must decide carefully where to apply it. Many current use cases sit in the back office and in risk management decisioning rather than in customer-facing roles, and he said understanding of customer queries has already improved. He expects most banks to keep a human in the loop rather than move to fully autonomous systems. He also noted that banks are at different stages, with some ahead and others still catching up.

Looking 18 to 24 months ahead, Ramamoorthy expects the cost of AI to normalise, since large models with billions of parameters are currently being used for narrow tasks that could be served more efficiently. He anticipates use cases aligning with that rebalanced cost base and stronger data security safeguards arriving. On YES Bank's own position, he said the bank has built capabilities around good bots and context-driven engagement, but wants to do more. The AI Fest was designed as a collaborative marketplace, bringing in partners and vendors, with the aim of generating around 100 use cases that emerge from employees rather than from technology teams alone. He said the first edition was open only to YES Bank employees so that colleagues could learn about AI's possibilities in one curated setting.

Articles.Title: Inside YES Bank’s AI playbook: Turning experimentation into enterprise-wide transformation - ET CIO
