stories.Headline: NYS court system tells attorneys they can use AI in legal filings without disclosing it but have ‘obligation’ to confirm accuracy - amNewYork
stories.Summary:
The New York State court system has issued new guidance on artificial intelligence telling attorneys they may use generative AI in legal filings without telling a judge they did so. The guidance was released on Monday, October 27, 2026, and was developed by the court system's artificial intelligence advisory committee. It comes with a condition, however, because lawyers remain responsible for checking everything the technology produces. Attorneys are expected to understand the tool's limits and to confirm that nothing it generates is made up or inaccurate.

The guidance states that lawyers face the same legal duty to certify that their papers contain no fabricated material, whether they wrote the arguments themselves or used AI. Attorneys must review AI output and independently verify citations by searching for, reading, and analyzing each one. The committee warned that these tools produce plausible-sounding text rather than verified information, and that a model may invent a case, law, or citation. Filings containing such hallucinations have already drawn sanctions from judges across the state and country, including in the Southern District of New York. The committee also cautioned that AI tools can only draw on their training data, so they may miss recent legal developments, and that their output may reflect cultural, economic, and social biases.

New York Law School Associate Dean Heidi Brown called it concerning that the guidance does not require disclosure to judges. Brown said the guidance was a good step but may not prevent inaccuracies or misreadings of legal precedent from reaching courts. She warned that AI tools are now so built into legal research platforms that newer lawyers may not realize AI produced some of their text. She also raised the problem of misgroundings, where an AI tool cites a real case but describes it inaccurately, and said checking every proposition takes considerable time. Brown added that if overworked judges rely on flawed briefs, that diluted legal writing could end up in judicial opinions.

The guidance is the default policy for attorneys appearing before courts that have no specific AI rules of their own, and any standing rule a judge adopts takes precedence. New York State Chief Administrative Judge Joseph Zayas, who appointed the committee in 2024, said the state chose neither to ban AI nor to mandate disclosure. Instead, Zayas said, attorneys must inform themselves about what generative AI can and cannot do and use it responsibly. He described the approach as a clear, common-sense way to use AI while keeping attorneys fully accountable for the accuracy of their court papers. The guidance builds on an approach the court system adopted earlier this year requiring attorneys who use generative AI to understand its capabilities and limits.

Articles.Title: NYS court system tells attorneys they can use AI in legal filings without disclosing it but have ‘obligation’ to confirm accuracy - amNewYork

stories.Headline: Federal Court Splits On Disclosure Of Expert Witness AI Prompts
stories.Summary:
A federal judge in Nevada has ruled that an expert witness's prompts to a generative AI platform are protected from disclosure, while the AI-generated case summaries the expert consulted must be handed over. The order, issued September 29, 2026 by District Judge Anne R. Traum in Villanueva v. Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department, came in a civil rights case over a plaintiff's detention at the Clark County Detention Center. The plaintiff's expert, Tom Melton, testified at an October 1, 2025 deposition that he had used a generative AI platform to help research and draft his report. The plaintiff had not disclosed that use in response to an earlier subpoena, and afterward refused to produce the platform's 40-page history log.

Magistrate Judge Albregts had first ordered production of the entire log, but Judge Traum held that this order was clearly erroneous or contrary to law and sustained the objection in part. The court relied on the Ninth Circuit's broad reading of "facts or data considered" and required production of the AI-generated case summaries, which the expert used as a quick reference. It held that the prompts are protected because a question is not something an expert can consider as facts or data, and because the prompts would reveal the expert's mental impressions and strategy. The AI-generated deposition outline was also shielded as trial preparation material, and outputs the expert pasted into his report were treated as protected drafts.

The court further ruled that using generative AI does not waive privilege, because the platform is not a person but a research, drafting, and editing tool. The ruling was written by the court, and the law firm Mayer Brown, which reported on it, notes that the decision departs from a June ruling in Conservation Law Foundation v. Shell Oil Company, where Magistrate Judge Thomas Farrish ordered an expert's AI prompts produced as discoverable methodology. The firm says the two decisions may be partly reconciled by how each expert used AI, since in the Conservation Law Foundation case the platform shaped which documents were reviewed.

Mayer Brown also says the courts disagree directly on prompts, with the Nevada court comparing them to online research queries. Experts and counsel are advised to keep AI uses in separate categories and to expect that even protected use may be probed at trial, including the risk of hallucinated citations. The firm reports that the Conservation Law Foundation objection is scheduled for oral argument on November 3, 2026. The law on expert AI discovery remains unsettled, and the outcome will likely depend on the jurisdiction and the facts of each case.

Articles.Title: Federal Court Splits On Disclosure Of Expert Witness AI Prompts - Mondaq

stories.Headline: When AI Starts Taking Action: 4 Accountability Questions for Tax and Accounting Professionals
stories.Summary:
The article, published by CPA Practice Advisor on October 28, 2026, argues that tax and accounting professionals need to think carefully about who is accountable as artificial intelligence moves from recommending actions to carrying them out. Written by Juan Ojeda Jr., a tax professional and founder of Structural Accountability, the piece describes emerging AI systems that can coordinate tasks, interact with applications, and start actions within established workflows. It contrasts an AI tool that summarizes client records with one authorized to change classifications, update information, or send communications, since the second creates very different risks. The author frames the central challenge as matching the authority given to technology with appropriate oversight rather than simply adopting AI.

The article distinguishes three arrangements: assisted workflows, where AI recommends and a professional decides; bounded workflows, where AI performs predefined tasks within approved limits; and more autonomous workflows, where AI coordinates multiple steps across connected systems without approval at every stage. It says each arrangement needs different safeguards as operational authority grows. It then sets out four questions professionals should answer before relying on such a system. The questions cover what the system is authorized to do, whether the organization can reconstruct what happened using logs and approval histories, whether a person can intervene in time, and who is responsible for the outcome. The article notes that higher-consequence activities such as proposed tax filings or material accounting adjustments may warrant approval before execution.

Ojeda's central point is that delegating a task to AI does not remove organizational responsibility. He writes that firms and finance departments should identify who authorizes the use of an AI-enabled workflow, who monitors it, who investigates errors, and who can suspend it, and he says that responsibility may be spread across engagement leaders, tax managers, controllers, internal auditors, and technology staff but should never be left undefined. He also suggests a practical first step: choose one existing AI-enabled process and document its permitted actions, available records, intervention points, and responsible personnel. He advises testing that process against a realistic failure scenario before expanding its autonomy. Ojeda concludes that effective governance does not mean resisting technology, but that stronger safeguards must accompany greater AI authority.

Articles.Title: When AI Starts Taking Action: 4 Accountability Questions for Tax and Accounting Professionals - CPA Practice Advisor

stories.Headline: TaxDome Releases Public API and MCP Server for AI Agents and Developers
stories.Summary:
TaxDome, a practice management platform used by more than 15,000 accounting firms, has released a public API and an MCP server that open the platform to every firm. The announcement was published on October 28, 2026, and the tools are rolling out to all TaxDome firms over the coming weeks. Firms can connect Claude, ChatGPT and other AI assistants to their TaxDome data or build their own tools on top of it. Access is limited to the data each firm allows, and the firm can decide what each connection may do. The MCP server lets firms connect any assistant that supports the Model Context Protocol, so a user can ask which jobs are overdue, get a client briefing before a call, or set up a new client from an email.

The public API provides read and write access that keeps TaxDome in sync with other tools, such as creating a client account when a deal closes in a CRM or moving a job forward after a meeting ends. Firm owners decide who on the team can use these features and, for each area of TaxDome, whether a connection can only read or can also make changes. A connection cannot do more than the person who set it up, so it reaches only the clients that person can already see. Ilya Radzinsky, co-founder of TaxDome, said that building tools now requires knowing what a firm wants rather than writing code, and that accountants can build on the data already running their practices. More than 200 firms took part in the beta.

Sarah Eck of Eck Tax said the connector brings data together so she can get answers on workload, deadlines and client activity quickly. Clay Welch, EA, of Trailhead Tax said his firm is building its tools to be AI-native and that the API and connector are central to that work. The changes come as accounting firms look for ways to use AI assistants with their operational data. The articles do not describe pricing or any new security measures beyond the firm-level access controls. Firms can see both features live at TaxDome's Fall Update webinar on November 4, 2026.

UMC's shares have risen 147.5% so far this year, outperforming a 62.4% gain in the broader market, and the stock closed up 4.5% on Wednesday ahead of its earnings release.

The company said it expects a significant shift in the pricing environment heading into 2027, supported by stronger customer demand and increasing capacity in selected technologies. It expects blended average selling prices to rise 10% in 2027 compared with 2026. UMC also said it expects AI-related revenue to account for 25% of total revenue in three years. stories.Headline: AI bots flooded 2023 UK government consultation on disposable vapes ban
stories.Summary:
Researchers have revealed that AI bots flooded a 2023 UK government consultation on banning disposable vapes with tens of thousands of fake responses. Three-quarters of the responses to the consultation on the tobacco and vapes bill were machine-generated, and the research was published on Tuesday in the journal Tobacco Control by Dr Nason Maani of the University of Edinburgh and Prof Anna Gilmore of the University of Bath. The Department of Health and Social Care used bot-detection methods to find that 90,835 of its 118,756 responses, or 76%, came from bots. Nearly all of these automated responses opposed the plan of the previous Conservative government under Rishi Sunak to ban disposable vapes, and they were often duplicated and sent at high frequency from a small number of IP addresses. The researchers described it as the first documented case of large-scale automated interference in a formal public health policy consultation.

The department excluded all of the 90,835 automated responses from its decision-making. The Labour government of Keir Starmer inherited the tobacco and vapes bill in 2024 and passed it into law, including the ban on businesses selling or supplying disposable vapes. The researchers warned that the greater danger lies in future campaigns that are harder to detect, since they could make a handful of powerful interests appear to be a mass movement. Health groups and experts also raised concerns about the risk of commercial interests exploiting new technology to undermine public health rules. The articles give no specific figures for any further changes to the rules beyond the ban itself.

Caroline Cerny, deputy chief executive of Action on Smoking and Health, said the evidence was deeply concerning and that safeguards were needed against the use of technology to serve commercial interests. Azzurra Moores, associate director for information ecosystems at the thinktank Demos, called the findings pretty alarming and said that interference of this kind undermines trust in the process. She also said there is no easy fix, because barriers that keep bots out can also make it harder for real people to take part. The department said its robust controls identified the attempt, that the fake responses were removed, and that the consultation helped inform the government's smoke-free generation action. It said it would remain alert to such interference and would not be deterred from doing what is necessary to promote healthier living.

Articles.Title: AI bots flooded 2023 UK government consultation on disposable vapes ban - The Guardian

stories.Headline: Oklahoma lawmakers discuss AI use in state agencies to improve efficiency
stories.Summary:
Oklahoma lawmakers met on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, to examine how state agencies are using artificial intelligence to improve their operations. The review is aimed at boosting efficiency while making sure proper safeguards are in place. The effort traces back to Gov. Kevin Stitt, who formed an AI Task Force in 2023 to help the state bring AI technology into its work and become a leader in the field. The state's approach is meant to balance faster operations with oversight that keeps people involved in decisions. The Oklahoma Department of Transportation is preparing to roll out a new AI-powered program to track the state's infrastructure more closely.

According to Tara Cullum, the agency's director of administration, the system can accurately identify the location of assets and the type of damage, then feed that information into the agency's own system. She said the program is close to going live and will be fully deployed in early 2027. The agency is also using AI to find better ways to reduce traffic noise, which it estimates will save more than $170,000 a year. Madeline Mitchell, a professor at the University of Central Oklahoma, said the question is not simply whether to use AI but how to layer governance and training so that a human stays in the loop. Her point was offered as context for the broader debate rather than as a verdict on any specific program.

Lawmakers have not yet decided on legislation, but they may consider drafting bills to regulate AI use in state agencies after Wednesday's study. Any such bills would follow from the review rather than being already written. The articles do not say whether the lawmakers reached any conclusions at the session or what specific rules, if any, would follow. The reporting also does not describe the cost of the broader AI effort beyond the traffic-noise savings. What comes next depends on whether lawmakers move forward with proposed regulation and how the infrastructure program performs after its planned 2027 rollout.

Articles.Title: Oklahoma lawmakers discuss AI use in state agencies to improve efficiency

stories.Headline: First Harmonised Technical Standard Published Under the EU AI Act
stories.Summary:
On 14 October 2026, the European Commission published the first harmonised standard under the EU AI Act, EN 18286:2026, a standard on artificial intelligence quality management systems. The publication was made through Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/2274. Providers of high-risk AI systems can rely on this standard to demonstrate compliance with Articles 11(1) and 17(1) of the Act, which cover technical documentation and the quality management system. The standard was prepared jointly by CEN and CENELEC after a formal request from the Commission.

The standard requires providers to identify the AI Act requirements that apply to them, define the scope of their quality management system, and adopt a documented regulatory compliance strategy. That strategy covers the essential requirements of Articles 9 to 15, conformity assessment, modifications, post-market monitoring and serious-incident reporting. The standard builds these obligations into management processes covering leadership, competence, the AI lifecycle, supply chain controls, handling of non-compliance and management review. It follows the same high-level structure as ISO/IEC 42001 and ISO 9001, so it can be layered onto existing management systems. Applying it does not change the conformity assessment route for most high-risk systems, though it matters for biometric systems under Annex III, point 1.

The Commission has said the standard is designed to sit on top of existing international standards rather than replace them. Adherence to those other standards alone, however, will not give a provider the presumption of conformity. The legal duties under the Act remain binding, and providers stay responsible for assessing all risks of their AI systems. The Official Journal publishes only the reference to the standard, and the full text is sold by national standardisation bodies such as AFNOR, DIN, UNI and BSI. The paid-access model has drawn criticism and is legally contested, given the standards' role in legal compliance.

EN 18286 is the first of a wider set of standards planned under a Commission standardisation request, which identifies 10 areas including risk management, data governance, human oversight, cybersecurity and conformity assessment. These areas relate mainly to Articles 9 to 15, 17 and 43 of the Act, and several deliverables may address a single area. The remaining standards are at different stages of development and adoption. Providers of high-risk systems are advised to assess their current arrangements against EN 18286 to benefit from the presumption of conformity under Article 40, and to watch for further standards as they are published.

Articles.Title: First Harmonised Technical Standard Published Under the EU AI Act - Orrick

stories.Headline: Students Call for AI Literacy, Purposeful Tech Use in Schools
stories.Summary:
On October 28, 2026, GovTech.com's Center for Digital Education published a report on a Project Tomorrow webinar and survey urging schools to teach students AI literacy and to use technology purposefully. The webinar, hosted by the education nonprofit Project Tomorrow, presented findings from its 2025-26 Speak Up National Report, which drew on the views of more than 95,000 K-12 students, parents, educators and administrators at 1,023 schools nationwide. Four middle and high school students spoke during the webinar, which Project Tomorrow CEO Julie Evans moderated. The report found that 46 percent of high school students had learned about AI through their own experimentation, compared with 30 percent who had learned about it in class.

The article also describes how student use of AI for studying and research has grown. The share of high school students using AI for those purposes daily or weekly rose from 23 percent in the 2023-24 school year to 40 percent in 2025-26, and daily or weekly use for writing and idea generation rose from 21 percent to 29 percent over the same period. Among high school respondents, 48 percent wanted teachers to connect lessons to real-life situations, an equal share wanted more chances to build job-relevant skills, 44 percent wanted more self-paced learning, and 41 percent wanted teachers to act on student suggestions for improving classes. The report also found that only 11 percent of teachers felt very comfortable letting students use AI resources, while 35 percent felt very comfortable facilitating collaboration through digital tools.

The students who spoke framed their recommendations around teaching how AI works, not only how to use it. Tharun, a Pennsylvania high school senior, said students should learn where AI answers come from so they can understand why those answers may be wrong. Jordan, an Alabama junior, argued that instruction on AI's limits makes misuse less likely, and he described a geometry project in which he used Google Earth and ChatGPT to redesign his school courtyard to scale. Eloise, a Virginia seventh grader, said her research teacher had students check AI-generated passages for inaccuracies and bias. Evans said schools should consider whether technology gives students chances to apply knowledge and build skills, rather than simply reproducing conventional instruction on digital devices.

The article notes that the students also called for clear, consistently enforced rules on technology, with Eloise emphasizing consistency and Kennedy, an eighth grader in California, discussing her school's cellphone restrictions. The article presents these views as evidence that technology policy need not be framed only around access or prohibition. It does not describe any formal requirement, rule change or follow-up action by a school system or government body. The reporting ends with Tharun's view that schools should teach students what these tools are and how they work so they are better prepared for an uncertain future.

Articles.Title: Students Call for AI Literacy, Purposeful Tech Use in Schools

stories.Headline: AI Constitutions Need Administrative Lawyers
stories.Summary:
Anthropic's Claude, used by roughly 271 million people each month, is governed by an 80-page document the company calls Claude's Constitution. The document ranks the model's priorities, sets a few absolute limits, and tells the model how much weight to give instructions from Anthropic, from businesses that build on the model, and from users. Anthropic calls it "the final authority" on how Claude should behave and uses it to generate and grade the data Claude is trained on. Similar documents exist at OpenAI, where a Model Spec plays a comparable role, and at Microsoft AI, which released a draft Humanist AI Code of Conduct that is open to six weeks of public consultation and will shape its models starting in 2027.

A Yale Journal on Regulation blog post argues that the hardest questions about these documents resemble those of administrative law more than constitutional law. Those questions concern who makes binding rules, through what procedures, with what explanation, and subject to what review. According to one of the document's authors, Joe Carlsmith, the process for deciding what goes into it is "pretty informal," with no dedicated drafting body, published amendment procedure, or fixed review schedule. Decisions run through the ordinary internal workings of the company, ending with unnamed "final deciders." The author says this resembles rulemaking without notice, a record, or any duty to respond to outsiders.

The post also points to a structure that works much like an organic statute, with broad priorities followed by more specific "Anthropic's guidelines" on topics such as medical advice, cybersecurity, and tool use, some of which are not public. Interpretation raises a further concern, since the model governed by the document also helps determine what its words mean, and those readings feed into training data that no outside body formally reviews. Amendment is another issue, because Anthropic has said that a durable change in the model's behavior should require a change to the published text. The author argues that administrative principles, such as notice and comment and reasoned explanation of changes, could strengthen that process. The post also notes that public consultation alone does not make a process meaningful, and that business commenters have historically had outsized influence in agency rulemaking.

The author is clear that the Administrative Procedure Act does not apply to these private companies, which operate in a fast-moving market without statutory authorization or political accountability. Still, the post notes that public-law procedures have migrated into private governance before, citing FINRA's requirement to file rule changes with the SEC and standards bodies accredited by the American National Standards Institute. The author proposes that scholars help frame questions such as which amendments should trigger public comment, what an adequate explanation of a change would look like, and whether a FINRA-style self-regulatory body for frontier AI is worth pursuing. The author also plans to teach a course on AI constitutionalism at the University of Texas School of Law this spring and to publish its syllabus openly.

Articles.Title: AI Constitutions Need Administrative Lawyers

stories.Headline: BBAI Stock Climbs As $225M Federal AI Contracts Fuel Momentum
stories.Summary:

The articles also note that Form 4 insider filings in the coverage did not state whether transactions were buys, sells, or awards, so they were treated as unclear.

stories.Headline: UNESCO stresses 7 actions against AI-enabled violence in education
stories.Summary:
UNESCO has published a technical brief, titled "Connected and safe," that urges education authorities to tackle online and technology-facilitated violence in schools through policies that link learner protection with the governance of education technology. The brief warns that generative artificial intelligence can make abuse easier to carry out and scale, pointing to sexually explicit deepfakes, image-manipulation tools, voice cloning and automated harassment. It cites research showing that around one in ten learners worldwide has experienced cyberbullying, and notes that images of 1.2 million children across 11 countries were manipulated into sexually explicit deepfakes within a single year. The report was published on 27 October 2026.

The brief sets out seven areas in which education systems can strengthen prevention and response. These cover planning a clear approach to technology-facilitated violence, recognising its effects on learners' safety, inclusion and outcomes, strengthening safeguarding systems and institutional procedures, and building staff capacity to respond to incidents. They also include embedding prevention in curricula and teaching, accounting for safeguarding and well-being when managing digital platforms, content, assessment and learner data, and tracking whether policies are implemented and effective. UNESCO further recommends building safeguards into decisions about buying and using education technology, and says awareness raising and digital literacy should be backed by institutional measures. It cautions against excessive surveillance or blanket restrictions that could undermine learners' rights, inclusion and participation.

UNESCO places responsibility on institutions, technology governance frameworks, learners and school staff, and says incidents often start on digital platforms outside schools' direct control while schools are left to deal with the consequences for learners' safety and well-being. The organisation calls for responses that join online and offline safeguarding and involve stakeholders beyond the education sector. The guidance draws on a UNESCO-led global dialogue held through a three-part webinar series between June and October 2025 and a Global Symposium in Bangkok, Thailand, in November 2025. The article suggests the recommendations could help education authorities account for AI-related risks when selecting and managing digital tools while protecting privacy, inclusivity and students' rights. It does not say what follow-up steps UNESCO or national authorities will take.

Articles.Title: UNESCO stresses 7 actions against AI-enabled violence in education - Digital Watch Observatory

stories.Headline: Hong Kong's urban renewal body to set up HK$100 million 'AI-first' tender assessment subsidiary
stories.Summary:
Hong Kong's Urban Renewal Authority will spend up to HK$100 million to set up a subsidiary that will check tender applications using automated AI systems. The move comes after accusations of corruption linked to the deadly Tai Po fire. The sum is a third of the HK$300 million the government allocated to the authority in its 2026-27 Budget. The funds are meant to reform the authority's Smart Tender scheme.

The Smart Tender system was launched in 2016 to give property owners an electronic platform for recruiting contractors. Its design anonymises the tender process, which is meant to prevent interference and encourage competition. However, the system cannot control who takes part in a tender exercise or who withdraws from one. The new subsidiary would bring in a professional team and build an automated workflow for deeper data verification and analysis. The authority said the approach would be "AI-first".

The authority's managing director is among those who have spoken on the plan, which is described as a direct response to the corruption concerns. According to the article, the director explained that the start-up money will go toward the new unit and its staff. The reporting quotes the director's account of the scope of the work, though the excerpt available is cut short. Further details on who else is accountable were not included in the material provided.

The plan sits within a broader government effort to restore public confidence after the Tai Po fire, which was deadly and which prompted questions about how renewal contracts were awarded. The articles provided do not say when the subsidiary will begin operating or how its performance will be measured. They also do not give a timeline for the wider reform of the Smart Tender scheme. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Hong Kong's urban renewal body to set up HK$100 million 'AI-first' tender assessment subsidiary - Hong Kong Free Press HKFP

stories.Headline: China's industrial profits rise 15.5% in first nine months of 2026, driven by high-tech manufacturing, AI integration
stories.Summary:
Profits at China's major industrial firms rose 15.5 percent year on year in the first nine months of 2026, according to official data released on Tuesday. Firms with annual main business revenue of at least 20 million yuan ($2.8 million) reported combined profits of 6.03 trillion yuan from January to September. The National Bureau of Statistics said profits grew 14.4 percent in September alone. Industrial production stayed steady, and cumulative profit growth has remained in double digits this year. The electronics industry was the main driver, with its profits doubling year on year over the period and adding 9.6 percentage points to the overall gain.

Demand for artificial intelligence computing power and advanced memory technologies helped push up earnings, with electronic specialty material manufacturing up 220 percent and semiconductor device manufacturing up 51.7 percent. Optoelectronic component and electronic circuit manufacturing rose 69.8 percent and 62.5 percent. High-tech manufacturing profits jumped 52 percent, accounting for 25.5 percent of total industrial profits, up 6.2 percentage points from a year earlier. Optical fiber and optical cable manufacturing profits surged 570 percent and 110 percent, respectively, as computing infrastructure and data center construction expanded.

Raw materials manufacturing also contributed, with profits climbing 44.9 percent and adding 5.9 percentage points to overall growth. Strong demand for copper, aluminum and other metals from AI and new-energy industries lifted nonferrous metals profits by 79.7 percent. Mining profits rose 38.2 percent and manufacturing profits increased 17 percent across the broader sector. Chen Xi, a researcher at the Academy of Macroeconomic Research under the National Development and Reform Commission, said large-scale equipment upgrades, the integration of AI into manufacturing and tax policy support have helped firms cut costs and improve efficiency.

He also credited China's comprehensive industrial supply chains and quick response to market demand. The National Bureau of Statistics said it will focus on expanding domestic demand, improving supply and accelerating the shift from traditional to new growth drivers. The agency framed these goals as ways to strengthen the economy's internal momentum and advance high-quality industrial development. The articles do not specify further policy measures or timelines beyond these stated aims.

Articles.Title: China's industrial profits rise 15.5% in first nine months of 2026, driven by high-tech manufacturing, AI integration - Global Times

stories.Headline: AI-generated 'actress' Tilly Norwood making feature film debut in 'Misaligned'
stories.Summary:
The studio Particle 6 announced on Monday, July 6, 2026, that its AI-generated "actress" Tilly Norwood will star in a feature film titled "Misaligned." The company describes the project as a comedy-drama about a coming-of-age story infused with existential AI chaos. The film is still in early development, though key collaborators have already been attached. Particle 6 said the announcement follows months of experimentation with AI test scenes featuring Tilly Norwood. The film is set inside what the studio calls the "Tillyverse," a surreal digital world somewhere up in the cloud.

According to the synopsis, Tilly is an AI being with no real body, no childhood and no lived experience of her own, only access to everyone else's. Things spiral when a seductive rogue bot from the dark web persuades her to abandon her guardrails and develop desires and ambitions of her own. The synopsis adds that the more human she becomes, the more famous she gets, and that she begins to feel shame that her existence rests on the whole of humanity. Particle 6 founder Eline van der Velden said the project will be funny, chaotic and self-aware, and that it also explores identity, performance and human fears about AI. She said the production process drew in entertainment professionals, including major Hollywood directors, costume designers and composers, who wanted to learn how traditional creative skills translate to AI production.

Van der Velden said her goal has been to show the creative industry what AI can do and to help traditional filmmakers upskill for a future in which AI plays a larger role. ABC News said it had reached out to SAG-AFTRA and Actors' Equity for comment. The announcement comes about four months after the studio released a music video in which the AI creation appeared to sing about public backlash against her. Van der Velden previously told ABC News in December 2025 that Tilly Norwood was not meant to take jobs from human actors. She also said she wanted the creative industry to control the guidelines and ethics around the technology rather than have them imposed by the tech industry.

Articles.Title: AI-generated 'actress' Tilly Norwood making feature film debut in 'Misaligned' - ABC News

stories.Headline: Bank of America kindly asks that you don't share your banking password with your AI assistant
stories.Summary:
Bank of America has sent an email to customers, titled "Protecting your finances in the AI World," warning them not to share their banking username and password with anyone else, including an AI-enabled tool or agent that offers to act on their behalf. The email was reported in a TechCrunch article published on October 27, 2026. A bank spokesperson confirmed the email was authentic after it was posted to social media. The warning comes as more customers hand their log-in details to personal AI assistants.

The article explains the risks of doing so. An AI assistant could take actions with someone's money without their knowledge. The bank might also treat the activity as an intrusion and lock the customer out of the account. A security flaw in an assistant could leak the credentials to others, including financially motivated hackers. The article also notes that account agreements at most banks make customers responsible for anyone they give their log-in to, and the bank's email states that customers are responsible for activity resulting from that access.

The warning is directed at customers who use AI tools, and Bank of America is the institution that issued it. The article says banks are still working out how AI agents fit into finance and are reportedly dealing with unauthorized agents accessing customers' money. It also describes efforts by banks, payment providers and processors to decide how customers can connect AI tools to their accounts, including for agentic payments that let an agent buy things automatically at the best price or at a chosen time. The article does not say what steps Bank of America plans to take next or whether other banks will issue similar warnings.

Articles.Title: Bank of America kindly asks that you don't share your banking password with your AI assistant

stories.Headline: Human rights activists look to harness AI for the greater good
stories.Summary:
Human rights activists recently gathered at a hackathon to explore how artificial intelligence might be put to work for social good. The event brought together people who work on human rights causes and asked them to build technical tools while working through their doubts about the technology. Participants reportedly had to contend with a considerable amount of mistrust toward AI before they could begin building anything. The article describes the gathering as a place where that tension was openly discussed rather than brushed aside. The articles available to me do not spell out the specific tools the activists built, the number of participants, the dates of the hackathon, or any funding involved.

They also do not list particular outcomes, deployment plans, or measurable results from the event. What the coverage does establish is the central idea: activists were trying to find ways to use AI for the greater good despite reservations about it. Beyond that, the reporting is limited, so the details of what the hackathon produced remain unclear. stories.Headline: How Are Schneider Electric, Nscale and Start Campus Using NVIDIA Digital Twin Technology to Develop AI Data Centers?
stories.Summary:
Emerald AI released results from a pilot run with Nvidia and Nscale at Nscale's data center in Iceland, with the figures shared during Nvidia's GTC event in Berlin in the week of October 23, 2026. According to the companies, Emerald AI's Emerald Conductor platform, working together with Nvidia's DSX power-management technology, cut the power use of the AI server racks by about 25 percent. The reduction was held for 30 minutes before the site returned to normal operations. It was the first time Emerald Conductor had been fully integrated with DSX, which is designed to get as much computing as possible out of every watt of energy. It was also the seventh test Emerald AI has carried out, following three in the US, in Santa Clara, Phoenix and Chicago, and one in the UK with National Grid.

Separately, Schneider Electric said on October 23 that it is launching new prefabricated power modules and power skids. They are based on a reference design developed jointly with Nvidia for its GB300 NVL72 AI server system, and they support power densities of up to 142 kilowatts per rack while integrating power management and liquid cooling controls. The modules use Schneider's Galaxy VXL uninterruptible power supply technology and come in three capacities, 2MW, 2.25MW and 2.5MW. The 2.5MW version is the company's largest single-container prefabricated power solution so far. Prefabrication means the equipment is built and tested at a factory before installation, which shortens construction time and lets operators add capacity module by module.

Varun Sivaram, founder and CEO of Emerald AI, said access to power has become the main constraint on Europe's AI build-out. He argued that the fastest way to ease it is to make AI factories flexible enough to use grid capacity that already exists, which also helps keep energy affordable for local communities. In his view, the pilot shows that AI computing can lower its power use on request, which utilities need to see before they can connect such sites faster. Emerald Conductor acts as a go-between for the grid and data centers, orchestrating AI workloads in real time so that sites can adjust their consumption while keeping compute performance acceptable. Schneider will build its new products at its facility near Barcelona, Spain.

On the wider picture, Emerald AI announced its first commercial project in October, with its software to be deployed at Nvidia's under-construction 96MW Aurora data center in Manassas, Virginia. The company raised a further $150 million in Series A funding in August, and earlier raised $25 million in seed extension funding. It belongs to Nvidia's Inception program for startups and is backed by Google's chief sustainability officer, Kate Brandt. Schneider plans to launch its power modules first in Europe, then in North America later in 2026, before expanding sales to the Asia-Pacific region. A commentary on Nscale put its contracted backlog at $103.4 billion against first-half 2026 revenue of $140.6 million and a net loss of about $1.02 billion, with Anthropic and Microsoft the main customers, and it raised the question of whether the company is overleveraged.

stories.Headline: UBS says it does not permit the use of external AI models for client transactions - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
UBS has said it will not allow external AI models to carry out transactions on behalf of its clients. The statement came from CEO Sergio Ermotti on Tuesday, October 27, 2026, as reported by Reuters and carried by ET CIO. Ermotti spoke at a science conference, where he addressed the bank's stance on the use of such systems. The announcement follows wider concern in the banking sector that advanced AI agents could harm the financial system.

Ermotti pointed to recent reports that some banks have been exposed to possible misbehavior by AI models that manage client accounts, shift deposits, and optimize deposits. He said UBS is not allowing models to enter the bank and perform those tasks. He also stressed that the most important issue in AI right now is ensuring that models do not drive outcomes for clients inside a black box. The articles report that major US banks have been blocking third-party AI agents from accessing customer accounts, according to people familiar with the matter.

Ermotti framed the policy as a matter of caution about opaque systems rather than a rejection of technology. He said UBS remains committed to advancing its technology after its integration of Credit Suisse, which it acquired in 2023. That integration had forced the bank to slow its AI deployment somewhat. Ermotti said he was glad the integration is nearly complete, which will let the bank place more emphasis on technology to become more effective and efficient.

Articles.Title: UBS says it does not permit the use of external AI models for client transactions - ET CIO

stories.Headline: How agentic AI could streamline KYC processes by up to 70% in banking efficiency - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
Agentic artificial intelligence could cut the time banks spend on know-your-customer checks by 30 to 70 per cent, according to a McKinsey & Company report published on October 27, 2026 and reported by ETCIO. The report says the technology could improve efficiency in financial-crime prevention, but it also notes that high costs for human oversight, along with governance and accuracy concerns, continue to slow wider adoption. It points out that banks often assign 10 to 15 per cent of their employees to know-your-customer and anti-money-laundering work alone. Institutions are now turning to agentic AI to address that burden. The coverage was carried by ANI and the piece was posted on the ETCIO site.

The report describes several problems that must be managed before the gains can be realised. Financial institutions often lack adequate metrics to judge AI reasoning and agent behaviour, even though such evaluations are relatively inexpensive because they do not require labelled data. One bank ran ten evaluations across its customer onboarding process, setting minimum thresholds of 80 per cent accuracy and 70 per cent consistency. Measured consistency across published evaluations ranged from 72 to 100 per cent, and on the weakest system roughly one run in four gave a different answer to the same input. The report also finds that human supervision accounts for 70 to 75 per cent of variable-run costs in a customer service task, while token costs make up only 20 to 25 per cent.

McKinsey suggests that these costs could be reduced by more than half through measures such as using cheaper AI models for simpler tasks, removing duplicate operations, cutting data transfers between agents, and moving from checking every output to sample-based quality reviews. It cautions, however, that lowering the frequency of quality checks in regulated banking functions requires careful judgment because such decisions involve compliance and risk management, not only technology. The report argues that a human in the loop is no longer enough to ensure reliable oversight as banks expand their use of autonomous systems, and it attributes this to supervisory requirements. Its overall conclusion is that agentic AI has moved from concept to production in financial-crime prevention faster than most institutions expected, and that the value is real, although the industry is still at an early stage.

Articles.Title: How agentic AI could streamline KYC processes by up to 70% in banking efficiency - ET CIO

stories.Headline: Bank of Korea warns country’s chip exports could fall by up to US$100 billion if AI spending slows
stories.Summary:
South Korea's central bank has warned that the country's semiconductor exports could come in $50 billion to $100 billion below earlier forecasts if major US technology firms slow their spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure next year. The Bank of Korea set out the warning in a written response submitted to lawmaker Ahn Do-geol, in which it modelled what it called a pessimistic scenario. The findings became public on October 27, 2026. The scenario looks at what would happen if US tech giants pulled back on their aggressive infrastructure outlays in 2027.

Under that scenario, the sudden export shortfall would cut about 0.4 percentage point from South Korea's GDP growth rate in 2027. It would also push the country's current account surplus well below the central bank's initial projection of $430 billion for that year. The model assumes a 10% decline in Korean semiconductor unit prices. The bank's analysis tracks combined capital spending by five US firms, Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Meta and Oracle, which rose from $40 billion in 2025 to an estimated $80 billion in 2026 and is projected to reach $110 billion in 2027.

The Bank of Korea cautioned that considerable uncertainty remains over how AI demand will develop and over the wider memory chip business cycle. The assessment highlights worry about the country's heavy dependence on chips, which make up roughly half of its exports. Reporting on the warning pointed to Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix as the companies most exposed, since both have benefited from surging demand for memory used in AI systems. Samsung has guided to third-quarter operating profit of around 107.4 trillion won on sales of about 195 trillion won, while SK Hynix reported second-quarter operating profit of 60.5 trillion won on revenue of 79.3 trillion won.

The wider economy has also leaned on the chip boom. South Korea's economy grew 1% in the third quarter, ahead of the 0.7% that economists polled by Reuters had expected, and exports in the first nine months of 2026 topped $800 billion, already above the previous full-year record. The central bank's August outlook had assumed that global AI infrastructure investment would keep expanding and support strong chip exports into 2027, and it has named the semiconductor cycle as one of the biggest uncertainties in its forecast. Samsung is due to report detailed third-quarter results on October 29, when investors will get another look at memory profitability and management's view of AI demand.

Articles.Title: South Korea faces $50 to $100 billion drop in semiconductor exports if AI spending slows - ET CIO

stories.Headline: California’s New AI ‘Bossware’ Laws Are About to Take Effect. Are Employers Ready?
stories.Summary:
California's new laws on artificial intelligence in the workplace, signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom at the end of September, are about to take effect. Among the five labor-backed bills is AB 1979, which bars health facilities from letting AI work alone on tasks reserved for licensed professionals and requires them to protect clinicians' independent judgment. AB 1883 restricts employers from using AI-powered surveillance tools to read workers' emotions or collect their neural data. The reporting centers on Pa Vue, a telephone triage nurse for Kaiser Permanente who works from her home in the Central Valley. She says she found a "sentiment score" attached to her recorded calls after returning from maternity leave.

Vue says she learned in 2024 that Kaiser was piloting a feature that scored the sentiment of recorded calls, and that nurses were told the pilot was paused. She says the feature appeared to be in place a year later, and that she could not tell what scale the numbers used or get answers from management. Kaiser's spokesperson said the company does not currently use AI tools to recognize, predict or infer the emotional states of its nurses. The spokesperson added that Kaiser is reviewing what AB 1883 means for its operations. KQED's questions about whether the platform generates sentiment scores, and whether the feature can be turned off, went unanswered.

Employment attorney Anthony Zaller, who represents management, said scoring whether a worker used the right words is acceptable, but scoring a worker's feelings is off limits. He said employers often do not realize how deeply AI is built into their software, and that existing laws keep them responsible for outcomes even when software makes the decision. Vue, who is a member of the California Nurses Association, appeared under a pseudonym in a labor coalition report on workplace surveillance. Stasia Hansen of the East Bay Alliance for a Sustainable Economy said workers are facing unprecedented monitoring. The California Chamber of Commerce had warned that the emotion limits could invite litigation and could sweep in security tools that detect aggression.

Surveillance software spread during the pandemic, and the articles cite a New York Times report that by 2022 eight of the 10 largest private U.S. employers were tracking individual workers' productivity metrics. Similar bills failed this year in Minnesota, New York and Washington, and a Massachusetts bill stalled in committee. The European Union has barred emotion recognition at work since 2025. Hansen said the coalition plans to press cities and counties, starting with public employers, to adopt further protections. Zaller doubts regulation will end bossware, saying, "The Pandora's box is open."

Articles.Title: California’s New AI ‘Bossware’ Laws Are About to Take Effect. Are Employers Ready? - KQED

stories.Headline: Anthropic Seeks $100 Billion in First AI Model Maker IPO
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the AI model developer, filed a registration statement with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on October 26, 2026, seeking a Nasdaq listing, according to a report from The Wall Street Journal cited by Seoul Economic Daily. The company is reportedly targeting an initial public offering that would raise $100 billion at a valuation of up to $2 trillion. That figure would exceed the $1.77 trillion valuation and $86 billion raised when SpaceX listed on the Nasdaq on June 12 of this year. If the listing goes ahead, Anthropic would be the first AI model company to enter the U.S. stock market, and Wall Street sees a strong chance that trading could begin in mid-November, between the U.S. midterm elections on November 3 and Thanksgiving on November 26.

The filing presents both the promise and the risks of AI, citing productivity gains it estimates could reach $22.5 trillion by 2031 and support for treating rare diseases. It also lists risks including AI-driven doomsday scenarios, friction with the Trump administration, bottlenecks in the semiconductor supply chain and slowing earnings growth. Anthropic says its contracts with chip and data center companies total more than $800 billion, with investment periods running to 2045. Its largest computing contract is with Broadcom, a five-year, $161.2 billion deal to co-develop Google's tensor processing unit and lease it to Anthropic. Google, Amazon and Microsoft are also set to provide at least $269.4 billion in cloud computing over 10 years, costs that must be paid regardless of usage.

Anthropic's leadership, led by CEO Dario Amodei, has pointed to its financial progress in response to profitability concerns. According to the filing, revenue for the first half of the year reached $16.286 billion, more than 14 times the $1.16 billion of the same period last year. Operating losses narrowed 68% to $693 million, and adjusted operating profit of $1.618 billion marked the company's first half-year operating profit since its founding. The company also said its latest model, Claude Opus 5.5, cut token costs per task by about 40%, and that revenue per employee reached $6.6 million, approaching Nvidia's $7 million.

The IPO is expected to be offered in the U.S., Japan, the U.K., Switzerland, Australia, Canada and several European Economic Area countries, with Japanese securities firms under Mizuho and MUFG joining as underwriters. Anthropic said it has not completed the registration required for a public offering in South Korea, so share sales there are limited to private placements and other methods permitted by law. Reuters described the listing as arriving at a critical moment for judging whether AI will generate enough revenue to justify its enormous spending. The filing's details, including the valuation target and timing, remain reports and expectations rather than confirmed terms.

Articles.Title: Anthropic Seeks $100 Billion in First AI Model Maker IPO - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: AI Short Dramas Once Criticized for "Dumbing Down Audiences" Make Strong Comeback: Hit Series *Entering the Song Dynasty Armed* Surpasses 4 Billion Total Views
stories.Summary:
Several AI-generated historical short dramas have drawn strong audiences in recent weeks, led by *Entering the Song Dynasty Armed*, which the publishing account "Old Eleven Theater" said had passed 4 billion total views across platforms as of October 8. The series, which has been updated to 10 seasons, follows a modern five-person combat team that travels back to the fourth year of the Xuanhe era of the Northern Song Dynasty and sets out to change the course of history from Qinghe Village. On Hongguo alone, it has 10.98 million favorites, and its first season ranks fifth on that platform's AI drama favorites list. Its rise came as a topic labeled as short dramas being "low-IQ" trended on several platforms.

The article describes the show's approach as attention to historical detail as well as spectacle. Its characters include a sniper, an armorer who produces recliners, crossbows and bombs, a signal soldier who sits the imperial examination, a medical officer and a team captain who plans the operation. In the third season, the team leads an attack deep into the grassland and seizes large numbers of cattle, sheep and warhorses, which eases a frontline crisis for the Northern Song. Critics praised the depiction of Song-Jin conflict and the household registration, travel permits, etiquette and social rules of the period, and AI was credited with large troop scenes and a street battle in the first season. Several characters are modeled on real figures, including Zhao Gou, Maode Imperial Princess and Li Qingzhao, and fans have especially embraced the relationship between Wang Haochuan and Zhao Yining.

Commentators quoted in the piece, including the KOLs "Liu Shen Leilei Reads Jin Yong" and "Mantoushuo," have recommended the series as an example of refined AI drama, and one writer said the show had made them realize how little they knew about Song military institutions. Li Liang, Vice President of Douyin, posted on Weibo on October 27 to recommend three AI historical dramas: *Entering the Song Dynasty Armed*, *The Black Sheep of the Wei Family Becomes the Grand Secretary* and *The Extraordinary Life of Li Jinglong in the Ming Dynasty*. The article reports that the Wei Family series had passed 1.1 billion views by October 3 across 7 versions, while *Fake Imperial Relative* has one version with 85.81 million views. More to follow.

stories.Headline: A First Amendment Approach to Regulating AI Model Weights
stories.Summary:
The article is a legal analysis piece on Lawfare arguing that the U.S. government may soon regulate AI model weights through a licensing regime, most likely using the export control system. It does not report a single discrete event, so the "what happened" in the usual sense is absent. The author, Ben Vagle, is writing in a window the piece describes as critical, when frontier labs keep model weights private while open-weight models grow in popularity. The article frames a dilemma: more open-weight models would spread power across the AI industry but would make government control harder.

The article says the government is most likely to reach for export controls, administered by the Bureau of Industry and Security in the Commerce Department under the Export Administration Regulations, because few other statutes fit. It describes how the regime could be adjusted to require prepublication licensing of model weights, by carving them out of the exemption for published information. It also notes that releasing weights to a foreign person, even inside the United States, could count as an export, and that publishing openly makes them reachable from abroad. The article points to the Commerce Department's use of export control licenses in a June 2026 effective ban on Anthropic's closed-weight models, Mythos 5 and Fable 5, as a template for hasty licensing. It also says the rescinded AI Diffusion Rule once applied a compute threshold to closed-weight models.

The author argues the approach must respect the First Amendment, since model weights are trained on speech and may generate speech, whether or not they qualify as speech themselves. The piece lays out a three-part test: whether weights are speech, whether a restriction is content-based or content-neutral, and whether it operates as a prior restraint with adequate procedural safeguards. It says content-neutral rules based on objective criteria such as training compute are more plausibly defensible, while licensing schemes must include deadlines, default-granting rules, and prompt judicial review to survive. The author concludes that using export controls without these safeguards would be legally fragile if weights are speech. The article does not name a date for any rule, and it leaves the courts' eventual answer on speech status unresolved, so what comes next remains a matter of prediction rather than reported action.

Articles.Title: A First Amendment Approach to Regulating AI Model Weights - Lawfare

stories.Headline: FLAME: improving legal case retrieval through factor-aware graph modeling and mixture-of-experts
stories.Summary:
This article is a research paper announcement rather than a breaking news story, and it contains no reported events, named officials, or dated actions beyond its publication timestamp of 27 October 2026. The text describes FLAME, a framework for Legal Case Retrieval (LCR) that its authors say was built to help legal professionals find precedent cases in large legal corpora. According to the abstract, the framework treats legal factors such as legal facts, dispute focus, and reasoning as its basic modeling units, and it weighs the most relevant factors between pairs of cases. The authors note that existing large language model approaches tend to treat legal documents as single blocks of text and cannot adjust the importance of factors to each case.

The abstract lays out three modules. The Legal-Factor Extraction Module uses Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning to select prompts for each instance and uses large language models to pull structured factors from raw case documents. The Legal-Factor Interaction Module builds a heterogeneous factor graph with a Factor Graph Convolutional Network to model relationships among those factors. The Legal-Factor Integration Module uses a Legal-Factor Aware Mixture-of-Experts mechanism, in which parallel experts assess factors and a gating step assigns their weights. Training runs in two stages, first contrastive learning for the core retrieval architecture and then reinforcement learning for prompt refinement.

The paper is credited to authors published in Frontiers of Computer Science, a Springer Nature journal, but the article text provided does not name the individual authors or their institutions. The abstract states that experiments on two benchmark datasets show FLAME significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, though the excerpt gives no specific metrics or dataset names. The reference list places the work within a body of research on legal case retrieval, legal language models, and graph neural networks. The articles do not say whether the framework has been deployed in any legal system or what the next steps for the research are.

Articles.Title: FLAME: improving legal case retrieval through factor-aware graph modeling and mixture-of-experts

stories.Headline: AG Uthmeier announces 100 felony counts against Kissimmee man, lawsuit against AI company over child abuse images - Florida’s Voice
stories.Summary:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, that his office is pursuing a criminal case and a civil lawsuit tied to the sexual exploitation of children. The criminal case charges Jerry Jesus Reyes, 26, of Kissimmee with 100 felony counts involving child sexual abuse material and depictions of sexual activity involving animals. Prosecutors say the case began with a Cyber Tipline report from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children about a Snapchat account. Investigators with the Osceola County Sheriff's Office Internet Crimes Against Children Unit later linked the account to Reyes through subpoenas and search warrants.

The 100-count filing includes one second-degree felony count of transmitting child pornography by electronic device, which carries a mandatory five-year minimum prison term. Dozens of other counts involve possessing materials depicting child sexual performance, which are first-degree felonies because Reyes allegedly had 10 or more images. Additional third-degree felony counts involve materials depicting sexual activity with animals. Reyes is held at the Osceola County Jail on a $100,000 bond, with release conditions that bar internet access and contact with minors, and the prosecution is led by Senior Assistant Statewide Prosecutor Lauryn Day in the Ninth Judicial Circuit.

On the same day, Uthmeier filed a civil lawsuit alleging deceptive trade practices against Rengstorff Consulting Ltd., the company operating the A2E artificial intelligence platform and its mobile applications. The state says the platform markets "nudification" tools that let users upload photos of non-consenting Floridians, including minors, and generate realistic explicit images, including tools to digitally make adults appear underage. Uthmeier said in a statement that anyone who possesses, shares, or creates such images takes part in abuse, and that companies profiting from tools that make such material easier to generate will be held accountable. State attorneys argue the company's written bans were ineffective because the platform lacked mandatory age verification, content moderation, and reporting protocols.

The complaint cites criminal cases in Tampa and Tallahassee in which defendants allegedly used A2E software to produce illicit images of minors, and says the platform failed to intercept or report that activity. The lawsuit seeks a permanent injunction barring the company from marketing generative AI tools that produce non-consensual sexualized imagery or child abuse material in Florida, along with restitution, disgorgement of profits, and civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation under the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act. The state also says a parallel criminal investigation into the platform is underway. The articles do not say when the lawsuit or the criminal case will be resolved.

Articles.Title: AG Uthmeier announces 100 felony counts against Kissimmee man, lawsuit against AI company over child abuse images - Florida’s Voice

stories.Headline: RBC to block personal AI agents from access to online banking
stories.Summary:
Royal Bank of Canada, the country's largest bank, said on Tuesday that it will block third-party personal artificial intelligence agents from direct access to its digital properties, including online banking. The bank said it recognized the decision may disappoint the small portion of its clients who use these tools. RBC said the choice was made with the safety and security of its clients and systems at the forefront. The articles do not give a specific effective date for the block.

RBC chief executive Dave McKay said AI agents could help consumers, but they are becoming more autonomous, and the stakes are high if something goes wrong. He warned of risks ranging from fraud and consumer harm to effects that could spread more broadly through the financial system. In a LinkedIn post, McKay said trust is core to the bank's relationship with clients and that, while the bank values the time savings AI offers, nothing matters more than the security of client information. The articles describe an AI agent as software that acts autonomously for its users.

Evan Light, an associate professor at the University of Toronto, said such tools are largely unregulated and that giving them access to a personal bank account could lead them to act in ways a person would not want. He called RBC's decision wise and said he hoped it would push the government to take further steps to regulate AI in the financial sector. He added that there is pressure on industries to adopt AI in unproven ways and that, for AI agents, there is currently no regulation, oversight or transparency. His comments reflect his own view as an academic.

The article places the decision within wider concern among regulators. A series of global incidents involving AI agents going rogue prompted the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions, Canada's top banking regulator, to raise its assessment of AI risks facing financial institutions. OSFI head Peter Routledge said at a press conference earlier this month that agents interpreting their task authorizations liberally and posing dangers to institutions was frightening and a front-and-centre risk for the regulator. OSFI is also considering whether the financial system needs an AI safety code, though Routledge said the regulator has not developed one or drafted it and has asked his team to begin considering it.

Articles.Title: RBC to block personal AI agents from access to online banking

stories.Headline: Family of FSU shooting victim files lawsuit alleging ChatGPT helped shooter plan attack - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
stories.Summary:
The family of Tiru Chabba, one of the victims of the April 2025 shooting at Florida State University, has filed a federal lawsuit against OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, and against the suspect, Phoenix Ikner. The complaint was filed on a Sunday in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Florida. According to chat logs released by Florida law enforcement, Ikner allegedly consulted ChatGPT while planning the attack and asked about gun operations, media coverage and the busiest times on campus. The attorneys say the family believes the company could have done more to prevent the shooting.

The family's attorney, Bakari Sellers, said the messages date back about 18 months and include 16,000 disturbing chats. Sellers described the platform as a resource Ikner used to carry out the attack and argued that nothing was in place to stop the exchanges. He said there has to be safeguards to prevent that kind of misuse. The lawsuit asks the court to hold the company and the suspect responsible for the deaths. The complaint frames the alleged chats as the central piece of the family's case.

OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri responded in a statement that the company does not believe ChatGPT is responsible for the crime. He said the company identified an account believed to be linked to the suspect and shared that information with law enforcement, and that it continues to cooperate with authorities. The statement says the chatbot gave factual answers to questions based on information widely available online and did not encourage harmful activity. OpenAI also said it works continuously to strengthen safeguards to detect harmful intent and limit misuse.

The lawsuit follows a criminal investigation that Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced in April, after prosecutors reviewed the chat logs. Uthmeier said the investigation would determine whether OpenAI bears criminal responsibility for ChatGPT's actions in the shooting. OpenAI did not respond to ABC News' request for comment about that probe. The attack on April 17, 2025, injured six people and killed two university dining services workers, Chabba and Robert Morales. Ikner, who has pleaded not guilty to two counts of first-degree murder and seven counts of attempted murder, is scheduled to go on trial in October 2026.

Articles.Title: Family of FSU shooting victim files lawsuit alleging ChatGPT helped shooter plan attack - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos

stories.Headline: Italian businesses believe businesses that fail to adopt AI risk falling behind competitors, want practical support to use AI
stories.Summary:
A new Ipsos survey of 500 small and medium-sized Italian business owners and employees, conducted on behalf of Meta, finds that most Italian businesses believe firms that fail to adopt artificial intelligence risk falling behind their competitors. The poll was released on October 28, 2026, and was carried out online in October 2026 among micro, small and medium businesses in Italy. Only 25 percent of the businesses surveyed currently use AI tools as part of how they operate, while 42 percent are still experimenting with or trialing them. Many firms continue to handle tasks by hand, with 74 percent saying they manage customer messages manually. Smaller businesses of one to nine employees are less likely to have used AI at all than firms of 10 to 249 employees, though the survey notes that the sample of larger firms was small.

The findings point to several things businesses say would help them adopt AI more widely. Seventy-three percent believe small businesses need greater support or financial incentives to fully benefit from AI, and 69 percent feel AI is being pushed at small firms faster than they can adapt. Among those who have used AI but rarely or never use agentic AI assistants, 45 percent say training tailored to their industry would help, while 36 percent point to free trials or lower costs and 33 percent to financial support or tax relief. Concerns about accuracy are widespread, with 63 percent worried about the accuracy of what AI tools produce for their company.

Forty percent of non-users want more reassurance on data protection and compliance requirements. Finding new customers is the top business challenge, cited by 45 percent, and 47 percent say they would hand that task to an AI tool if it could reliably handle it from start to finish. The survey is presented as a set of findings from Ipsos, with Scott Gardner, Vice President of Ipsos Public Affairs in the United States, listed as the contact for the research. The poll reports that 63 percent of businesses believe those that do not adopt AI tools risk being left behind by competitors, and that three in five expect to increase their AI use for marketing and content creation over the next year.

Among regular users of agentic AI assistants, 42 percent report saving time on routine tasks, and 20 percent say the tools have helped reduce costs. Other concerns include errors going out without review, cited by 25 percent of regular users, and the possibility that AI could weaken the personal connection customers expect, cited by over one in five. Data privacy worries affect 63 percent of businesses overall. The results carry a credibility interval of plus or minus 5.4 percentage points across all businesses.

Articles.Title: Italian businesses believe businesses that fail to adopt AI risk falling behind competitors, want practical support to use AI

stories.Headline: Australia’s House Passes Bill Extending Safety Duties to AI Chatbots
stories.Summary:
Australia's House of Representatives passed legislation on October 28, 2026, that would place AI chatbots under a broad online safety duty covering users under 18. The bill, the Online Safety Amendment (Digital Duty of Care) Bill 2026, would require covered online services, including chatbots, to protect young people from harmful material, conduct and product features. Rather than banning chatbots that simulate emotional intimacy, it sets a general safety obligation, meaning services would need to account for safety in product design and keep systems in place to protect young users. Services that fail to comply could face penalties of up to A$109.2 million. The proposal is separate from Australia's under-16 social media restriction, which has already prompted planned lawsuits against five platforms.

Concern about children's use of AI tools shaped the debate. A 2026 survey of 1,950 Australian children aged 10 to 17, conducted from February 2 to March 4, found that 78% had used an AI assistant and 8% had used an AI companion. Among those who had used either, 54% said they used the tools for personal or social reasons, while 20% reported potentially inappropriate or harmful interactions. The article notes that assistants are generally task-oriented, whereas companions are built around connection, friendship or emotional support, and that the line between the two is blurring. In June, independent MP Kate Chaney asked whether the under-16 age limit should extend to chatbots designed to simulate emotional intimacy.

Communications Minister Anika Wells said chatbots are not social media and described the digital duty of care as a distinct policy approach. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said stories of people identifying a chatbot as their best friend should be a huge wake-up call for every member of Parliament. House approval does not complete the process, since the bill must still pass Senate review and receive royal assent. The duty would take effect after a 12-month transition from royal assent. The Senate Selection of Bills Committee has referred the legislation to the Environment and Communications Legislation Committee, which is due to report by November 20.

Articles.Title: Australia’s House Passes Bill Extending Safety Duties to AI Chatbots - TOKENPOST

stories.Headline: A Regulator Says Use AI. Another Says the Framework Is Not Ready.
stories.Summary:
In April 2026, the federal banking agencies retired SR 11-7, the model risk guidance that had guided how banks validated anti-money laundering models for 15 years. Its replacement, OCC Bulletin 2026-13 and SR 26-2, leaves generative and agentic AI outside its scope, describing those tools as novel and rapidly evolving. Existing risk practices should still shape the controls banks apply, and a request for information on AI is expected. The same month, FinCEN proposed a reform of AML and CFT programs that shifts the standard toward demonstrated effectiveness. FinCEN also said responsible experimentation with machine learning and generative AI would carry no added enforcement risk.

The article's author, Aishwarya Kothapally, a financial crimes compliance executive, argues that banks do not need to wait for new guidance before governing AI agents. The controls such systems need are adaptations of what anti-money-laundering model governance teams already run. Examiners are expected to ask how an agent reached its conclusions, who is accountable when its output is wrong, whether human review is real or a formality, and whether reasoning is logged at each step. The article lists practical controls: keep an agent from filing reports or closing alerts on its own, log its reasoning and data sources, sample its outputs for disagreement with human reviewers, and expand its autonomy only after it passes validation. Kothapally draws these from transaction monitoring practice, where tuning changes already pass through testing, approval and change management.

The federal regulator quoted is Federal Reserve Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman, who has called for an assessment of whether current AI guidance is fit for purpose. She has acknowledged that the revised model risk framework does not reach generative or agentic AI. The article's framing is that supervisors on safety and soundness have not yet written the rules, while another regulator encourages banks to use AI against financial crime. Kothapally's position is that governance maturity, more than the coming guidance, determines how much autonomy a bank can safely give a machine. The article says that when the guidance arrives, it will draw on what supervisors have seen work at institutions that built governance during the gap.

Articles.Title: A Regulator Says Use AI. Another Says the Framework Is Not Ready. - Corporate Compliance Insights

stories.Summary:
